2.2 Quantum Entanglement
Quantum entanglement is a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, indicating non-classical
correlations between the quantum states of subsystems within a larger system. In a bipartite system,
entanglement is exemplified by a state vector |ψ⟩in the combined Hilbert space H=HA⊗ H B,
which defies decomposition into independent states of HAandHB. A representative example is
the Bell state |Ψ−⟩=1√
2(|0A⟩ ⊗ |1B⟩ − |1A⟩ ⊗ |0B⟩). In multipartite systems, entanglement
demonstrates even more complex interdependencies, involving correlations among three or more
subsystems, illustrating a comprehensive web of quantum relationships that cannot be simplified into
products of any subgroupings.
This intricate property is recognized as an invaluable resource for quantum computing, particularly
for its capacity to facilitate the manipulation of quantum states, enabling quantum algorithms to tackle
problems with exponential complexity—tasks that are unmanageable for classical algorithms [30 –32].
QNNs, including QCNNs, benefit immensely from quantum entanglement and superposition. These
features allow for a richer representation of features and more dynamic learning processes than is
possible with classical systems [28]. Recent studies highlight that QNNs rich in qubit entanglement
3

show enhanced generalizability [18], making them more adept at learning from limited data by
capturing and leveraging quantum correlations that are otherwise inaccessible to classical models.
Multipartite entanglement, in particular, is essential for managing complex quantum state operations,
which is critical for the advancement of quantum computing applications [19, 20].
However, while entanglement enhances the potential of quantum networks, it also introduces chal-
lenges such as the occurrence of barren plateaus in training landscapes, particularly in highly entangled
bipartite systems. These barren plateaus, where gradients vanish, can impede the trainability of
QNNs [21].
In this study, we evaluate the quantum entanglement properties of the QCNN model using a suite
of metrics: logarithmic negativity, coherent information, and entangling capability. These measures
each offer a unique lens through which to view the extent and impact of quantum entanglement
within QNNs, providing deeper insights into its critical role in enhancing the generalizability and
operational efficiency of these advanced neural network architectures.
2.2.1 Logarithmic Negativity
Logarithmic negativity quantifies the degree of entanglement in a bipartite quantum state, ρ. It is
defined as:
EN(ρ) := log2|ρTA|1, (4)
where ρTArepresents the partial transpose of the density matrix with respect to subsystem A.
Although not a convex function, logarithmic negativity does not increase under local operations and
classical communication (LOCC) [33, 34]. This property is significant in quantum communication
and computation, where such operations are commonplace. Higher values of logarithmic negativity
indicate that a quantum state will maintain a greater level of entanglement when subjected to
LOCC, making it a valuable metric for comparing entanglement across different states. Furthermore,
logarithmic negativity serves as an upper bound on the amount of distillable entanglement, which
refers to the process of converting less pure entangled states into more pure, maximally entangled
states. These states are essential for advanced quantum tasks such as quantum teleportation and
dense coding [33, 34]. Recent research, including studies on near-term quantum devices like noisy
intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, highlights its application in estimating entanglement
within quantum neural networks [35].
2.2.2 Coherent Information
Coherent information of a bipartite quantum state ρis defined by the equation:
IC(ρ) =S(ρA)−S(ρ), (5)
where S(ρ)represents the von Neumann entropy of the state ρ, and ρArefers to subsystem A’s
reduced state. Coherent information measures the capacity to preserve quantum information across a
noisy quantum channel and is constrained by the principle that it cannot increase through quantum
information processing [36, 37].
This concept is fundamental to understanding quantum entanglement as it is linked through the
inequalities:
EF(ρ)≥ED(ρ)≥IC(ρ), (6)
where EF(ρ)andED(ρ)represent the entanglement of formation and entanglement distillation,
respectively [38, 39]. Specifically, EF(ρ)measures the minimum entanglement needed to form a
stateρusing LOCC, reflecting the potential entanglement that could be generated from ρ. Conversely,
ED(ρ)involves converting multiple copies of ρinto fewer, more highly entangled states with high
probability, also via LOCC. This indicates that a higher ED(ρ)value signifies a state’s effectiveness
in transforming into highly entangled states crucial for quantum computing tasks.
The relationship defined by these inequalities underscores coherent information as a practical and
fundamental measure of quantum state entanglement. Its computational simplicity further enhances its
utility in evaluating entanglement within hybrid quantum-classical machine learning frameworks [40].
2.2.3 Entangling Capability
The entangling capability of a quantum neural network is a crucial metric that quantifies the circuit’s
ability to effectively explore the solution space of a machine learning task and capture intricate

parameters, calculating the average of the Meyer-Wallach measure across these samples [43, 44]:

A score of 0 in the entangling capability indicates that the circuit produces only product states, while
a score of 1 signifies consistent production of highly entangled states. This metric has become a
standard measure for assessing a variational quantum circuit’s ability to generate entangled states in
recent research [45–47].
3 Experiments
Our experiments leveraged the Pennylane library [48], a cornerstone in quantum machine learning re-
search known for its comprehensive quantum simulator. This simulator facilitates the implementation
of quantum circuits using conventional CPU resources, effectively emulating operations typically
carried out by quantum processing units. Additionally, the integration of Pennylane with PyTorch
supports tensor operations and automated gradient calculations, allowing for a seamless transition
between classical computing techniques and quantum computational frameworks [49].
The computational infrastructure for our experiments consisted of a Linux server (Kernel version
3.10.0-1160.el7.x86-64) equipped with an x86-64 architecture processor and 40 physical cores.
This setup provided the necessary computational power for efficient parallel processing, crucial for
handling the computationally intensive nature of our tasks. Notably, our experimental analysis relied
solely on CPU resources; we did not utilize GPUs or quantum computing hardware such as NISQ
devices. This approach highlights the resource efficiency and adaptability of our methodology to
standard computing environments.
3.1 Quantum Supremacy of Generalizability
To evaluate the generalizability of the QCNN, we employed the Scikit-Learn Digits dataset, which
consists of images of handwritten digits 0 through 9, represented in an 8 ×8 pixel array [50]. Given
the dataset’s structure, with 10 classes and 64 features per image, it aligns well with the QCNN’s
capacity, where six qubits encode each image’s features.
Following the architectural framework established by Kottmann et al. [51], the QCNN implemented in
this study features distinct quantum-specific operations designed to process quantum data efficiently
(see Figure 1). Each image feature is encoded into the amplitude of a quantum state using six
qubits. The network employs a sequence of quantum gates in the convolutional layer, including two
single-qubit U3 gates and three Ising interactions per pair of qubits, followed by additional U3 gates.
The pooling layer utilizes conditional single-qubit unitaries to reduce the system’s size by half. The
final output of the QCNN is derived from the measurement statistics of the dense layer, constructed
using an arbitrary unitary gate sequence.
For a direct comparison of quantum and classical approaches, a classical CNN was also developed,
mirroring the QCNN’s layer structure but with limited trainable parameters, including four filters per
convolutional layer. Details on the architecture and parameters can be found in Appendix B.
In this study, we prioritize scenarios with inherently limited data availability, focusing on the efficiency
of learning from minimal data. We designed our experiments to assess the QCNN models’ ability to
extrapolate from limited data by using a larger test set than the training set to evaluate generalizability
more effectively. To this end, we tested the QCNN’s performance with an increasing number of

Abstract  67 
Early life stress (ELS), such as abuse , neglect, and maltreatment , is a well -known 68 
risk factor for mental illness. However, it is unclear how ELS affects the brain and cognitive 69 
development. Identifying specific relationships of ELS with the genetic and brain -related 70 
underpinnings of cognitive development may reveal bio logical mechanisms responsible for 71 
the negative impact of ELS and those that lead to individual differences in sensitivity (or 72 
resilience) to ELS. In this study, to investigate the interlinked processes of cognitive 73 
development, we analyzed the multimodal data of DNA genotypes, brain imaging (MRI), and 74 
neuropsychological assessment (NIH Toolbox) outcomes of 4,276 children (ages 9 to 10 75 
years, European ancestry ; male=2,005, female=2,271 ) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive 76 
Development (ABCD) study. We estima ted the genetic influence on cognitive capacity using 77 
genome -wide polygenic scores (GPSs). Our regression and mediation analyses revealed 78 
significant causal relationships for the gene -brain -cognition pathway: Brain structural 79 
development significantly medi ated the genetic influence on cognitive development ( partial 80 
mediation effect = 0.016, P FWE<0.001 ). Interestingly, within the triangular relationship, we 81 
found a significant moderation effect of abuse  only on the gene -to-brain pathway ( Index of 82 
Moderated M ediation = -0.007; 95% CI= -0.012 ~ -0.002; P FWE<0.05 ). These findings 83 
indicate the negative modulatory effects of ELS on the genetic influence on brain structural 84 
development that lead to disadvantageous neurocognitive development in prepubertal 85 
children.   86 

Introduction  87 
Early life stress (ELS), such as abuse  and neglect , is a well -known major risk factor 88 
for maladaptive cognition, behaviors, and psychiatric disorders  (De Bellis, 2001; Pechtel & 89 
Pizzagalli, 2011; Pesonen et al., 2013; Saleh et al., 2017)  with long -term sequelae  (Peña et 90 
al., 2017) . ELS modulates the expression of the genes responsible for stress physiology, 91 
emotion regulation, cognitive control, and learning and memory  (Chen & Baram, 2016; Fuge 92 
et al., 2014; McGowa n et al., 2009; Niwa et al., 2013 ; Koenen et al., 2003 ). Animal literature 93 
shows a causal effect of ELS on cognition and behaviors  (Adjimann et al., 2021; Aisa et al., 94 
2007; Bock et al., 2012; Brunson et al., 2005; Dong et al., 2018; Ivy et al., 2010; Molet et al., 95 
2016; Radley et al., 2008; Spinelli et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2021)  and the epi -/genetic 96 
mechanisms within the brain  (Alviña et al., 2021; Arabadzisz et al., 2010; Kronman et al., 97 
2021; Wang et al., 2011) . In humans, similar mechanisms may be involved in 98 
psychopathology  (De Bellis et al., 2002; Jackowski et al., 2008) , stress physiology  (Fuge et 99 
al., 2014) , or emotion regulation  (Caspi et al., 2003; Gatt et al., 2009; McLaughlin et al., 100 
2016) .  101 
Although extensive literature shows associations of ELS with poor cognitive 102 
outcomes and brain functional and structural representations  (Chen & Baram, 2016; Pechtel 103 
& Pizzagalli, 2011; Saleh et al., 2017) , exactly how ELS affects cognitive capacity in humans 104 
remains unclear. Moreover, the impact of ELS on the development of the brain and cognition 105 
in children remains unknown. Addressing these questions will provide much -needed insight 106 
into who, when, and where to intervene regarding the negative neurocognitive outcome s of 107 
ELS. Considering the well -known impact of ELS on cognition  (Koenen et al., 2003; Pechtel & 108 
Pizzagalli, 2011) , we hypothesize that ELS is likely to modulate genetic influences on brain 109 
developm ent as well as cognitive development  (Pechtel & Pizzagalli, 2011; Peña et al., 110 
2017) . 111 

Cognitive development involves multiple dynamic processes that are regulated by the 112 
complex interplay of geneti c and environmental factors  (Harden et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2018; 113 
van der Sluis et al., 2008) . Despite its significant impact, however, less is known about the 114 
biological mechanisms of how ea rly environmental factors such as ELS, interact with genetic 115 
influences and impact cognitive development in children. The recent development of the 116 
genome -wide polygenic score approach (GPS) allows individual genetic loadings for 117 
cognitive capacity (e.g., accounting for up to 13% of the variance in cognitive outcomes in 118 
adults  (Plomin & von Stumm, 2018) ) to be estimated quantitatively. Using this rigorous 119 
computational approach, we aimed to test whether E LS modulates the gene -brain -cognition 120 
development process.  121 
This study had two main questions. First, does a gene -brain -cognition pathway exist 122 
during developmental periods? If so, does ELS negatively affect the causal pathway? We 123 
investigated these questio ns using multimodal data, including genetics, brain imaging, 124 
psychological data, and cognitive testing in large samples of prepubertal children (ages 9 to 125 
10 years) with a wide range of sociodemographic characteristics.   126 

Methods  127 
Experimental Design  128 
Study Participants  129 
Participants were enrolled in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) 130 
study, an ongoing longitudinal multisite study of brain development and health of youth in the 131 
United States. We used the deidentified neuroimaging, demograp hic, genetic, and 132 
behavioral data from the ABCD 2.0 Data Release  (Jernigan & Jernigan, 2019) , these data 133 
were collected across 21 sites from 2015 to 2018. The participants were 11,875 children 134 
from the U .S. who were aged 9 -10 years  (Karcher & Barch, 2021) . After removing 135 
participants who had at least one missing value from genetic, neuroimaging, and ELS data, 136 
our study cohort comprised 4,276 unrelated c hildren of European ancestry with a mean age 137 
of 9-10 years from the ABCD study  (Karcher & Barch, 2021) . The demographic 138 
characteristics of the patients, stratified by records of ELS experience, are summa rized in  139 
Table 1 (Table 1-1) and Figure 1.  140 
  141 
Genotype data for Genome -wide polygenic scores (GPS)  142 
Saliva samples were collected from study participants and were genotyped using the 143 
Affymetrix NIDA Smokescreen array (733,293 SNPs) at the Rutgers University Cell and DNA 144 
Repository. We removed any inferiorly genotyped SNPs with thresholds of (i) genotype call 145 
rate<95%, (ii) sample call rate<95%, and (iii) rare variants with minor allele frequency 146 
(MAF)<1%. We imputed the data using the Michigan Impu tation Server  (Das et al., 2016)  147 
based on the 1000 Genome phase 3 reference panel with Eagle ver2.4 phased output  (Loh 148 
et al., 2016) . For the imputed 12,046,090 SNPs, we additionally removed data from any 149 

individuals with >5% missing genotypes; extreme heterozygosity (F coefficient > 3 standard 150 
deviation from the population mean); and SNPs with <0.4 imputation INFO score, >5% 151 
missingness rate, <1% MAF a nd Hardy -Weinberg equilibrium (p<10-6). Genetic ancestry was 152 
determined with the fastSTRUCTURE algorithm  (Raj et al., 2014) , available from ABCD 153 
release 3.0. Our analysis was restricted to individuals wi th European ancestry to control for 154 
population stratification. We estimated both kinship coefficients (K.C.s) and principal 155 
components (P.C.s) to control familial relatedness and ancestry admixture using PC -Air 156 
(Conomos et al., 2015)  and PC -Relate  (Conomos et al., 2016) . We selected unrelated 157 
samples that were inferred to be more distant than 4th -degree relativ es (K.C.>0.022) and 158 
removed any genetic outliers that fell significantly outside (>6 S.D. limits) the center in P.C. 159 
space. In the rest of this paper, we used genotype data (11,301,999 variants) of 8,523 160 
unrelated European samples after Q.C., and the first  ten ancestrally informative P.C.s were 161 
used as covariates in all the reported analyses ( Supplementary Figure 1 ). 162 
To assess the subject -level genetic propensity for cognitive ability, we computed 163 
genome -wide polygenic scores (GPS) for cognitive performance  (CP) and educational 164 
attainment (EA) using publicly available GWAS summary statistics based on the European 165 
population  (Lee et al., 2018) . The GPSs were constructed using PRSice2  (Choi & O’Reilly, 166 
2019) , adjusting for the first ten principal components (P.C.s) of the genotype data to control 167 
for population stratification.  168 
 169 
Brain Imaging -Anatomical Imaging  170 
T1-weighted (T1w) 3D structural MRI images were  acquired in the ABCD study. We 171 
processed the images following established protocols  (Casey et al., 2018; Garavan et al., 172 
2018) : The gradient nonlinearity distortion correction method was performed  on structural 173 
MRI scans to improve geometric accuracy and image intensity reproducibility  (Jovicich et al., 174 

2006) . Based on tissue segmentation and sparse spatial smoothing, intensity nonuniformity 175 
was corrected. Then, the data were then resampled with 1 mm isotropic voxels into rigid 176 
alignment with an atlas -derived brain.  177 
Cortical surface reconstruction was applied using the following procedures: structural 178 
MRI scans were processed using FreeSurfer v6.0  (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu ) for 179 
cortical surface reconstruction  (Dale et al., 1999) , which includes skull -stripping  (Ségonne et 180 
al., 2004) , white matter segmentation and initial mesh creation  (Dale et al., 1999) , correction 181 
of topological defects, surface optimization  (Fischl et al., 2001; Ségonne et al., 2007) , and 182 
nonlinear registration to a spherical surface -based atlas  (Fischl et al., 1999) . 183 
  184 
Brain Imagi ng-Diffusion Spectrum Imaging  185 
We used the diffusion spectrum images from the ABCD study that were 186 
preprocessed using the following protocol  (Hagler et al., 2019)  by the ABCD Data Analysis 187 
and Informatics  Center (DAIC). Eddy current distortion correction was used with a nonlinear 188 
estimation using diffusion gradient orientations and amplitudes to predict the pattern of 189 
distortion  (Zhuang et al., 2006) . Head motion was corrected by registering images 190 
synthesized from tensor fit  (Hagler et al., 2009) . Diffusion gradients were adjusted for head 191 
rotation  (Hagler et al., 2009; Leemans & Jones, 2009) . To identify and replace dark slices 192 
due to abrupt head motion, we used robust diffusion tensor estimation  (Chang et al., 2005) . 193 
B0 distortion was corrected with the reversing gradient method  (Holland et al., 2010) . 194 
Gradient nonlinearity distortion correction was applied  (Jovicich et al., 2006) . The data were 195 
resampled to a standard orientation with an isotropic resolution of 1.5 mm.  196 
To estimate accurate brain imaging phenotypes, we used individual connectome 197 
data. We applied MRtrix3  (Tournier et al., 2019)  for whole -brain white matter tract estimation 198 
and individualized connectome generation. For connectivity metrics, we used streamline 199 

counts associated with fiber connection strength  (Cha et al., 2015, 2016)  associated with 200 
fiber integrity. We decreased noise  (Veraart et al., 2016) , and performed bias correction with 201 
the Advanced Normalizat ion Tools (ANTs) pipeline’s N4 algorithm  (Tustison et al., 2010) . To 202 
obtain a connectivity index with a white matter pathway  (Ciccarelli et al., 2006) , we 203 
performed probabilistic tractography by second -order integration over fiber orientation 204 
distributions  (Calamante et al., 2010) , with random seeding across the brain and target 205 
streamline counts of 2 0 million. These initial tractograms were filtered from preliminary 206 
tractograms using spherical -deconvolution informed filtering (2:1 ratio). With a final 207 
streamline count of 10 million, we generated an 84 x 84 whole -brain connectome matrix for 208 
each partic ipant using the T1 -based parcellation and segmentation in FreeSurfer. This 209 
pipeline ensured that individual participants' connectomes were restricted to their own 210 
neuroanatomy. We carried out the computation on the supercomputers at Argonne 211 
Leadership Comp uting Facility Theta and Texas Advanced Computing Center Stampede2.  212 
  213 
Dimensionality reduction of brain data  214 
To extract brain morphometric representations correlated with genetic influence on 215 
intelligence, we first performed generalized linear model analysis using cognitive capacity 216 
GPSs as independent variables and neuroimaging data as dependent variables adjusted to 217 
covariates (e.g., age, sex, maternal education, income, BMI, study site, and marital status). 218 
Among three different types of neuroimagi ng data (structural MRI, DTI -count, and DTI -FA), 219 
only brain morphometric features (i.e., structural MRI) showed significant associations with 220 
cognitive capacity GPSs ( PFWE < 0.05 ; Figure 2, Supplementary Figure 2, Supplementary 221 
Table 3) (Bedre, 2021) . We then performed principal component analysis to extract 222 
representations from brain morphological features associated with CP GPS or EA GPS (R 223 
version 3.4.1). We used the first principal components as repre sentations of the brain.  224 

NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery data  225 
NIH Toolbox Cognitive Function Tests  (Gershon et al., 2013)  were used to assess 226 
various levels of general cognitive ability of the participants. For each child, summary scores 227 
from the NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery were provided, including the crystallized intelligence 228 
composite score (mainly measuring prior learn ing and past experiences about language), 229 
the fluid intelligence composite score (mainly measuring abstract reasoning and learning 230 
ability in novel situations), and total intelligence composite score, which is the combination of 231 
both crystallized and fluid  intelligence composite scores  (Cattell, 1963; Weintraub et al., 232 
2013) . The crystallized intelligence composite score is a composite of the Picture Vocabulary 233 
Test and the Oral Reading Recognition Test outcomes,  and the fluid intelligence composite 234 
score is a composite of the Dimensional Change Card Sort Test , the Flanker Inhibitory 235 
Contro l and Attention Test , the Picture Sequence Memory Test , the List Sorting Working 236 
Memory Test , and the Pattern Co mparison Processing Speed Test outcomes. Total 237 
intelligence composite score is a representation of general intelligence and is an aggregation 238 
of all the tests  (Akshoomoff et al., 2013) . 239 
  240 
Early life stre ss 241 
We derived ELS measures based on child exposure domains in the ABCD study  242 
(Hoffman et al., 2019)  (Supplementary Table 4). ELS measures were divided into three 243 
main categories: household challenges, neglect, and abuse . Subcategories of ELS data 244 
were as follows:  parental separation or divorce , criminal household member , household 245 
substance abuse , mental illness in household , mother treated violently  in household 246 
challenges , emotional neglect , physical neglect  in neglect ; and physical abuse  and sexual 247 
abuse  in abuse . We extracted the items of each subscale from the following various 248 
measurement tools (participant - or parent -reported): ABCD Family Environment Scale - 249 

Family Conflict Subscale Modified from PhenX, ABCD Diagnostic Interview for DSM -5 250 
Traumatic Events, ABCD Family History Assessment, ABCD Parent Demographics Survey, 251 
ABCD Children’s Report of Parental Behavioral Invent ory, and ABCD Parental Monitoring 252 
Survey. We averaged the measurements for each subcategory and transformed them into z 253 
scores. The higher the score, the more stressful experiences children had.  254 
  255 
Statistical Analysis  256 
We performed a generalized linear model for three types of relationships — GPS - 257 
brain, GPS -intelligence composite scores, and brain -intelligence composite scores. We 258 
included the following covariates into those models: age, sex, maternal education, parental 259 
income, BMI, study site, a nd marital status. Family ID was not included because our analysis 260 
was performed in the dataset of unrelated individuals after excluding any relatives fourth - 261 
degree or closer during the genetic QC process. We used familywise error (i.e., Bonferroni 262 
correct ion) in each type of relationship for multiple comparison corrections.  263

EEGUnity: Open-Source Tool in Facilitating Unified EEG Datasets
Towards Large-Scale EEG Model
Chengxuan Qin∗1,2, Rui Yang†1, Wenlong You1,2, Zhige Chen3, Longsheng Zhu1,2, Mengjie
Huang4, and Zidong Wang5
1School of Advanced Technology, Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou, 215123, China
2School of Electrical Engineering, Electronics and Computer Science, University of Liverpool,
Liverpool, L69 3BX, United Kingdom
3Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, SAR
4Design School, Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou, 215123, China
5Department of Computer Science, Brunel University London, Uxbridge, Middlesex, UB8 3PH,
United Kingdom
October 11, 2024
Abstract
The increasing number of dispersed EEG dataset pub-
lications and the advancement of large-scale Electroen-
cephalogram (EEG) models have increased the demand
for practical tools to manage diverse EEG datasets.
However, the inherent complexity of EEG data, char-
acterized by variability in content data, metadata, and
data formats, poses challenges for integrating multi-
ple datasets and conducting large-scale EEG model re-
search. To tackle the challenges, this paper introduces
EEGUnity, an open-source tool that incorporates mod-
ules of “EEG Parser”, “Correction”, “Batch Process-
ing”, and “Large Language Model Boost”. Leveraging
the functionality of such modules, EEGUnity facilitates
the efficient management of multiple EEG datasets, such
as intelligent data structure inference, data cleaning,
and data unification. In addition, the capabilities of EE-
GUnity ensure high data quality and consistency, pro-
viding a reliable foundation for large-scale EEG data re-
search. EEGUnity is evaluated across 25 EEG datasets
from different sources, offering several typical batch pro-
cessing workflows. The results demonstrate the high
performance and flexibility of EEGUnity in parsing and
data processing. The project code is publicly available
at github.com/Baizhige/EEGUnity.
Keywords: Brain-Computer-Interface, Electroen-
cephalogram Data Integration, Large-Scale Model,
Open-Source Software
∗C.Qin8@liverpool.ac.uk
†Corresponding author: R.Yang@xjtlu.edu.cn
1This research has been approved by University Ethics Com-
mittee of Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University with proposal num-
ber EXT20-01-07 on March 31 2020, and is partially supported
by: National Natural Science Foundation of China (72401233),
Jiangsu Provincial Qinglan Project, Natural Science Founda-
tion of the Jiangsu Higher Education Institutions of China
(23KJB520038), and Research Enhancement Fund of XJTLU
(REF-23-01-008).1 Introduction
Brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are really pushing
the limits, being able to record over not just days, weeks,
but months, years at a time [27]. The proposal of BCI
systems has encouraged many researchers to actively
explore brain signals and apply BCI systems in vari-
ous fields: game interaction entertainment, robot con-
trol, emotion recognition, fatigue detection, sleep qual-
ity assessment, and clinical fields [2, 10, 28, 34, 36, 40].
With the increasing exploration of BCI systems, the de-
mand for neuro-monitoring capabilities has significantly
increased. EEG is applied in various BCI systems to
collect active electrical signals from the brain. To meet
diverse requirements, numerous EEG-based BCI system
paradigms have been proposed [1]. The paradigms allow
for the selection of an appropriate approach to gather
extensive brain electrical signals to form EEG datasets
that provide foundational knowledge of specific patterns
in the brain [33, 48].
In recent years, there has been a marked increase in
both the quantity and demand for EEG data publica-
tions. On the one hand, online databases such as Zenodo
[7] and PhysioNet [8] have a vast and growing collection
of diverse EEG datasets. On the other hand, a study
[15] on large EEG models employing over 20 datasets
demonstrates the ever-increasing need to process large-
scale EEG data. Nevertheless, the inherent characteris-
tics of EEG data present a challenge in data processing
[20, 49]. The challenge is primarily attributed to three
key factors:
•Differences in content data : Variations in the
configuration of electrodes, characteristics of the
sensor, and circuit structures can lead to signifi-
cant differences in the dimensions and distribution
of EEG data [29, 42, 43];
•Differences in metadata : Variations in the la-
1arXiv:2410.07196v1  [eess.SP]  24 Sep 2024

beling criteria for metadata (such as channel names
and events annotation), along with the absence or
errors in standard information, can lead to incon-
sistencies in annotation [9];
•Differences in data formats : Variations in data
formats (such as gdf, edf, mat, csv, txt) complicate
the standardization and processing steps of data,
demonstrating that the processing pipeline must be
tailored for each study [9, 30].
The challenges above indicate an urgent need for an
efficient large-scale EEG data management tool to sim-
plify data standardization and processing steps, eventu-
ally improving data processing efficiency. Table 1 sum-
marizes highly integrated EEG data processing tools,
covering their openness and supported platforms. Vari-
ous EEG data processing tools with comprehensive func-
tionality are widely used in multiple EEG research.
Some of the common open-source tools include SPM
[22], EEGLAB [4], FieldTrip [30], Brainstorm [35], and
MNE-Python [9], offering flexible and powerful analysis
capabilities to meet diverse research needs. Addition-
ally, commercial software such as NeuroScan CURRY
[39] and BESA [17] are also available.
Despite the significant advantages in functionality and
broad applicability offered by existing tools, the tools
listed in Table 1 exhibit shortcomings when handling
large-scale data. Specifically, the existing tools offer
flexible processing for individual datasets, but lack spe-
cialized management methods to simultaneously handle
multiple datasets with varying content data, metadata,
and formats. Therefore, current tools are limited in ef-
fectively managing and analyzing heterogeneous EEG
data from various sources. As the quantity and demand
for EEG datasets continue to increase, the shortcomings
become particularly evident, affecting research efficiency
and the reliability of results. Therefore, an urgent need
is to enhance EEG data processing capability for han-
dling large-scale EEG data.
In this paper, a novel EEG data processing tool
named EEGUnity is proposed, aiming to unify diverse
EEG datasets from all over the world, as reflected in its
name. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the objective of EEGU-
nity is to manage multiple datasets, efficiently process
large-scale data, and enhance data processing efficiency.
The introduction of EEGUnity addresses the limitations
of existing tools in handling large-scale EEG data and
provides a new approach to the unified management and
processing of EEG data. EEGUnity offers several inno-

effectively manage and process heterogeneous EEG data
from different sources, enhancing data consistency and
comparability.
Based on the above discussions, the main contribu-
tions of this paper can be summarized as follows:
•The proposal of a new concept for efficiently man-
aging and processing large-scale EEG data through
a unified platform;
•The proposal of EEGUnity, a tool specifically de-
signed for EEG data processing, supporting the
management of multiple datasets, thereby address-
ing the challenges of data heterogeneity;
•The intelligent integration of features into EEG
Unity, including data structure inference, correc-
tion, cleaning, and unification, ensuring high data

data foundation for EEG research.
The remaining structure of this paper is arranged as

tails, giving readers comprehensive background infor-

Section 4 comprehensively analyzes the advantages and

EEGUnity is currently a Python package focused
on managing multiple EEG datasets. The EEGUnity
package includes a core Python class— UnifiedDataset ,
along with functions for creating, modifying, and
merging on the UnifiedDataset . The Python
class UnifiedDataset is designed to provide a uni-
fied interface for different operations to datasets.
Users can efficiently manage multiple datasets through
UnifiedDataset , thereby gaining the capability to han-
dle large-scale EEG data.
The usage for managing datasets in EEGUnity is very
convenient, following a two-step process: 1) instanti-
ating a UnifiedDataset ; 2) performing batch process-
ing based on the UnifiedDataset . There are three ap-
proaches for managing datasets in EEGUnity, as shown

•The second approach is illustrated in Fig.

remains accessible on the user’s system, the result-
ingUnifiedDataset instance is equivalent to one
that would have been instantiated directly via an

quickly reload a dataset and save any modification
made to the metadata.
•The third approach is illustrated in Fig.
2C. EEGUnity supports the instantiation
of UnifiedDataset by integrating multiple

Compared to other processing tools, EEGUnity offers
the following innovative features:
•Data Scale Capabilities : EEGUnity is designed
to process large-scale EEG datasets, supporting the
integration of multiple datasets and large-scale data
operations;
•Functional Scope : EEGUnity processes diverse

•Compatibility and Flexibility : EEGUnity sup-
ports intelligent data structure inference using pre-

2.2 Implementation Details of UnifiedDataset
In EEGUnity, the parser for EEG data and the
unified interface are integrated within a Python class
UnifiedDataset .UnifiedDataset includes a compre-
hensive set of methods and attributes to provide a uni-
fied interface, as shown in Fig. 3. The functions can be
categorized into four modules:
•EEG parser module : This module facilitates the
intelligent parsing of EEG data across diverse for-
mats, including but not limited to edf, gdf, mat,
txt, and csv. The EEG data files are initially
processed using standard readers, such as parser
functions in MNE-Python. If standard readers
are insufficient, non-standard readers are employed,
which are boosted by pre-defined code and another
module in EEGUnity—large language model boost
module;
•Correction module : This module offers a user-
friendly interface to facilitate the correction of
dataset annotations. On the one hand, the module
allows users to visually inspect and modify anno-

the other hand, the module provides several correc-
tion methods, by built-in functions and the large

3

•Batch processing interface module : This mod-
ule provides batch processing functionality. On
the one hand, this module enables users to cus-

a variety of built-in functions for EEG data process-
ing, such as data cleaning, denoising, quality assess-
ment, channel alignment, and standardization.
•Large language model boost module : This
module enhances the capabilities of other modules
within UnifiedDataset by leveraging existing large

enables advanced functionalities, including intelli-

2.3 Implementation Details of Locator
In the design of EEGUnity, a critical component sup-
porting the functionality of EEGUnity is the Locator .
During the instantiation of UnifiedDataset , attributes
for each EEG data file are stored in the Locator ,
which is structured using a DataFrame from the Pan-

•Basic attributes include file path, domain tag,
file type, EEG channel configuration, sampling rate,
duration, and completeness check;
•Advanced attributes are linked to specific sub-

cording to user requirements.
Based on the design of Locator , users can calibrate
the dataset by visually inspecting and modifying the
Locator file in a spreadsheet-like environment, either
programmatically or manually. The metadata specified
by the Locator takes precedence over those in source
data. In such a design, EEGUnity allows users to
quickly correct metadata through the locator without
modifying the source files.3 Typical Batch Processing Workflow in

Addressing the Current Challenges of Quantum
Machine Learning through Multi-Chip Ensembles
Anonymous Author(s)
Affiliation
Address
email
Abstract
Practical Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is challenged by noise, limited scal- 1
ability, and poor trainability in Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) on current 2
hardware. We propose a multi-chip ensemble VQC framework that systematically 3
overcomes these hurdles. By partitioning high-dimensional computations across 4
ensembles of smaller, independently operating quantum chips and leveraging con- 5
trolled inter-chip entanglement boundaries, our approach demonstrably mitigates 6
barren plateaus, enhances generalization, and uniquely reduces both quantum error 7
bias and variance simultaneously without additional mitigation overhead. This al- 8
lows for robust processing of large-scale data, as validated on standard benchmarks 9
(MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10) and a real-world PhysioNet EEG dataset, 10
aligning with emerging modular quantum hardware and paving the way for more 11
scalable QML. 12
1 Introduction 13
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has emerged as a promising approach to leverage quantum 14
properties like superposition and entanglement for computational advantage in diverse domains [1, 2], 15
from chemistry [3, 4] and materials science [5, 6] to healthcare [7, 8] and high-energy physics [9, 10]. 16
However, QML faces critical challenges due to noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware 17
limitations [11, 12], including noise, limited coherence, sparse connectivity, and the emergence of 18
barren plateaus—regions where gradients vanish exponentially with system size [13, 14]. These 19
factors severely hamper scalability and trainability of QML models, particularly variational quantum 20
circuits (VQCs) [15]. 21
We introduce multi-chip ensemble VQCs to address these challenges through a novel modular ar- 22
chitecture that processes input subsets on multiple independent quantum processors with classical 23
aggregation of quantum measurement outputs. This approach offers four key advantages over previ- 24
ous distributed quantum strategies: (1) high-dimensional data processing without lossy dimension 25
reduction; (2) barren plateau mitigation through controlled entanglement; (3) enhanced generalization 26
via implicit regularization; and (4) simultaneous reduction of both bias and variance in quantum 27
errors—an improvement over traditional error mitigation techniques that typically trade one for the 28
other. 29
Our theoretical framework formally establishes these benefits through analysis of entanglement 30
properties, gradient variance scaling, and noise propagation. Experimental validation demonstrates 31
significant performance improvements over both classical baselines and single-chip QML approaches 32
under realistic noise conditions. The architecture maintains compatibility with current hardware and 33
aligns with modular quantum computing roadmaps [16 –18], providing a practical pathway toward 34
scalable QML on near-term quantum devices. 35
Submitted to 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025). Do not distribute.

2 Background 36
2.1 Status-Quo: Single-Chip VQCs 37
In VQCs, the input data xis first encoded into a quantum state ρ(x). A parameterized unitary 38
operator U(θ)then acts on this state, where θrepresents the tunable parameters of the quantum 39
circuit. The evolution of the quantum state is given as U(θ)ρ(x)U†(θ). Measurements are then 40
performed on the U(θ)ρ(x)U†(θ)to produce classical outputs. 41
The output is represented by the function: 42
fθ(x) =Tr[HU(θ)ρ(x)U†(θ)], (1)
where fθ(x)represents the output of the quantum model, derived from the expected value of 43
measurements Tr [HU(θ)ρ(x)U†(θ)]performed by the Hermitian operator H. This expected value 44
reflects the average outcomes based on the probability distribution of measurement results. 45
During training, the parameters θare adjusted to optimize the performance of the quantum circuit 46
fθ(x)by minimizing the loss function L(x, y;θ)over the training dataset D={(xi, yi)}i. For 47
example, the loss function for a regression task may be L(x, y;θ) =P
i∥fθ(xi)−yi∥2. The value 48
of the loss L(x, y;θ)(or of its gradient) are estimated on a quantum circuit are then fed into a 49
classical optimizer, which attempts to solve the optimization task arg min θL(x, y;θ). 50
VQCs leverage the parameter-shift rule to compute analytical gradients by evaluating circuits at 51
shifted parameter values [19]. This enables seamless integration with classical components through 52
backpropagation, supporting end-to-end training of hybrid quantum-classical models. 53
2.2 Limitations of VQC 54
VQCs are hybrid quantum-classical algorithms designed to utilize the computational power of 55
NISQ devices. They parameterize quantum circuits to solve optimization problems, where a classical 56
optimizer iteratively updates parameters to minimize a cost function. By leveraging quantum hardware 57
for state preparation and measurement, and classical resources for optimization, VQCs bridge the 58
gap between NISQ limitations and real-world computational demands. This hybrid approach has 59
enabled applications in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and QML, making VQCs a 60
cornerstone of near-term quantum computing research [20]. 61
Despite their potential, VQCs face significant challenges due to the limitations of current quan- 62
tum hardware and algorithmic scalability [11]. While theoretically capable of achieving quantum 63
advantage, these limitations hinder their ability to solve high-dimensional and complex problems: 64
Scalability Current NISQ devices are restricted to tens or low hundreds of qubits, with limited 65
coherence times and sparse qubit connectivity [11]. While it is possible to process high-dimensional 66
data with limited number of qubits using amplitude encoding, it requires exponential circuit depth 67
[21–23]. As quantum noise grows exponentially with circuit depth [24], large-scale quantum circuits 68
are often infeasible. These constraints prevent VQCs from processing high-dimensional datasets or 69
representing rich quantum states essential for tasks like classification and regression. 70
Trainability Barren plateaus—regions in the optimization landscape where gradients vanish—are 71
a significant obstacle to VQC optimization [13 –15]. Gradients often vanish exponentially with 72
the number of qubits, making optimization difficult for many problems [25]. Noise and random 73
parameter initialization exacerbate these challenges, creating uninformative and noisy loss landscapes 74
that hinder effective parameter updates [26]. These factors reduce the generalizability of VQCs on 75
complex datasets and limit their utility in QML. 76
Noise Resilience Noise, inherent to NISQ hardware, affects all stages of VQC execution, from 77
state preparation to measurements [20]. Noise arises from interactions between qubits and their 78
environment, introducing errors in quantum gates, measurements, and state preparation. This 79
limits circuit depth and computational accuracy [12]. Accumulated noise reduces circuit fidelity 80
exponentially with depth, limiting the expressibility of VQCs and exacerbating barren plateau 81
issues [26]. These combined effects restrict VQCs to shallow circuits, narrowing the range of 82
problems they can address. 83
2

In summary, while VQCs represent a critical step toward quantum advantage in the NISQ era, their 84
practical utility is constrained by challenges in scalability, trainability, and noise resilience. Address- 85
ing these limitations is crucial to translating their theoretical promise into impactful applications in 86
artificial intelligence and beyond. 87
2.3 Comparison with Related Works 88
2.3.1 Distributed QML Approaches 89
The inherent limitations of NISQ devices have spurred approaches to distribute quantum computations 90
across multiple smaller processing units. While distributed quantum computing has been studied 91
extensively [27 –30] and applied to variational algorithms like variational quantum eigensolvers 92
[31, 32] and quantum approximate optimization algorithms [33], its application to QML remains 93
nascent [34, 35]. Frameworks such as QUDIO [36] demonstrate that distributed approaches can 94
accelerate convergence and reduce circuit depth on current hardware. However, most distributed 95
QML research focuses on empirical scaling or data partitioning without addressing the theoretical 96
foundations of critical QML challenges [34–39]. 97
2.3.2 Limitations of existing Distributed QML strategies 98
Current distributed QML approaches face four principal limitations. First, circuit cutting techniques 99
[37, 39] fragment large circuits into smaller segments but incur exponential sampling overhead, 100
undermining their practical scalability. Second, communication-based methods [40] that integrate mid- 101
circuit classical information exchange suffer from latency and coherence disruptions. Third, feature- 102
based partitioning approaches [38] divide input data across multiple circuits with classical output 103
aggregation, but restrict aggregation to a simple arithmetic mean and lack theoretical foundations 104
regarding trainability, generalization, and noise resilience. Fourth, quantum federated learning 105
methods [41], while promising for privacy preservation, remain primarily heuristic without rigorous 106
analysis of fundamental QML challenges. 107
These limitations coalesce around three critical gaps: (1) insufficient theoretical analysis of barren 108
plateaus, quantum bias-variance trade-offs, and noise resilience; (2) empirical evaluations restricted 109
to small-scale, noiseless simulations with limited insight into real hardware performance; and (3) 110
minimal consideration of compatibility with emerging modular quantum hardware architectures being 111
developed by industry. These gaps highlight the need for theoretically grounded, hardware-compatible 112
distributed QML frameworks that address fundamental quantum learning challenges. 113
2.3.3 Novel contribution of the present work 114
We propose a novel multi-chip ensemble VQC framework that addresses the limitations above both 115
theoretically and empirically. Our contributions are as follows: 116
Theoretical Rigor We provide formal analysis linking entanglement to trainability and general- 117
ization. Specifically, we prove that restricting inter-chip entanglement increases gradient variance 118
(mitigating barren plateaus) and improves generalization by regulating model complexity via the 119
quantum bias–variance trade-off (Appendix B, C, D, E). 120
Noise Resilience without Overhead Unlike traditional error mitigation techniques that reduce 121
error bias at the cost of increased variance [42], our method reduces both simultaneously through 122
architectural design. This is analytically proven (Appendix F) and empirically validated under 123
depolarizing and amplitude damping noise. 124
Scalability and Hardware Compatibility We extend beyond simple summation aggregation 125
of individual quantum circuit outputs [38] to general classical post-processing functions that can 126
be optimized for specific tasks. The proposed framework processes high-dimensional data using 127
ensembles of shallow circuits, enabling scalability without increasing qubit count per chip. Our 128
architecture aligns with modular quantum hardware roadmaps (e.g., IBM, IonQ, Rigetti), making it 129
forward-compatible with near-term devices [16–18]. 130
3

Unified Resolution of QML Challenges To the best of our knowledge, this is the first distributed 131
QML approach to simultaneously and systematically address scalability, trainability (barren plateaus), 132
generalizability, and noise resilience, supported by both theoretical guarantees and large-scale 133
empirical results. 134
In summary, our work fills a critical gap in the field by advancing distributed QML from engineering 135
patchwork to a principled and scalable learning framework. It is both practically implementable on 136
near-term hardware and theoretically grounded to tackle foundational QML limitations. 137
3 Multi-Chip Ensemble VQCs 138
(a) Single-chip VQC
 (b) Multi-chip Ensemble VQC
Figure 1: Comparison between Single-chip vs Multi-chip Ensemble VQCs . (a) Conventional
single-chip approach processes entire input Xthrough a single large VQC. (b) Multi-chip ensemble
partitions input into subvectors ( x1, ...xk), each processed by independent smaller VQCs on separate
chips with outputs classically combined to produce Y. This distributed architecture enhances
scalability, trainability, and noise resilience.
3.1 Multi-Chip Ensemble Framework Overview 139
Multi-chip ensemble VQC introduces a novel architecture that combines kdisjoint quantum chips 140
with each chip comprised of small l-qubits quantum subcircuits to create a n-qubit large quantum 141
circuit ( n=k×l) (Figure 1b). Here, each quantum chip has individual subcircuit Ui(θi), acting on 142
l-qubits. Crucially, there are no gates connecting different chips–so the total action is: 143
UMC(θ) =kO

This indicates that there are no cross-chip entanglement in the multi-chip ensemble VQCs. 144
To perform computations on multiple quantum chips, the input data space Rnis partitioned into 145
ksmaller subspaces, where Rn=Rℓ× ··· × Rℓ(ktimes). Each input x∈Rnis split into k 146
concatenated subvectors x= [x1,x2, . . . ,xk], where xi∈Rℓcorresponds to the input for the i-th 147
quantum chip. 148
Each subvector xi∈Rℓis then processed by an independent quantum circuit Ui(θi)on a separate 149
quantum chip, where each circuit operates on ℓ-qubits. The quantum state preparation for each 150
subcircuit follows ρi(xi) =Vi(xi)�⊗ℓ|0⟩⟨0|⊗ℓ

The measurement outputs from the ksubcircuits are classically combined to produce the final output. 153
Specifically, each subcircuit measures an observable Hito produce an expectation value: 154
fθi(xi) =Tr[HiUi(θi)ρi(xi)U†

Here, Hican vary across subcircuits or be identical, depending on the application. For example, 155
in image classifications, Hicould correspond to observables encoding class probabilities. The 156
circuit outputs fθ1(x1), ..., f θk(xk)are then combined through a classical function g:Rk→Rmto 157
produce a final output: 158
fθ(x) =g(fθ1(x1), ..., f θk(xk)). (4)
4

The choice of combination function gdepends on the specific learning task. For instance, it could be 159
a weighted sum for regression tasks or a more complex nonlinear function implemented via a shallow 160
neural network for classification tasks. 161
The training procedure for multi-chip ensemble VQC maintains the hybrid quantum-classical nature 162
of traditional VQCs while incorporating the distributed architecture. The parameters θ={θ1, ...,θk} 163
are optimized jointly to minimize the overall loss function: 164
L(x, y;θ) =Lensemble (fθ(x), y), (5)
where Ldenote a task-dependent loss function (e.g., mean squared error for regression or cross- 165
entropy for classification), fθ(x)the multi-chip ensemble VQC’s prediction, and ythe target outcome. 166
Notably, the gradients for each subcircuit can be computed independently and in parallel, enabling 167
efficient training even as the number of subcircuits kincreases. This parallelization of both inference 168
and training represents a significant advantage over single-chip approaches, particularly for high- 169
dimensional data processing. 170
3.2 Compatibility with Current and Near-Future Quantum Hardware 171
The multi-chip ensemble VQC framework aligns naturally with both current NISQ devices and 172
emerging modular quantum architectures [11, 12, 43, 44]. By distributing computations across 173
multiple smaller chips without requiring inter-chip quantum communication, our approach works 174
within existing hardware constraints while anticipating future developments. 175
Current NISQ hardware faces fundamental limitations in qubit count, coherence time, and connectivity 176
[11, 45]. Our approach addresses these challenges by confining operations to smaller, high-coherence 177
regions and using classical aggregation instead of noisy inter-chip quantum gates. This design enables 178
processing of high-dimensional data even with modest qubit counts per chip. 179
This architecture maps directly to emerging industry roadmaps, including IBM’s quantum interconnect 180
strategy [16], Rigetti’s modular superconducting systems [18], and IonQ’s reconfigurable multicore 181
architecture [17]. For detailed hardware compatibility analysis, see Appendix A. 182
3.3 Entanglement in Multi-Chip Ensembles 183
Quantum entanglement fundamentally determines QML models’ expressibility, trainability, and 184
generalizability. Our multi-chip ensemble architecture introduces a controlled entanglement structure: 185
quantum connections exist only within each chip, not between chips. This design creates quantifiably 186
lower global entanglement compared to single-chip circuits (see Appendix B for formal proofs). 187
This controlled entanglement simultaneously addresses two critical QML challenges while accepting a 188
constrained Hilbert space [46 –48]. First, it mitigates barren plateaus [49 –51] by preventing the global 189
entanglement patterns that trigger this phenomenon. Second, it reduces overfitting by constraining 190
the model’s representational capacity [52], effectively implementing implicit regularization. 191
Our approach demonstrates that optimal QML performance requires calibrating entanglement appro- 192
priately rather than maximizing it—a principle systematically implemented through our multi-chip 193
ensemble architecture. 194
4 Advantages of Multi-Chip Ensembles 195
Here, we present the advantages of multi-chip ensemble VQCs over the conventional single-chip 196
VQCs. We show that given a fixed number of total qubits, applying multi-chip ensemble approach to 197
single-chip VQCs can improve scalability, trainability, generalizability, and noise resilience of the 198
model. 199
4.1 Improved Scalability 200
Single-chip VQCs face inherent scalability constraints: processing n-dimensional data typically 201
requires nqubits, often necessitating classical dimension reduction techniques that introduce infor- 202
mation loss (Figure 3a). While amplitude encoding theoretically enables encoding 2n-dimensional 203
5

data with nqubits, its practical implementation requires prohibitively deep circuits and complex state 204
preparation for current NISQ hardware [21–23]. 205
Our multi-chip ensemble VQCs overcome this limitation by distributing computational load across 206
kindependent quantum chips, each processing l=n/k dimensions of the input data (Figure 3c). 207
This horizontal scaling approach eliminates mandatory dimension reduction—a small circuit with 208
10 physical qubits, replicated 200 times, can process 2,000-dimensional data that would otherwise 209
require 2,000 qubits in a single-chip implementation. 210
This architecture offers additional advantages through strategic feature allocation: correlated features 211
can be grouped on the same chip while independent features are distributed across different chips, 212
aligning naturally with the clustered correlation structure often present in real-world datasets. Each 213
subcircuit can thus specialize in specific feature subspaces, preserving nuanced patterns that might be 214
lost with global dimension reduction. 215

landscape where gradients vanish exponentially with system size [13, 14]. These plateaus emerge 218

Spatiotemporal Learning of Brain Dynamics from
fMRI Using Frequency-Specific Multi-Band
Attention for Cognitive and Psychiatric
Applications
Sangyoon Bae1, Junbeom Kwon2, Shinjae Yoo3, Jiook Cha1,4,5*
1Interdisciplinary Program in Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National
University, Gwanak-ro 1, Seoul, 08826, Seoul, South Korea.
2Department of Psychology, University of Texas at Austin, Dean
Keeton Street, Austin, 78712, Texas, United States.
3Computational Science Initiative, Brookhaven National Laboratory,
Brookhaven Avenue, Shirley, 11967, NewYork, United States.
4Department of Psychology, Seoul National University, Gwanak-ro 1,
Seoul, 08826, Seoul, South Korea.
5Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Seoul National
University, Gwanak-ro 1, Seoul, 08826, Seoul, South Korea.
*Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): connectome@snu.ac.kr;
Contributing authors: stellasybae@snu.ac.kr;
Abstract
A central challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the brain’s com-
plex nonlinear dynamics give rise to emergent properties underlying adaptive
cognition and behavior across spatial and temporal scales. These dynamics
exhibit scale-free and multifractal properties, shaping the adaptive reconfigu-
ration of neural networks. However, conventional neuroimaging models remain
constrained by assumptions of linearity and stationarity, limiting their capacity
to fully characterize these intricate processes. Transformer-based architectures,
known for capturing long-range dependencies in sequential data, naturally align
with the brain’s intrinsically hierarchical and temporal organization. Here, we
introduce Multi-Band Brain Net (MBBN), a transformer-based deep learning
framework that explicitly models frequency-specific spatiotemporal brain dynam-
ics from fMRI by integrating scale-free network principles with frequency-resolved
multi-band self-attention mechanisms.
1

Trained on three large-scale neuroimaging cohorts (UK Biobank, ABCD,
ABIDE) totaling 45,951 individuals, MBBN reveals previously undetectable
frequency-dependent intrinsic network interactions , shedding new light
on distinct connectivity disruptions across psychiatric conditions (ADHD, ASD,
depression). This extensive validation demonstrates robust generalizability and
highlights core neural principles conserved across populations and developmental
stages.
Specifically, MBBN achieves up to 30.59% higher predictive accuracy than
state-of-the-art deep learning and conventional connectome-based methods,
demonstrating the advantage of frequency-informed spatiotemporal modeling in
capturing latent neural computations. Furthermore, MBBN’s attention-based
interpretability reveals novel frequency-specific biomarkers for neurodevelopmen-
tal disorders, offering mechanistic insights into the hierarchical organization of
brain function.
By providing a principled, interpretable framework for dissecting spatiotempo-
ral learning mechanisms, MBBN advances methodological rigor and provides
new insight into how dynamic neural computations underpin cognitive func-
tion and psychiatric vulnerability, with implications for brain decoding, cognitive
neuroscience, and precision psychiatry.
Keywords: Spatiotemporal learning, Transformer, fMRI, Knowledge-guided Deep
Neural Network, Neural Dynamics
1 Introduction
Understanding the brain’s dynamic processes is essential for unraveling the mecha-
nisms underlying adaptive cognition and behavior. These processes influence critical
functions such as learning, decision-making, and social interactions, and their dysreg-
ulation is closely linked to mental health conditions ([66, 34, 57, 7]). While functional
magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has been instrumental in probing brain activity,
many conventional analytical methods remain constrained by assumptions of linearity,
stationary, static connectivity. Approaches ranging from mass-univariate statistical
tests and seed-based correlations to static functional connectivity maps often treat the
brain as a relatively fixed system, thus failing to capture the temporal fluctuations,
nonlinear interactions, and adaptive reconfigurations that characterize real neural
dynamics. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly transformer-
based architectures, have begun to address these shortcomings by modeling brain
activity as a continuously evolving network of interdependent processes ([38, 3, 72,
49]).
However, a critical gap remains in understanding and modeling two fundamental
properties of neural dynamics: scale-free dynamics andmultifractal structures .
These properties are essential for comprehending the brain’s hierarchical complexity
and adaptability ([52, 64, 34]). Scale-free dynamics , characterized by power-law
relationships (Equation 1), reveal how neural activity maintains consistent patterns
across different timescales and modalities. These dynamics play crucial roles in brain
2

maturation and state transitions, with temporal variability serving as a key regulatory
mechanism ([60, 67]). The power-law exponent ( β) varies across brain regions and
states, providing valuable insights into neural network heterogeneity and serving as a
potential marker for neurological and psychiatric disorders ([69, 46]).
Multifractality extends this framework by incorporating multiple scaling dimen-
sions and power-law behaviors ([63, 23, 53]), offering a sophisticated approach to
understanding the brain’s nested, hierarchical organization ([29, 15]). This property
manifests in distinct frequency-dependent patterns that reflect neural adaptability and
functional specialization ([47]). Evidence from fMRI, ECoG, and EEG studies suggests
that these multifractal principles drive frequency-specific changes in connectivity and
topological organization, particularly in properties such as small-worldness and mod-
ularity ([1, 54]). Understanding these patterns is crucial for developing more effective
diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
To address these challenges, we introduce the Multi-Band Brain Net (MBBN) ,
a novel framework based on Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transform-
ers (BERT) that integrates scale-free property-based frequency decomposition with
advanced self-attention mechanisms and network theory concepts like communica-
bility (Figure 1). MBBN divides fMRI BOLD signals into distinct frequency bands,
enabling the capture of band-specific functional and topological properties. This
approach provides a neurobiologically informed framework for modeling the brain’s
multifractal and scale-free dynamics. The model features two key strengths: Firstly,
its self-attention weighted connectivity dynamically models functional connectivity by
capturing complex, nonlinear interactions and time-varying relationships between
brain regions, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional static, correlation-
based linear representations . Secondly, a communicability-inspired pretraining
loss function optimizes for biologically meaningful connectivity patterns. By leverag-
ing these advances, MBBN not only provides deeper insights into brain function but
also identifies frequency-specific markers for neurological and psychiatric disorders,
offering a powerful new tool for clinical neuroscience research and applications.

2 Results
2.1 Comparison of Model Performance Across Various
Downstream Tasks
To evaluate model performance, we trained MBBN from scratch on multiple down-
stream tasks spanning biological, cognitive, and clinical domains, using both the
HCP-MMP1 and Schaefer atlases across the UKB and ABCD datasets. MBBN con-
sistently outperformed baseline models across all tasks. For biological phenotype
prediction (sex classification), MBBN achieved notable gains of up to 11.6% on UKB
and 18.88% on ABCD using the HCP-MMP1 atlas, with similar improvements using
the Schaefer atlas (9.06% on UKB, 14.78% on ABCD). In cognitive assessment tasks,
fluid intelligence prediction showed substantial improvements on the ABCD dataset
(up to 18.88% with HCP-MMP1, 8.03% with Schaefer). For clinical applications,
depression prediction on the UKB dataset demonstrated meaningful gains (up to 9.42%
with HCP-MMP1, 6.98% with Schaefer). Comprehensive performance comparisons,
including task-specific metrics and statistical analyses, are detailed in Appendix.
2.2 Communicability-based masking loss improves fine-tuning
performance over random masking loss.
A key component of our methodology was a pretraining loss function designed to
mask nodes with high communicability within the brain network. This strategy was
predicated on the hypothesis that selectively reconstructing these highly influential
nodes during pretraining would better represent the complex communication patterns
within the brain. To validate this hypothesis and evaluate the downstream impact
of this pretraining strategy, MBBN was subsequently fine-tuned on two clinically rel-
evant classification tasks: ADHD classification using the ABCD dataset, and ASD
classification using the ABIDE dataset. These datasets and tasks were chosen for their
established clinical significance and high prevalence rates.
Fine-tuning experiments revealed a clear advantage for the MBBN-high model,
which employed a pretraining strategy that selectively masked nodes with high commu-
nicability. This approach resulted in significant performance improvements compared
to baselines: a 5.55% gain in ADHD classification accuracy and a remarkable 30.59%
gain in ASD classification accuracy. In contrast, models using random node masking
(MBBN-random ) or masking nodes with low communicability ( MBBN-low ) showed
inferior performance, even compared to the MBBN model trained from scratch
(MBBN-from scratch ). These findings underscore the critical role of communicability-
based pretraining in effectively leveraging the underlying network structure of the
data to enhance predictive performance. Complete results and statistical details are
available in Appendix ??.

ASD-related connectivity patterns exhibited localized differences compared to
healthy controls (HC), with varying effects across frequency ranges (Figure 3). In the
high-frequency range (Figure 3 D), connectivity differences were observed in regions
such as PGi (PG inferior) and 47m (Area 47 medial), potentially linked to challenges
in socio-emotional and executive functions. In the low-frequency range (Figure 3 E),

In both the ABCD and ABIDE datasets, analysis of false positive and false negative

3 Methods
3.1 Preprocessing
The ABCD, UKB, and ABIDE datasets underwent initial preprocessing prior to anal-
ysis. In the ABCD study, a bandpass filter ranging from 0.009 to 0.08 Hz was applied
to harmonize multi-site data [30]. In the UKB study, a bandpass filter ranging from
0.008 to 0.1 Hz was used to minimize the effects of heart rate variability and hemo-
dynamic response delays [44]. In the ABIDE study, a finite impulse response (FIR)
filter with a passband of 0.01–0.1 Hz [36] was employed to facilitate multi-site data
integration. For the present study, additional preprocessing was performed on the
resting-state BOLD data. The following preprocessing procedures were applied to each
participant’s resting-state BOLD data: First, skull-stripping, slice-timing correction,
and spatial normalization to MNI space were conducted using fMRIPrep ([21]). Sub-
sequently, head motion artifacts and signals from white matter were removed using
component-based noise correction (CompCor) [4]. The mean time-series signals from
predefined regions of interest (ROIs) were extracted using the Nilearn package, with
HCP-MMP1 symmetric ([27]) and Schaefer 400 ([55]) atlases employed for ROI def-
initions. Participants whose data contained voxels with NaN values, typically arising
8

from the regression of unreliable white-matter signals, were excluded from the analy-
sis. Additionally, to minimize spurious signal fluctuations due to scanner instability,
the first 20 volumes of each time-series were discarded.
For deep neural network training, uniform sequence lengths across all partici-
pants were required. To standardize the sequence length, it was set to the smallest
multiple of 8 that was greater than or equal to the shortest sequence length in the
dataset, optimizing computational efficiency for GPU-based matrix operations. The
final sequence lengths for the datasets were as follows: UK Biobank (UKB) 464, Ado-
lescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) 348, and Autism Brain Imaging Data
Exchange (ABIDE) 280.
3.2 Dataset
Demographic and diagnosis distribution details for the three datasets (UKB, ABCD,
ABIDE) are summarized in Table 1. The UK Biobank (UKB) dataset, which includes
41,283 participants, was used for pretraining due to its large sample size and broad
demographic representation. This extensive dataset enabled the model to capture
generalizable brain dynamics patterns. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Develop-
ment (ABCD) dataset, consisting of 4,527 participants (including individuals with
ADHD and healthy controls), and the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE)
dataset, which includes 141 participants (comprising individuals with ASD and healthy
controls), were employed for fine-tuning to capture disorder-specific patterns.

Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=yzkSU5zdwD
Abstract
Scaling up language models has been shown to predictably improve performance and sample
eﬃciency on a wide range of downstream tasks. This paper instead discusses an unpredictable
phenomenon that we refer to as emergent abilities of large language models. We consider an
ability to be emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.
Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating the performance of
smaller models. The existence of such emergence raises the question of whether additional
scaling could potentially further expand the range of capabilities of language models.
1 Introduction
Language models have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP) in recent years. It is now well-known
that increasing the scale of language models (e.g., training compute, model parameters, etc.) can lead to
better performance and sample eﬃciency on a range of downstream NLP tasks (Devlin et al., 2019; Brown
et al., 2020, inter alia ). In many cases, the eﬀect of scale on performance can often be methodologically
predicted via scaling laws—for example, scaling curves for cross-entropy loss have been shown to empirically
span more than seven orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). On the other hand,
performance for certain downstream tasks counterintuitively does not appear to continuously improve as a
function of scale, and such tasks cannot be predicted ahead of time (Ganguli et al., 2022).
In this paper, we will discuss the unpredictable phenomena of emergent abilities of large language models.
Emergence as an idea has been long discussed in domains such as physics, biology, and computer science
(Anderson, 1972; Hwang et al., 2012; Forrest, 1990; Corradini & O’Connor, 2010; Harper & Lewis, 2012, inter
1arXiv:2206.07682v2  [cs.CL]  26 Oct 2022

Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (08/2022)
alia). We will consider the following general deﬁnition of emergence, adapted from Steinhardt (2022) and
rooted in a 1972 essay called “More Is Diﬀerent” by Nobel prize-winning physicist Philip Anderson (Anderson,
1972):
Emergence is when quantitative changes in a system result in qualitative changes in behavior.
Here we will explore emergence with respect to model scale, as measured by training compute and number of
model parameters. Speciﬁcally, we deﬁne emergent abilities of large language models as abilities that are
not present in smaller-scale models but are present in large-scale models; thus they cannot be predicted by
simply extrapolating the performance improvements on smaller-scale models (§2).1We survey emergent
abilities as observed in a range of prior work, categorizing them in settings such as few-shot prompting (§3)
and augmented prompting strategies (§4). Emergence motivates future research on why such abilities are
acquired and whether more scaling will lead to further emergent abilities, which we highlight as important
questions for the ﬁeld (§5).
2 Emergent Abilities Deﬁnition
As a broad concept, emergence is often used informally and can be reasonably interpreted in many diﬀerent
ways. In this paper, we will consider a focused deﬁnition of emergent abilities of large language models:
An ability is emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models.
Emergent abilities would not have been directly predicted by extrapolating a scaling law (i.e. consistent
performance improvements) from small-scale models. When visualized via a scaling curve ( x-axis: model
scale, y-axis: performance), emergent abilities show a clear pattern—performance is near-random until a
certain critical threshold of scale is reached, after which performance increases to substantially above random.
This qualitative change is also known as a phase transition —a dramatic change in overall behavior that would
not have been foreseen by examining smaller-scale systems (Huberman & Hogg, 1987).
Today’s language models have been scaled primarily along three factors: amount of computation, number
of model parameters, and training dataset size (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). In this paper,
we will analyze scaling curves by plotting the performance of diﬀerent models where training compute for
each model is measured in FLOPs on the x-axis (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). Because language models trained
with more compute tend to also have more parameters, we additionally show plots with number of model
parameters as the x-axis in Appendix D (see Figure 11 and Figure 12, as well as Figure 4 and Figure 10).
Using training FLOPs or model parameters as the x-axis produces curves with similar shapes due to the fact
that most dense Transformer language model families have scaled training compute roughly proportionally
with model parameters (Kaplan et al., 2020).
Training dataset size is also an important factor, but we do not plot capabilities against it because many
language model families use a ﬁxed number of training examples for all model sizes (Brown et al., 2020; Rae
et al., 2021; Chowdhery et al., 2022). Although we focus on training computation and model size here, there
is not a single proxy that adequately captures all aspects of scale. For example, Chinchilla (Hoﬀmann et al.,
2022) has one-fourth as many parameters as Gopher (Rae et al., 2021) but uses similar training compute; and
sparse mixture-of-expert models have more parameters per training/inference compute than dense models
(Fedus et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021). Overall, it may be wise to view emergence as a function of many
correlated variables. For example, later in Figure 4 we will also plot emergence as a function of WikiText103
perplexity (Merity et al., 2016), which happens to closely correlate with training computation for Gopher/
Chinchilla (though this correlation may not hold in the long-run).
Note that the scale at which an ability is ﬁrst observed to emerge depends on a number of factors and is
not an immutable property of the ability. For instance, emergence may occur with less training compute
1This survey focuses on pre-trained Transformer language models. Emergent abilities in NLP more broadly, however, could
go back to Miller et al. (2004), Liang (2005), or earlier.
2

Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (08/2022)
or fewer model parameters for models trained on higher-quality data. Conversely, emergent abilities also
crucially depend on other factors such as not being limited by the amount of data, its quality, or the number
of parameters in the model. Today’s language models are likely not trained optimally (Hoﬀmann et al., 2022),
and our understanding of how to best train models will evolve over time. Our goal in this paper is not to
characterize or claim that a speciﬁc scale is required to observe emergent abilities, but rather, we aim to
discuss examples of emergent behavior in prior work.

ularized by GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020).2In prompting, a pre-trained
