The ability to perform a task via few-shot prompting is emergent when a model has random performance
until a certain scale, after which performance increases to well-above random. Figure 2 shows eight such
emergent abilities spanning ﬁve language model families from various work.
BIG-Bench. Figure 2A–D depicts four emergent few-shot prompted tasks from BIG-Bench, a crowd-sourced
suite of over 200 benchmarks for language model evaluation (BIG-Bench, 2022). Figure 2A shows an arithmetic
benchmark that tests 3-digit addition and subtraction, as well as 2-digit multiplication. GPT-3 and LaMDA
(Thoppilan et al., 2022) have close-to-zero performance for several orders of magnitude of training compute,
before performance jumps to sharply above random at 2·1022training FLOPs (13B parameters) for GPT-3,
and 1023training FLOPs (68B parameters) for LaMDA. Similar emergent behavior also occurs at around the
same model scale for other tasks, such as transliterating from the International Phonetic Alphabet (Figure 2B),
recovering a word from its scrambled letters (Figure 2C), and Persian question-answering (Figure 2D). Even
more emergent abilities from BIG-Bench are given in Appendix E.
TruthfulQA. Figure 2E shows few-shot prompted performance on the TruthfulQA benchmark, which
measures the ability to answer questions truthfully (Lin et al., 2021). This benchmark is adversarially curated
against GPT-3 models, which do not perform above random, even when scaled to the largest model size.
Small Gopher models also do not perform above random until scaled up to the largest model of 5·1023
training FLOPs (280B parameters), for which performance jumps to more than 20% above random (Rae
et al., 2021).
Grounded conceptual mappings. Figure 2F shows the task of grounded conceptual mappings, where
language models must learn to map a conceptual domain, such as a cardinal direction, represented in a
textual grid world (Patel & Pavlick, 2022). Again, performance only jumps to above random using the largest
GPT-3 model.
Multi-task language understanding. Figure 2G shows the Massive Multi-task Language Understanding
(MMLU) benchmark, which aggregates 57 tests covering a range of topics including math, history, law, and
more (Hendrycks et al., 2021a). For GPT-3, Gopher, and Chinchilla, models of ∼1022training FLOPs ( ∼10B
parameters) or smaller do not perform better than guessing on average over all the topics, scaling up to 3–5
·1023training FLOPs (70B–280B parameters) enables performance to substantially surpass random. This
result is striking because it could imply that the ability to solve knowledge-based questions spanning a large
collection of topics might require scaling up past this threshold (for dense language models without retrieval
or access to external memory).
2Though GPT-3 popularized prompting, the task setup has existed since before GPT-3 (Trinh & Le, 2018; McCann et al.,
2018; Radford et al., 2019; Raﬀel et al., 2020).

4 Augmented Prompting Strategies
Although few-shot prompting is perhaps currently the most common way of interacting with large language
models, recent work has proposed several other prompting and ﬁnetuning strategies to further augment the
abilities of language models. If a technique shows no improvement or is harmful when compared to the
baseline of not using the technique until applied to a model of a large-enough scale, we also consider the
technique an emergent ability.

Multi-step reasoning. Reasoning tasks, especially those involving multiple steps, have been challenging for
language models and NLP models more broadly (Rae et al., 2021; Bommasani et al., 2021; Nye et al., 2021). A
recent prompting strategy called chain-of-thought prompting enables language models to solve such problems
by guiding them to produce a sequence of intermediate steps before giving the ﬁnal answer (Cobbe et al., 2021;
Wei et al., 2022b; Suzgun et al., 2022). As shown in Figure 3A, chain of thought prompting only surpasses
standard prompting without intermediate steps when scaled to 1023training FLOPs ( ∼100B parameters).
A similar emergence in performance gain was also observed when augmenting few-shot prompting with
explanations that came after the ﬁnal answer (Lampinen et al., 2022).
Instruction following. Another growing line of work aims to better enable language models to perform
new tasks simply by reading instructions describing the task (without few-shot exemplars). By ﬁnetuning
on a mixture of tasks phrased as instructions, language models have been shown to respond appropriately
to instructions describing an unseen task (Ouyang et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022a; Sanh et al., 2022; Chung
et al., 2022). As shown in Figure 3B, Wei et al. (2022a) found that this instruction-ﬁnetuning technique hurts
performance for models of 7·1021training FLOPs (8B parameters) or smaller, and only improves performance
when scaled to 1023training FLOPs ( ∼100B parameters) (though Sanh et al. (2022) found shortly after that
this instruction-following behavior could be also induced by ﬁnetuning smaller encoder-decoder T5 models).
Programexecution. Considercomputational tasksinvolving multiple steps, suchas addinglarge numbers or
executing computer programs. Nye et al. (2021) show that ﬁnetuning language models to predict intermediate
outputs (“scratchpad”) enables them to successfully execute such multi-step computations. As shown in
Figure 3C, on 8-digit addition, using a scratchpad only helps for models of ∼9·1019training FLOPs (40M
parameters) or larger.
Model calibration. Finally, an important direction for deployment of language models studies is calibration ,
which measures whether models can predict which questions they will be able to answer correctly. Kadavath
et al. (2022) compared two ways of measuring calibration: a True/False technique, where models ﬁrst propose
answers and then evaluate the probability “P(True)” that their answers are correct, and more-standard
methods of calibration, which use the probability of the correct answer compared with other answer options.
As shown in Figure 3D, the superiority of the True/False technique only emerges when scaled to the largest
model scale of ∼3·1023training FLOPs (52B parameters).

1. INTRODUCTION
Task- based functional magnetic resonance imaging 
(fMRI) has been instrumental in cognitive neuroscience, 
offering insights into the functional neuroanatomy asso-
ciated with adaptive and maladaptive cognition and 
behavior. This method holds promise for predicting indi-
vidual cognitive functions and psychological disorders 
( Brodersen  et al.,  2011;  Frässle  et al.,  2020), often out-
performing resting- state fMRI in accuracy ( Gal,  Coldham, 
 et  al.,  2022;  Gal,  Tik,  et  al.,  2022;  Greene  et  al.,  2018; 
 Sripada  et  al.,  2020). Its utility extends to pre- surgical 
planning, where it aids in identifying functionally impaired brain regions, thus helping to reduce the risk of cognitive 
impairments post- surgery ( Niu  et al.,  2021;  Parker  Jones 
 et al.,  2017). However, implementing task- based fMRI in 
practical settings such as clinical practice is challenging. 
This is due to issues such as ensuring participant compli-
ance and motivation, as well as the necessity for strict 
experimental control. These issues become particularly 
pronounced in specific groups such as children, the 
elderly, and individuals with neurocognitive disorders or 
severe psychiatric conditions ( Bernstein- Eliav  &  Tavor, 
 2024;  Zhang  et al.,  2021).
As an alternative, recent research is steering toward 
predicting task reactivity using resting- state fMRI, which Predicting task- related brain activity from resting- state brain dynamics 
with fMRI Transformer
Junbeom Kwona, Jungwoo Seoa, Heehwan Wanga, Taesup Moona, Shinjae Yoob, Jiook Chaa
aSeoul National University, Seoul, South Korea
bBrookhaven National Lab, Upton, NY , United States
Corresponding Author: Jiook Cha (connectome@snu.ac.kr)
ABSTRACT
Accurate prediction of the brain’s task reactivity from resting- state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data 
remains a significant challenge in neuroscience. Traditional statistical approaches often fail to capture the complex, 
nonlinear spatiotemporal patterns of brain function. This study introduces SwiFUN (Swin fMRI UNet Transformer), a 
novel deep learning framework designed to predict 3D task activation maps directly from resting- state fMRI scans. 
SwiFUN leverages advanced techniques such as shifted window- based self- attention, which helps to understand 
complex patterns by focusing on varying parts of the data sequentially, and a contrastive learning strategy to better 
capture individual differences among subjects. When applied to predicting emotion- related task activation in adults 
(UK Biobank, n = 7,038) and children (ABCD, n = 4,944), SwiFUN consistently achieved higher overall prediction 
accuracy than existing methods across all contrasts; it demonstrated an improvement of up to 27% for the FACES- 
PLACES contrast in ABCD data. The resulting task activation maps revealed individual differences across cortical 
regions associated with sex, age, and depressive symptoms. This scalable, transformer- based approach potentially 
reduces the need for task- based fMRI in clinical settings, marking a promising direction for future neuroscience and 
clinical research that enhances our ability to understand and predict brain function.
Keywords: resting- state fMRI, deep learning, task activation prediction, individual differences

captures intrinsic brain activity patterns ( Bernstein- Eliav 
 &  Tavor,  2024). This approach is based on the close rela-
tionships between resting- state and active- state func-
tional networks ( Cole  et  al.,  2014;  Elliott  et  al.,  2019; 
 Smith  et al.,  2009), suggesting that the “connectivity fin-
gerprint” derived from resting- state fMRI reflects salient 
individual differences in cognitive functioning ( Finn  et al., 
 2015;  Ito  et al.,  2022;  Schultz  et al.,  2022). These finger -
prints have been shown to predict task activation across 
various cognitive tasks ( Cohen  et al.,  2020;  Cole  et al., 
 2016;  Tavor  et al.,  2016;  Tripathi  &  Somers,  2023;  Zheng 
 et al.,  2022), even in patients with neurological disorders 
( Niu  et  al.,  2021;  Parker  Jones  et  al.,  2017;  Tik  et  al., 
 2021). The consistent correlation between resting- state 
functional connectivity and task activation was validated 
across diverse sites, MRI vendors, and age groups in 
multiple cognitive tasks ( Tik  et al.,  2023). In addition, task 
activation maps derived by resting- state functional con-
nectivity achieved more accurate predictions of cognitive 
functioning than resting- state functional connectivity 
alone ( Gal,  Tik,  et  al.,  2022). Furthermore, researchers 
can investigate underlying functional connections of 
task- related cognitive processes by identifying resting- 
state functional connectivity predictive of task- induced 
brain activity ( Izakson  et al.,  2023;  Tik  et al.,  2021).
The advent of deep learning marks a significant evo-
lution in connectivity fingerprinting from fMRI data, 
enabling enhanced predictive accuracy and reliability. 
BrainSurfCNN, a surface- based deep convolutional neural 
network pre- trained on extensive datasets and fine- tuned 
for specific applications, has shown marked capability 
in predicting task activation maps from resting- state 
grayordinate fMRI data ( Ngo  et  al.,  2022;  M.  Nguyen 
 et al.,  2024). These models surpass traditional approaches 
that rely on rule- based features of the functional pat-
terns (e.g., independent component analysis followed 
by dual regression ( Tavor  et  al.,  2016), or stochastic 
probabilistic functional modes ( Zheng  et  al.,  2022)), 
which only partially capture the brain’s spatial and tem-
poral dynamics. Other recent studies suggested that 
applying deep learning models directly to volumetric 
fMRI data can better capture subtle individual differ -
ences in fMRI data than deep learning models relying on 
handcrafted features, showing outstanding predictive 
performance for cognitive and biological variables ( Kim 
 et al.,  2023;  Malkiel  et al.,  2022;  S.  Nguyen  et al.,  2020; 
 Rosenman  et al.,  2024). The question then arises: Can 
we predict task- related activations from resting- state brain 
activity by capturing spatiotemporal patterns directly 
from fMRI data?
In response to this challenge, we introduce SwiFUN 
(Swin fMRI Transformer with UNET), a pioneering end- to- 
end deep learning model designed to generate task activation maps from resting- state fMRI data. SwiFUN, 
leveraging the innovative Swin (shifted window) UNETR 
architecture ( Hatamizadeh  et  al.,  2022) and a Swin 4D 
fMRI Transformer ( Kim  et al.,  2023) combined with con-
trastive learning strategy ( Ngo  et al.,  2022), represents the 
first application of such technology in human neuroimag-
ing studies. Our findings suggest that SwiFUN can learn 
rich spatiotemporal representations from resting- state 
fMRI data, significantly improving the prediction of human 
brain activity during specific tasks. This novel approach 
may potentially transform neuroscience research, offering 
a more effective and inclusive method of exploring the 
functional neuroanatomy of cognition and behavior.
2. METHODS
2.1. Experimental setup
2.1.1. Data
We used 3- Tesla resting- state fMRI (rsfMRI) and task- 
based fMRI (tfMRI) data from participants in the UK Bio-
bank ( Sudlow  et  al.,  2015) and the Adolescent Brain 
Cognitive Development study ( Casey  et al.,  2018). In con-
trast to the conventional approach using rsfMRI data 
and tfMRI in surface space (CIFTI: (“grayordinate” sur -
face + volume)) ( Van  Essen  et al.,  2013), we used mini-
mally preprocessed rsfMRI data and volumetric z- score 
task activation maps related to specific tasks or visual 
stimuli. We masked out the irrelevant brain and nonbrain 
voxels using two brain atlas images to restrict the analy-
sis to the comparable brain regions as the ConnTask, a 
machine learning model depending on parcellation ( Gal, 
 Coldham,  et al.,  2022;  Gal,  Tik,  et al.,  2022;  Tavor  et al., 
 2016;  Tik  et al.,  2021,  2023). Specifically, we employed 
100 cortical parcels defined by  Schaefer  et  al.  (2018), 
which are assigned to one of the seven brain networks 
and widely used in the previous research ( Cohen  et al., 
 2020;  Gal,  Coldham,  et al.,  2022;  Gal,  Tik,  et al.,  2022; 
 Tavor  et al.,  2016), and Harvard– Oxford cortical and sub-
cortical structural atlases for evaluating the model’s per -
formance in predicting subcortical brain activity ( Desikan 
 et al.,  2006;  Frazier  et al.,  2005;  Goldstein  et al.,  2007; 
 Makris  et al.,  2006). As a result, a total of 132,032 (Schae-
fer) and 146,025 (Harvard– Oxford) valid voxels in task 
activation maps and each rsfMRI volume were selected 
for our analysis.
2.1.1.1. UK Biobank data. UK Biobank (UKB) is a 
large biomedical database that contains health- related 
information from half a million UK participants. To eval-
uate the model’s ability to generate task activation 
maps, we ran the analysis on the preprocessed rsfMRI 
and tfMRI of 7,038 individuals (age =54.971±7.53 years, 

3
J. Kwon, J. Seo, H. Wang et al. Imaging Neuroscience, Volume 3, 2025
52.7% female) from UK Biobank release 2. The detailed 
acquisition protocol and preprocessing process are 
described in  Miller  et al.  (2016) and  Alfaro- Almagro  et al. 
 (2018). The fMRI data have a resolution of 2.4  ×  2.4 × 
2.4 mm, having TR of 0.735 s and TE of 39 ms. The scan 
duration is 6 min (490 time points) for rsfMRI and 4 min 
(332 time points) for tfMRI. The initial preprocessing per -
formed by the UKB Brain imaging team includes motion 
correction, group- mean intensity normalization, high- 
pass temporal filtering, and EPI warping. Spatial smooth-
ing with a Gaussian kernel of FWHM 5 mm was applied 
to tfMRI scans before intensity normalization. Unlike tfMRI 
scans, the resulting rsfMRI scans were further ICA+FIX 
cleaned to remove structured artifacts ( Beckmann  & 
 Smith,  2004;  Salimi- Khorshidi  et al.,  2014). The task used 
is the Hariri faces/shapes “emotion” task, where partic-
ipants viewed faces or shapes sequentially in each block 
of trials. Z- statistics of three contrasts were estimated 
from tfMRI using FSL FEAT ( Woolrich  et  al.,  2004): 
SHAPES- BASELINE, FACES- BASELINE, and FACES- 
SHAPES ( Barch  et al.,  2013). The rsfMRI scans and task 
contrast maps were then registered to standard MNI 
space ( Grabner  et al.,  2006).
2.1.1.2. Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development 
data. Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) 
study is the largest longitudinal study of brain and cogni-
tive development in the United States. We used tfMRI 
scans during emotional n- back (EN- back) task from 
4,944 adolescents (age  =  9.95±0.63   years, 49.7% 
female) ( Casey  et al.,  2018) from release 2. The fMRI data 
have a resolution of 2.4  ×  2.4 ×  2.4  mm, having TR of 
0.8 s and TE of 30 ms. The scan duration is 5 min (383 
time points) for rsfMRI and 4.8 min (362 time points) for 
tfMRI. Using fMRIprep ( Esteban  et al.,  2019), an automated 
preprocessing pipeline for structural and functional MRI, 
we conducted brain extraction, slice time correction, and 
confounds estimation. Then, we spatially normalized 
fMRI data to the standard MNI space for the pediatric 
brains (i.e., MNIPediatricAsym space;  V.  Fonov  et  al., 
 2011;  V.  S.  Fonov  et al.,  2009). For rsfMRI, we additionally 
applied low- pass filtering, head movement correction, 
and artifact removal, regressing out signals from nongray 
matters (aCompcor). We applied spatial smoothing with a 
Gaussian kernel with FWHM of 5 mm to tfMRI and nor -
malized the signal of each voxel by the mean across the 
time of each voxel following  Chaarani  et al.  (2021).
We used a generalized linear model (GLM) to estimate 
the participants’ task- related brain activation map in the 
Emotional N- back task. We created a task model consid-
ering a block design following  Chaarani  et al.  (2021), with 
a task block duration of 24.5 s and a fixation block dura-
tion of 14 s. We used a total of nine conditions of blocks as GLM regressors (i.e., block of 0- back positive face, 
0- back negative face, 0- back neutral face, 0- back place, 
2- back positive face, 2- back negative face, 2- back neu-
tral face, 2- back place, and fixation). We used a total of 
15 nuisance regressors for GLM, including confounding 
variables calculated by fMRIPrep, such as average signal 
within brain mask, white matter mask, and CSF mask, as 
well as six motion parameters and their time derivatives. 
We used SPM’s canonical hemodynamic response func-
tion (double- gamma SPM model with time derivative). 
We used high- pass filtering with a Discrete Cosine Trans-
form (DCT) basis (cutoff freq = 1/128 Hz) to remove low- 
frequency fluctuations in the BOLD time series as the 
drift model. We censored frames with framewise dis-
placement (FD) of 0.9 mm or higher. We estimated four 
z- statistics maps for the following contrasts: PLACES- 
BASELINE, FACES- BASELINE, FACES- PLACES, and 
2BACK- 0BACK. For brevity, comparisons between spe-
cific stimuli and the baseline condition are expressed 
using only the stimulus name (e.g., FACES- BASELINE is 
denoted as FACES).
2.1.1.3. Feature extraction for resting- state functional 
modes. Previous studies have used resting- state func-
tional modes for predicting task activation maps ( Gal, 
 Coldham,  et al.,  2022;  Gal,  Tik,  et al.,  2022;  Tavor  et al., 
 2016;  Tik  et al.,  2021,  2023;  Zheng  et al.,  2022). Func-
tional modes refer to consistent spatial patterns of brain 
activity observed across different individuals. Group-  
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is widely used 
to extract the group- level functional modes from rsfMRI. 
The spatial maps from group- level ICA are data- driven 
parcellation that extracts independent components (IC) 
from fMRI data, each representing distinct brain func-
tional networks. We used two versions of group- level 
ICs (25 and 100) provided by UK Biobank (refer to  Miller 
 et al.  (2016) for the detailed process). The group- level 
parcellation results in UK Biobank are available at  
the following URL: http://biobank . ctsu . ox . ac . uk / crystal  
/ refer  . cgi ? id = 9028. We filtered out components consid-
ered artifactual from the initial 25 and 100 group- level 
ICs, leaving 21 and 55 ICs for the dual regression ( Miller 
 et al.,  2016).
To obtain the group- level functional modes of ABCD 
data, we carried out group- ICA on the rsfMRI of ABCD 
data. Group ICA was performed only on the specific 
training subjects, and we excluded them from the rest- to- 
task fMRI activation map prediction. Only genetically 
unrelated European subjects with at least 300 rsfMRI 
time points among healthy controls were selected. 
Healthy controls were defined as subjects with a Child 
Behavior Checklist (CBCL) total score of 60 or less and 
a normal KSAD diagnosis based on parent and child

Total number of subjects.questionnaires. This totaled 215 subjects, including 103 
males and 112 females. The rsfMRI data were spatially 
smoothed with a 5 mm kernel. Then, the group- PCA was 
applied to the fMRI data by MELODIC’s Incremental 
Group- PCA, generating 1,000 spatial eigenmaps ( Smith 
 et  al.,  2014). The eigenmaps were used to generate 
group- ICA spatial maps at multiple ICA dimensions by 
using FSL’s MELODIC function. The ICA dimensions 
used for our experiments were 25 and 45.
To derive functional modes for each subject, we per -
formed dual regression using the spatial group IC maps 
as templates ( Nickerson  et  al.,  2017). Before the dual 
regression, we masked the group IC maps and fMRI 
scans with a whole- brain mask to exclude unnecessary 
nonbrain voxels. The dual regression consists of two 
steps. In the first step, the fMRI data were regressed 
onto the spatial IC maps, resulting in the subject-  
specific time courses associated with each IC. In the 
second step, the previous subject- specific time courses 
were regressed onto the previous fMRI data, creating 
individual network- specific spatial IC maps. The individ-
ual network- specific spatial IC maps were then used for 
weighted seed- to- voxel analysis. The individual IC maps 
were used to regress against the individual rsfMRI time 
series, resulting in a single time series for each spatial 
map. Subsequently, each time series was correlated 
with the original fMRI data to generate connectivity 
maps for each spatial IC. The resulting connectivity fea-
tures have voxels with different dimensions based on 
the number of ICs.
2.1.2. Measures of model performance
We evaluated the predictive performance of task activa-
tion maps by assessing, firstly, the overall prediction 
accuracy and, secondly, how well an individual predicted 
map identifies individual variability as outlined in previ-

Quasi-Experimental Analysis Reveals Neuro-Genetic Susceptibility to Neighborhood Socioeconomic Adversity in Children’s Psychotic-Like Experiences

Junghoon Justin Park1, Minje Cho2, Eunji Lee3, Bo-Gyeom Kim3, Gakyung Kim4, Yoonjung Yoonie Joo3,5,6, Jiook Cha* 3,4,7

1. Interdisciplinary Program in Artificial Intelligence, College of Engineering, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

2. Department of Economics, Korea University, Seoul, South Korea

3. Department of Psychology, College of Social Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

4. Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, College of Natural Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

5. Department of Digital Health, Samsung Advanced Institute for Health Sciences & Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, Seoul, South Korea 

6. Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

7. Graduate School of Data Science, Seoul National University, South Korea

*Corresponding Author: Jiook Cha, PhD

Gwanak-ro 1, Building 16, Suite M512, Gwanakgu, Seoul, 08826, South Korea

Email: connectome@snu.ac.kr 

Author Contributions: J.J.P. and J.C. designed research; J.J.P. and M.C. performed research; J.J.P., M.C., E.L., B.-G.K., G.K., Y.Y.J. analyzed data; and J.J.P., M.C., and J.C. wrote the paper.

Competing Interest Statement: Authors have no competing interests. 

Keywords: Intertemporal reward valuation, Psychotic-like experiences, Causal machine learning, Childhood socioeconomic environment, Heterogeneous effects

Abstract

Socioeconomic deprivation is linked to psychiatric vulnerability in children, yet the sources of individual variability remain unclear. Using an instrumental‑variable random‑forest framework (IV Forest) in a longitudinal cohort of 2,135 children, we estimate the association between neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation and delay discounting and psychotic‑like experiences (PLEs) using variation in neighborhood adversity induced by state source‑of‑income anti‑discrimination laws. Under standard IV assumptions, higher neighborhood adversity relates to steeper delay discounting and higher PLEs on average, and these associations vary systematically across children. These findings support the behavioral poverty trap framework, which is a self-reinforcing cycle where poverty-induced psychological distress relates to decisions that may perpetuate economic hardship. Moving beyond average relationships, an integrated IV Forest model that combines delay discounting, prefrontal‑limbic morphometry, reward‑task activation, and polygenic scores delineates marked significant heterogeneity in associations between neighborhood adversity and PLEs across children. Children most vulnerable to neighborhood adversity showed a paradoxical pattern: higher genetic predisposition for cognitive achievement (GPS for cognitive performance, IQ, and educational attainment) combined with specific limbic alterations (reduced volumes, heightened reward-related activation). These findings challenge diathesis-stress models and support differential susceptibility theory. By identifying who is most vulnerable to neighborhood disadvantage and why, our results inform precision-medicine approaches to preventing childhood psychopathology and breaking cycles of socioeconomic disadvantage.

Introduction

A child's environment is a powerful predictor of their lifelong health and economic outcomes. Adverse childhood environments, such as low family income, malnutrition, physical or sexual abuse, and unsafe neighborhoods, are linked to an heightened risk of various mental or physical health issues, including psychosis (1-3), impoverished cognitive ability (1-3), anxiety, bipolar disorder, self-harm, depression (4-6), substance abuse, and obesity (2, 3, 7). Furthermore, these environments are associated with negative social outcomes, such as poor academic performance (8, 9), low income, unemployment (10, 11), higher rates of imprisonment, and increased likelihood of teen pregnancy (12, 13). Additionally, exposure to these adverse conditions in childhood is associated with a propensity for engaging in risky behaviors, including criminal activity (13, 14), excessive consumption of calorie-dense foods (15), substance use (16, 17), deficient self-control (18), and disrupted reward processing (19). 

One prominent framework, the “behavioral poverty trap,” posits that exposure to socioeconomic deprivation alters reward valuation, promoting impulsive decision-making that can lead to a range of suboptimal behavior and outcomes (20, 21). Individuals with steeper discounting of future rewards (i.e., value present rewards much higher than future rewards) are more likely to save less, invest less in their education, engage in criminal activities, exhibit lower academic performance, and accumulate less economic wealth (20, 22-24). Such impairments in intertemporal valuation are not only associated with financial and social disadvantages but are also linked to psychiatric disorders, including psychosis, attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and addiction (25, 26). 

In this paper, we focused on psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) as a key psychiatric outcome. Around 17% of 9-12 years old children report PLEs (27), individuals with PLEs at age 11 had greater risk of developing psychosis in adulthood (28, 29). Prior studies revealed that PLEs are correlated to heightened vulnerability to other psychopathologies (30) including suicidal behavior (1), mood, anxiety, and substance disorders (31-33) and exhibit the strongest association with environmental risk factors in comparison to other internalizing/externalizing symptoms during adolescence (2). 

The link between deprivation and PLEs is likely moderated by core neurodevelopmental processes, and we propose that delay discounting provides a critical window into these mechanisms (31, 34, 35). Delay discounting, which is evidenced by the extent to which individuals’ discount future rewards, pertains to their intertemporal decision-making and impulsive behavior. This measure of intertemporal choice is not merely a behavioral quirk but a quantifiable index of reward valuation governed by prefrontal-limbic circuits (25, 26). Children who experienced social adversities show steeper discounting of future rewards in adulthood (36, 37) and have higher PLEs (1, 2, 38). Comparative studies have demonstrated that individuals with psychosis discount future rewards more steeply than healthy controls (31, 34, 35), a pattern that is uniquely pronounced in psychosis compared to other psychopathologies such as primary mood disorders (34), major depressive disorder (34), and bipolar disorder (35). Crucially, the same mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic systems that regulate reward anticipation are heavily implicated in the pathophysiology of psychosis (1, 2, 38). This shared neurobiological foundation suggests that individual differences in these reward circuits could be a key mechanism determining how environmental stress translates into psychiatric symptoms.

This raises the central puzzle in developmental science: why do some children exhibit remarkable resilience to adversity while others are exquisitely vulnerable? Answering this requires dissecting individual-level heterogeneity, which likely arises from a complex interplay of genetic predispositions and neurodevelopmental factors (39-41). Traditional linear models are ill-equipped for this task, as they struggle to capture the high-dimensional, nonlinear gene-environment interactions that likely define a child's vulnerability (42, 43).

Here, we address this challenge by applying a causal machine learning framework to rich, longitudinal, multi-modal data—including genomics, structural and functional MRI, and behavior—from children aged 9-12 years old in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. Using instrumental variable (IV) random forests (henceforth IV Forest) (30, 44), we move beyond population-level associations to characterize the specific neuro-genetic patterns associated with vulnerability to the psychiatric risks of socioeconomic adversity. We focus specifically on neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation because it represents a critical environmental layer beyond individual family status. Neighborhood adversities during childhood have been associated with maladaptive neurocognitive development (6, 45, 46), psychiatric disorders (28, 29), and unfavorable social outcomes such as decreased income, reduced probability of college attendance, and limited employment opportunities (47, 48). This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in societies where housing discrimination based on family income or race/ethnicity restricts underprivileged families from selecting neighborhoods that present greater opportunities for upward social mobility, as observed in the United States (47).

This study first estimates the IV-based association between neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation, steeper delay discounting, and elevated PLEs. We then document heterogeneity in this link and observe a multi-modal pattern of vulnerability characterized by specific genetic predispositions, and limbic system structures and functions. Within this pattern, we found a paradoxical finding: a higher genetic predisposition for cognitive achievement is positively—rather than negatively—related to the psychiatric risks of a deprived socioeconomic environment.

Methods

Study Participants

The ABCD Study recruited participants from 21 research sites across the nation, utilizing a stratified, probability sampling method to capture the sociodemographic variation of the US population (49). We used the baseline, first year, and second year follow-up datasets included in ABCD Release 4.0, downloaded on February 10, 2022. 

To ensure the highest quality of data and internal validity for our analyses, we implemented the standardized preprocessing and quality control pipelines recommended by the ABCD Study consortium (50, 51). Of the initial 11,876 ABCD samples, participants not meeting the ABCD Study’s MRI quality control standards (N=3,275) were excluded. Similarly, for the delay discounting task, we applied the Johnson-Bickel validation criterion (52), as recommended by the ABCD behavioral workgroup (51), to exclude participants with inconsistent responses (i.e., indifferent point for a given delay larger than that of an indifference point for a longer delay) (N=5,293). We also removed participants without genotype data, MRI data, NIH Toolbox Cognitive Battery, delay discounting, residential address, ADI, and PLEs (N=1,173). Missing values of covariates were imputed using k-nearest neighbors. The final samples included 2,135 children from a variety of race/ethnic groups (Fig. 1). 

Data

Our primary exposure was neighborhood socioeconomic adversity, measured at baseline using the national percentile scores of the Area Deprivation Index (ADI) (2, 45). The primary outcomes were delay discounting, a model-free measure of reward impulsivity assessed at the 1-year follow-up (51), and PLEs, measured using the Prodromal Questionnaire-Brief Child version at 1- and 2-year follow-ups (53). A lower value of delay discounting denotes steeper discounting of future rewards; a higher value of PLE score indicates greater severity of PLEs. To identify moderators of vulnerability, we utilized a rich, multi-modal dataset including genome-wide polygenic scores (GPS) for cognitive and psychiatric traits, structural MRI measures of brain morphometry (50), and functional MRI data from a monetary incentive delay (MID) task (50). Detailed descriptions of all measures, tasks, and MRI processing pipelines are provided in the Supplementary Information.

To adjust for the potential confounding effects, sociodemographic covariates were included. Consistent with existing research on psychiatric disorders in ABCD samples (2, 53-55), we controlled for the child’s sex, age, race/ethnicity, caregiver’s relationship to a child, BMI, parental education, marital status of the caregiver, household income, parent’s age, and family history of psychiatric disorders. The family history of psychiatric disorders, measured as the proportion of first-degree relatives who experienced psychosis, depression, mania, suicidality, previous hospitalization, or professional help for mental health issues (2) was included as a covariate. Given that delay discounting and PLEs are associated with an individual's neurocognitive capabilities (56-58), NIH Toolbox total intelligence was used as a covariate. All covariates were from baseline year observations.

Statistical Analyses

Given the non-randomized, observational nature of the ABCD Study, potential confounding factors, such as genetic, environmental variables, and their unobserved common causes, can lead to biased estimations (59). A powerful and effective way to adjust such bias is the IV regression. Designed to isolate a quasi-random source of variation in the treatment/exposure variable, IV regression is an effective method to conduct quasi-experimental analysis using non-randomized, observational data for research in various domains, including economics (60, 61), psychology (62), neuroscience (63), and psychiatry (64).

Our instrument is the presence of state-level source of income (SOI) laws at baseline year assessment, which prohibit housing discrimination against voucher holders. These laws increase the landlords’ acceptance of housing vouchers, aiding low-income families in securing quality housing. As such, SOI laws are critical in enabling better residential environments by mitigating neighborhood socioeconomic adversity. That is, the implementation of these laws provides a natural experiment: it strongly predicts a family's neighborhood adversity (i.e., ADI) but is plausibly unrelated to the unobserved confounding factors that typically bias estimates. The IV analysis leverages this exogenous variation from SOI laws to estimate the associations of ADI with delay discounting and PLEs while mitigating bias from unobserved confounders (see Fig. 2A). We present theoretical explanations of the IV method and detailed justification of SOI laws as valid instrument in the Supplementary Information.

We used IV Forest (65, 66)—a random forest-based IV regression (60)—to adjust for unobserved confounding bias in identifying the potential relationship of ADI with delay discounting and PLEs. The IV Forest method provides nonparametric, doubly robust estimates of the average (group-level) and heterogeneous (individual-level) associations of ADI with these outcomes, interpreted under the IV assumptions (see Fig. 2B). This method is noted for delivering estimates with significantly lower mean-squared error compared to conventional k-nearest neighbor methods (65, 66). Furthermore, its use of independent subsamples for model construction and validation ensures honest, overfitting-resistant estimates of average and heterogeneous relationships (65-67). Notably, this method is particularly useful for analyzing the complex, nonlinear interactions between genetic and environmental factors and their link with neurocognitive development and PLEs, even within the confines of observational data (65). We used cluster‑robust inference with the ABCD Study site as the clustering unit for IV Forest estimates. The technical description of the IV Forest algorithm is detailed in the Supplementary Information.

Fig. 1 presents the analytical framework of our study, examining the associations of neighborhood socioeconomic adversity with children's decision-making and mental health. ADI, recorded in the baseline year, serves as an indicator of this socioeconomic adversity. We assessed the potential link between ADI and children’s intertemporal decision-making through delay discounting at a 1-year follow-up. PLEs, encompassing distress, delusional, and hallucinational symptoms, were evaluated at both 1-year and 2-year follow-ups. Our analysis spans multiple follow-up periods and PLE indicators to investigate the sustained influence of ADI over time and to explore differential associations with various PLE symptoms, particularly delusional versus hallucinational.

Results

The demographic characteristics of the final sample (N=2,135) are presented in Table 1. Within the sample, 46.14% were female, 76.63% of participants had married parents, the mean household income was $116,538, and 65.57% identified their race/ethnicity as white.

In our initial exploratory analysis, partial correlations were used to examine the relationship between psychopathological symptoms and delay discounting. Among the symptoms assessed (e.g., depression, anxiety, ADHD), only PLEs showed significant correlation with delay discounting (Spearman ρ = -0.067, p-FDR= 0.024 ~ ρ = -0.057, p-FDR= 0.035) (Table S1). This finding underscores the unique association between PLEs and delay discounting, laying the groundwork for subsequent investigations into how delay discounting—along with its genetic and neural correlates—may be associated with the heterogeneous relationship of neighborhood socioeconomic adversity with PLEs.

Neighborhood Socioeconomic Adversity is Associated with Steeper Delay Discounting and Higher PLEs

IV Forest analyses suggested that a higher ADI has significant associations with a steeper delay discounting (β= -1.73, p-FDR= 0.048) and a higher PLEs (distress score 1-year follow-up: β= 1.872, p-FDR= 0.048; distress score 2-year follow-up: β= 1.504, p-FDR= 0.039; delusional score 1-year follow-up: β= 5.97, p-FDR= 0.048; delusional score 2-year follow-up: β= 4.022, p-FDR=0.048; hallucinational score 1-year follow-up: β= 3.761, p-FDR= 0.048; hallucinational score 2-year follow-up: β= 4.786, p-FDR=0.039) (Table 2).

To evaluate the robustness of our findings from the IV Forest, we calculated the E-values for the average relationships from the IV Forest. The E-values quantify the minimum strength of association that unobserved confounders would need to possess with both ADI and the outcomes, conditional on the observed covariates in the IV Forest model, to nullify the observed relationships (68). E-values indicated that unobserved confounders would need to have a relative risk greater than 9.13 for delay discounting and between 7.32 and 457.03 for PLEs to account entirely for the observed effects (Table S2). This suggests a high threshold for unobserved confounding effects, thereby strengthening the validity of our analyses.

Supplementary analyses employing a conventional linear IV regression (60) and an alternative causal machine learning method, i.e., Double ML (69, 70), corroborated these findings. The conventional IV regression also showed that ADI has negative relationship with childhood delay discounting (β= -0.468, p-FDR= 0.03) and positive PLEs (distress score 1-year follow-up: β= 0.609, p-FDR= 0.011; distress score 2-year follow-up: β= 0.78, p-FDR= 0.003; delusional score 1-year follow-up: β= 0.486, p-FDR= 0.028; delusional score 2-year follow-up: β= 0.578, p-FDR= 0.013; hallucinational score 1-year follow-up: β= 0.604, p-FDR= 0.011; hallucinational score 2-year follow-up: β= 0.827, p-FDR= 0.003). The partial-linear IV model of the Double ML algorithm showed significant associations of ADI with children’s delay discounting (β= -0.429, p-FDR= 0.044), distress score PLEs (1-year follow-up: β= 0.495, p-FDR= 0.023; 2-year follow-up: β= 0.609, p-FDR= 0.005), hallucinational score PLEs (1-year follow-up: β= 0.498, p-FDR= 0.018; 2-year follow-up: β= 0.683, p-FDR= 0.002), and 2-year follow-up delusional score PLEs (β= 0.417, p-FDR= 0.044). The negative relationship of ADI with 1-year follow-up delusional score PLEs were marginally significant (β= 0.393, p-FDR= 0.051). The moderating role of white matter integrity in the association between screen time and inhibitory control in youth

Moonyoung Jang, MD, MS1,†, Jungyoun Janice Min, MS2, Seunghui Han, MS1, Kyung Hwa Lee, PhD1, Grace H. Chung3, Dongil Chung4, Sang Ah Lee, PhD2, Jiook Cha, PhD2, Jae-Won Kim, MD, PhD1,*

1Department of Psychiatry, Seoul National University Hospital and Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

2Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

3Department of Child Development and Family Studies, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

4Department of Biomedical Engineering, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, Republic of Korea

*Corresponding author

Professor Jae-Won Kim, M.D., Ph.D.

Department of Psychiatry, Seoul National University Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

101 Daehak-no, Jongro-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea, 03080

Tel.: +82 2 2072 3648

Fax: +82 2 747 2471

E-mail: kimjw412@snu.ac.kr

Abstract

Excessive screen time is consistently associated with impaired inhibitory control in youth, a key component of executive function. However, the neurobiological factors that may buffer this effect remain unclear. This study investigated (1) the association between screen time and inhibitory control and (2) whether white matter integrity moderates this relationship in children and adolescents. A total of 150 participants aged 7–17 years completed the Stroop Color and Word Test and diffusion-weighted MRI. Screen time was assessed via caregiver report. White matter integrity was indexed using track-weighted fractional anisotropy (FA) in eight tracts: bilateral superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) I/II, SLF III, arcuate fasciculus, and cingulum bundle. Moderation analyses were conducted using the PROCESS macro, controlling for age and gender with Bonferroni correction. Greater screen time was associated with poorer inhibitory control (r = .275, p < .001). FA in the right SLF I/II, SLF III, and arcuate fasciculus was inversely related to screen time. Crucially, the right SLF I/II significantly moderated the screen time–inhibitory control relationship (p = .005): the negative effect of screen time on inhibition was observed only at lower FA levels. No other tract showed significant moderation. White matter integrity may confer neurocognitive resilience to screen-related disruptions in inhibitory control. This finding identifies a neural biomarker of susceptibility to screen media exposure and supports the use of diffusion-based metrics to inform individualized intervention strategies in youth.

Keywords: Screen time, Inhibitory control, White matter integrity, Diffusion tensor imaging, Moderating effect

Introduction

Advancements in digital devices such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops have significantly increased access to digital technology across all age groups. Notably, screen use has increased most prominently among youth [1], a pattern attributed to several key factors: the growing prevalence of screen-based learning; the digitization of peer interactions through social networking platforms; and adolescents’ increasing reliance on digital media to fulfill emotional needs such as stress relief [2-4]. However, a growing body of evidence indicates that elevated screen time among youth is associated with developmental delays [5], cognitive impairments [6], sleep disturbances [7], attentional difficulties [8], heightened impulsivity [9], and elevated risk for both internalizing and externalizing psychopathology [10].

Among these findings, one particularly concerning report indicates that increased screen time is associated with reduced inhibitory control [6, 11, 12]. This is especially problematic, as diminished inhibitory control hinder ability of youth to regulate their screen time, potentially creating a vicious cycle in which impaired self-regulation leads to further increases in screen use [12, 13]. Inhibitory control is a critical construct in youth mental health research because it serves as a foundational component of the executive function system, and impairments in this domain can lead to cascading disruptions in higher-order cognitive processes, including working memory, attentional shifting, and planning [14-16]. Deficits in inhibitory control have also been closely linked to core symptoms, such as inattention and impulsivity, observed in prevalent adolescent psychiatric conditions, represented by attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) [17, 18].

While excessive screen use has been consistently associated with cognitive difficulties in youth, especially in inhibitory control, little is known about neurobiological factors that may buffer the negative effects of screen use. One promising candidate is white matter integrity. Given the neuroplastic nature of the developing brain, environmental factors such as screen exposure may significantly influence white matter development [19, 20]. In addition, white matter structure has been reported to be associated with inhibitory control [21, 22]. A previous study reported that reduced white matter integrity may lead to increased ADHD symptoms and greater screen time [23]. The integrity of white matter structure is most commonly indexed by fractional anisotropy (FA), a DTI-derived metric that reflects the directionality and coherence of white matter fibers [24]. Although FA can be extracted from multiple white matter tracts, we focus on the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), cingulum bundle, and arcuate fasciculus—tracts that have been consistently implicated in response inhibition [21, 22]. To our knowledge, no previous study has examined white matter integrity as a moderating factor in the relationship between screen time and inhibitory control in children and adolescents.

The aims of the present study are (1) to examine the association between screen time and inhibitory control, and (2) to evaluate whether the integrity of white matter tracts related to response inhibition moderates this association. We hypothesized that greater screen time would be associated with poorer inhibitory control, and that higher white matter integrity would exert a protective effect—buffering against the negative impact of screen use. (Figure 1) We assessed screen time in youth aged 7 to 17 and measured inhibitory control using the Stroop test. After evaluating the correlation between screen time and Stroop performance, we conducted a moderation analysis using FA values extracted from eight white matter tracts (bilateral superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) I/II, SLF III, arcuate fasciculus, and cingulum bundle) implicated in response inhibition.

Methods

Participants 

Participants were recruited from the WECANDOIT project (Wellness Effects on Childhood and Adolescent Neurocognitive Development Outcomes and Individual Trajectories) [Min et al.]. A total of 180 individuals (mean [SD] age = 14.12 [2.13] years, 94 female) were enrolled between February 2022 and September 2024 through Seoul National University and the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology. 

All participants completed diffusion-weighted MRI as well as a comprehensive set of neuropsychological assessments and structured questionnaires. The study included school-enrolled children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Individuals were excluded if they (1) had a diagnosed intellectual disability; (2) had a prior clinical diagnosis of a psychiatric or learning disorder; (3) lacked sufficient fluency in Korean to complete assessments reliably; (4) had color vision deficiencies; or (5) presented any contraindications for MRI scanning, including metallic implants or the possibility of pregnancy. 

Due to an unexpected shutdown and subsequent damage to the MRI scanner during the participant recruitment phase, MRI data were unavailable for 26 participants. Additionally, 4 participants were excluded from the MRI analysis due to contraindications such as the presence of piercings or excessive head motion during scanning. As a result, a total of 150 participants were included in the final analysis. After applying these criteria, a total of 150 participants were retained for the final analyses. The final analysis included 150 participants (mean [SD] age = 13.63 [1.94] years, 80 female), and their ages and gender distribution did not differ significantly from those of the 30 excluded participants. 

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants and their legal guardians. All study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board of Seoul National University (IRB Nos. 2112/004-006 and 2202/003-003).

Assessment of Screen Time and Inhibitory Control

To assess youths’ screen time, we adapted the Screen Time Questionnaire developed for the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study [25]. The adapted parent-report measure consisted of 23 items completed by the caregiver. Among these, 12 items assessed the daily average time spent on screen-based activities during weekdays and weekends, including: (1) watching TV or movies, (2) watching online videos, (3) playing video games, (4) texting via phone, tablet, or computer, (5) using social media, and (6) engaging in video chatting. An additional 6 items assessed problematic behaviors related to the child’s screen media use, including craving, withdrawal-like symptoms, dependence, functional impairment, and impaired control, as perceived by the parent. A further 4 items measured parental concerns and perceptions regarding the child’s online environment, such as exposure to harmful content, inappropriate behavior, and excessive engagement. Finally, 1 item asked parents to indicate which type of screen media their child used most frequently (non-scalar). A composite variable representing overall screen time was computed by summing all scalar items, excluding the non-scalar item indicating the most frequently used media type.

To evaluate inhibitory control, the Stroop Color and Word Test [26] was administered by trained clinical psychologists following standardized procedures. The Stroop interference score was derived by subtracting the raw reaction time obtained on the Color Naming task from that on the Color-Word Reading task. The resulting difference score was then converted into an age-normed T-score using the normative data provided in the Stroop test administration and scoring manual [27]. This T-score was used as a standardized index of inhibitory control, reflecting the ability to inhibit automatic responses to conflicting stimuli.

Diffusion MRI (dMRI) Acquisition  

Diffusion-weighted and structural MRI data were acquired using Siemens MAGNETOM Trio Tim 3T scanners, following acquisition and preprocessing protocols described in our previous manuscript [Min et al.]. Diffusion images were collected using a monopolar encoding scheme with a multiband acceleration factor of 3 and b-values of 0, 1000, 2000, and 3000 s/mm², totaling 114 diffusion directions. High-resolution T1-weighted anatomical images were obtained using a three-dimensional MPRAGE sequence (1 mm³ isotropic resolution) without multiband acceleration. All preprocessing steps and probabilistic tractography were performed on the Brainlife platform [28], using constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD), whole-brain random seeding, and a target of one million streamlines. This pipeline ensured standardized, reproducible diffusion processing across participants.

dMRI Preprocessing

White matter preprocessing was conducted using track-weighted fractional anisotropy (TW-FA), implemented with MRtrix3 tools, including the tckmap command [29], following standard MRI quality control prcedures. The analytical pipeline was based on our previous work [Min et al.], and prior methodological reports of the TW-FA framework [30, 31], and is summarized briefly here. Specifically, fractional anisotropy (FA) values were sampled along fiber streamlines, and voxel-wise TW-FA values were computed by averaging Gaussian-weighted FA estimates across all trajectories passing through each voxel. A full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of 15 mm was used for the Gaussian kernel to enhance sensitivity to focal white matter abnormalities. This approach enables anatomically informed diffusion mapping by incorporating directional smoothing derived from streamline-specific FA distributions.

White Matter Tract Selection

We selected tracts previously implicated in cognitive functions, particularly those associated with cognitive control network, based on prior literature [32-34]. The tracts included in the analysis were the left and right SLF I/II, SLF III, arcuate fasciculus, and cingulum bundle. (Figure 2)

Statistical analyses

To test potential gender effect, we first explored gender differences in screen time, Stroop interference score, and white matter FA values using independent samples t-tests. Given the wide range of age, we also examined whether these variables were associated with age using Pearson correlation analyses. To test our primary hypothesis that screen time is associated with Stroop interference scores, we evaluated the partial correlation between screen time and Stroop interference scores while controlling for age and gender. Additionally, partial correlations were conducted to examine the associations between FA values and Stroop interference scores, as well as between FA values and screen time, while controlling for age and gender. 

To address the second hypothesis—that white matter integrity moderates the relationship between screen time and inhibitory control—we conducted moderation analyses using the PROCESS macro for SPSS [35]. The Johnson–Neyman technique was applied to identify regions of significance in the interaction between screen time and FA. Conditional effects were examined at ±1 SD from the mean FA to aid interpretation. To mitigate Type I error due to multiple testing, Bonferroni correction was applied to adjust the significance threshold. Therefore, to account for multiple comparisons across the eight white matter fasciculi tested, a Bonferroni corrected p-value threshold was 0.006 derived by dividing the significance threshold (0.05) by 8. All statistical analyses were performed in SPSS (version 29.0.1.0, IBM Corp.).

Results

Demographic, Clinical, and Neuroimaging Characteristics

Demographic and clinical characteristics, along with white matter FA values, are summarized in Table 1. The Stroop interference score did not differ by gender and showed no significant correlation with age (all ps > .05). After applying Bonferroni correction, no gender differences were observed in FA values, and no significant associations with age were found (all ps > .05).

Association between Inhibitory Control and Screen Time

A partial correlation revealed that greater screen time was associated with increased Stroop interference score (r = .275, p < .001), controlling for age and gender (Figure 3).

Associations of White Matter Integrity with Screen Time and Inhibitory Control

Higher FA in the right SLF I/II (partial r = –.197, p = .017), the right SLF III (partial r = –.167, p = .043), and the right arcuate fasciculus (partial r = –.220, p = .007) was associated with lower screen time. No significant associations were observed for the left SLF I/II, SLF III, arcuate fasciculus, or bilateral cingulum (all ps > .05). However, FA values were not significantly correlated with Stroop interference scores after controlling for age and gender.

Moderation analysis: Relationship between screen time and response inhibition moderated by White Matter integrity

We observed a significant interaction for the right SLF I/II, which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (ΔR² = .049, b = –7.02, p = .005) (Table 2). That is, FA in the right SLF I/II significantly moderated the association between screen time and inhibitory control. Johnson–Neyman analysis showed that the screen time-Stroop interference score association was significant only at low FA in the right SLF I/II (–1 SD; b = 0.32, SE = 0.07, p < .001), not at high FA (+1 SD; b = 0.02, SE = 0.08, p = .83) (Figure 4). Interactions with the right cingulum (p = 0.015), right (p = .016) and left arcuate fasciculi (p = .046) did not survive Bonferroni correction. (Supplementary Table 1) The left SLF I/II, SLF III, cingulum, and right SLF III did not moderate the association between screen time and Stroop interference score (all ps > .05), and were therefore excluded from further interpretation. 

Discussion

The present study investigated the association between youth screen use and inhibitory control, and tested whether white matter integrity moderated this relationship. Greater screen time was associated with poorer inhibitory control, and white matter integrity moderated this association. Specifically, the negative association between screen time and inhibitory control was more pronounced among individuals with lower white matter integrity, whereas this effect was attenuated at higher levels of white matter integrity.

As we hypothesized, longer screen time was correlated with reduced inhibitory control. This result aligns with previous studies suggesting that youth who spent more time on screens tend to exhibit weaker inhibitory control [6, 11, 12]. Specifically, one meta-analysis reported that longer screen viewing time—including exposure to TV and video—was associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, including diminished response inhibition [11]. Another study found that screen time measured during infancy was correlated with performance on the Stroop test at age nine [6]. Additionally, a separate study reported that response inhibition, assessed using a Go/No-Go task, mediated the relationship between screen time and ADHD symptoms [12]. As suggested by numerous previous studies, the fast-paced content and frequent attentional shifts characteristic of digital media may undermine sustained attention and inhibitory control [36-38]. Furthermore, excessive use of digital media may displace cognitively enriching activities—such as physical exercise, sleep, and interpersonal interactions—that are essential for the development of executive functions, including the capacity for inhibitory control [39].

In line with our hypothesis, white matter integrity moderated the relationship between screen time and inhibitory control. The negative association between screen time and inhibitory control was evident only in youth with lower integrity in the right SLF I/II. Given that the SLF I/II supports top-down regulation and attentional control [34], youth with lower integrity in this tract may be more susceptible to disruptions in response inhibition posed by excessive screen time. In contrast, individuals with more robust white matter integrity of the SLF I/II may possess greater neurocognitive resilience [40], maintaining response control despite similar screen exposure. Although the SLF III, arcuate fasciculus, and cingulum have all been implicated in inhibitory control, only the SLF I/II showed a statistically significant moderating effect in the present study. This may be due to the SLF I/II’s more direct involvement in executive functions compared to the other tracts [41, 42]; however, this interpretation warrants further investigation in larger samples.

This study has some limitations. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether screen exposure alters inhibitory control and white matter integrity, or vice versa. Second, caregiver-reported screen time may be subject to recall bias, particularly for adolescents. Third, inhibitory control was assessed using a single Stroop measure, which may not fully capture this multifaceted construct. Future studies should incorporate prospective designs, multi-informant assessments of screen use, and diverse m

papers.content:
Referee expertise:

Referee #1: Neuroimaging & Psychiatry; ML

Referee #2: Neuroimaging & Psychiatry; ML

Referee #3: Psychiatric Genomics


Reviewers' comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):

This study aims to develop and validate a deep learning framework that integrates polygenic risk scores (PGS) with diffusion MRI-derived white matter features to predict the onset and developmental trajectory of depression. The authors utilized a large multi-ethnic youth cohort from the ABCD study (N=4,741) and an independent Korean cohort (N=108), applying PGS to pretrain the model and subsequently fine-tuning it on white matter imaging data for depression classification and prediction. Additionally, the model identified key white matter tracts associated with depression. The study demonstrates certain strengths in methodological design, sample size, cross-population validation, and biological interpretability. However, the methodological descriptions lack sufficient detail, and several analytical approaches, result interpretations, and writing aspects need improvement to enhance the rigor and clarity of the paper. Moreover, given the existence of numerous high-performing multimodal fusion approaches, the lack of comparison with such methods reduces the methodological novelty of this study. In conclusion, the current version lacks critical implementation details, raising concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of the reported findings.

1. Major Strengths
(1) The innovative use of PGS (including both depression PGS and composite PGS) for pretraining the white matter imaging model leverages potential gene-brain structural associations to improve downstream depression prediction; (2) Identification of depression-associated white matter tracts, contributing to biological interpretability; (3) Use of a large ABCD dataset and validation on an independent Korean cohort, as well as longitudinal evaluation of predictive performance; (4) Comprehensive experimental design, but insufficient detail in implementation limits reproducibility.

2. Major Concerns
The methodology and experimental details require substantial clarification and supplementation. While the authors conducted multiple experiments to demonstrate the method's effectiveness from different angles, it is strongly recommended that each experiment be briefly introduced with its purpose and procedure before presenting results, to help readers better follow the research flow. To further enhance clarity, a comprehensive schematic diagram of the entire pipeline (including data partitioning, model training, validation, and evaluation) is strongly encouraged, rather than limiting to the analytical process shown in Figure 1. Importantly, without sufficient methodological transparency, the credibility of the findings is significantly compromised.
Specific points requiring clarification include:
(1) How were the "10 matched subsets with diverse controls" generated (line 121)? Table S1 does not provide demographic details for each of the three stages of data usage. Please elaborate on the population characteristics used in each stage, and provide brief explanations for the variables in the demographic table rather than simply listing them without context. Also, please clarify whether the pretraining set (N=4,741) is completely independent of the fine-tuning/testing set to avoid data leakage. In Figure S1, a total of 5,248 ABCD participants were included in the study, yet the sum of samples used in the three stages (4,741 + 266 + 236) does not match this number, please explain the discrepancy.
(2) How were the "multimodal models trained without pretraining" implemented? Was it simply concatenation of multimodal features? Please specify the model construction in more detail. It is also recommended to compare the proposed method with established multimodal fusion approaches.
(3) Line 146 claims that the pretrained 3DCNN outperformed traditional machine learning models. Please clarify whether the training data, features, and evaluation protocols were consistent across the comparisons, otherwise, the comparison lacks validity.
(4) The performance difference between depression PGS and composite PGS models (e.g., AUROC 0.597 vs. 0.62 in Table 1) is not discussed. Please provide possible explanations or cite relevant supporting literature.
(5) In the Decision Curve Analysis section, please explain the basis for threshold selection and the clinical interpretation of net benefit values.
(6) The calculation and biological implications of PGS and composite PGS lack detailed explanation. Please supplement this information to ensure reproducibility.
(7) Please review the over 100 references cited in the manuscript to ensure their relevance and avoid excessive or redundant citations.
(8) Furthermore, making the used data and reproducible code publicly available (subject to ethical and legal constraints) would greatly strengthen the transparency, credibility, and broader impact of this study.

3. Minor Issues
(1) Carefully check the use of abbreviations: full terms should be provided upon first appearance, and brief explanations added when necessary to improve readability. Also, all abbreviations in figures and tables should be defined and explained. For instance, in Figure S1, the meaning of “SC data” should be clearly stated.
(2) Improve the quality of all figures, especially Figure 2C where axis labels are unclear, consider enlarging or bolding the font.
(3) Revise formatting issues throughout the manuscript, such as extra spaces, missing punctuation, etc..



Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

This study proposes a novel deep learning method that integrates brain white matter features with polygenic scores to enhance prediction performance for major depressive disorders in youth. The authors utilized a large dataset to fine-tune the model and demonstrated the scalability of their methodology across both sectional and ethnic groups. The manuscript requires significant clarification to be ready for publication. Additionally, several trivial writing and figure issues need to be addressed to improve readability.


Major Comments:

Clarification of Prior Literature (Line 35 vs. Line 42):
At line 35, the authors state that “studies have identified significant genetic correlations between measures of diffusion tensor imaging and depression-related traits.” However, this lacks specific details on how these correlations were determined. Moreover, this appears to contradict the statement at line 42 that “most studies have examined genetic and neuroimaging factors in isolation, failing to capture their complex interplay.” The authors should reconcile these two points and clearly specify what previous studies have done regarding genetic-neuroimaging associations.

Model Training and Validation Strategy (Line 67):
The manuscript lacks sufficient detail on how the 10-fold cross-validation was implemented. Specifically, it is unclear how the "Finetune" dataset (N=266) was used in the context of model training and evaluation. If the Finetune dataset was used both for tuning hyperparameters and reporting final performance metrics, this could lead to data leakage and inflated performance estimates (“double-dipping”). The authors should adopt standard machine learning nomenclature (e.g., training, validation, and test sets) and clarify the role each subset played in model development and evaluation.

Reporting of F1 Scores (Figure 2):
Figure 2 presents multiple F1 scores for each model, but it is not clear how these scores were obtained. Were they derived through nested cross-validation, or are they from repeated runs on held-out sets? Ideally, model comparisons should be based on performance on an independent test set. The authors should clarify their methodology and justify their approach.

Statistical Analysis of F1 Scores:
The manuscript lacks details on the statistical test on the F1 scores. It is mentioned in the supplementary maters that Wilcoxon rank sum test was used. As there are multiple models, it is better to first run a Kruskal-Wallis H test and run post-hoc test with multiple comparison correction.

Ambiguity in Table 1 Descriptions:
In Table 1, the entry “Only TW-FA with feature TW-FA” appears to be duplicated and lacks clarity. Additionally, the terminology conflates model types with input features. The table should indicate what machine learning models were used (e.g., SVM, XGBoost, or CNN), not just the features. A consistent and clear presentation of model type and input features is necessary.

Model Specificity for Depression Prediction:
The manuscript would benefit from a discussion of the specificity of the proposed model to major depressive disorder (MDD). Is the model specifically trained and validated for MDD, or could it be identifying general psychiatric risk? This has important implications for both clinical utility and interpretation.

Minor Comments:

Terminology Consistency (Tables 1 and 2):
The terms “composite PGS” and “cPGS” appear to refer to the same feature but are used inconsistently. Please standardize terminology throughout the manuscript for clarity.

Identical Results (Table 2):
In Table 2, the models “from-scratch 3DCNN TW-FA” and “Only TW-FA TW-FA” report identical results. Please verify whether this is accurate or a copy-paste error.

Table Formatting:
The headers in Tables 1 and 2 are repeated. Consider either removing redundant headers or presenting each section as a separate table to improve readability.

Figure Readability:
The font size used in the figures is too small and may be difficult to read, especially for visually impaired or older readers. Please increase the font size and ensure all labels are clearly legible.

Typographical Error (Line 826):
There is a typo at line 826: “Intendent” should likely be “Intended.”

Age Group Clarification (Line 795):
The phrase “Fine-tuned model evaluates 9–10y depression classification” is unclear. Does this refer to predicting depression diagnosis in participants aged 9–10 years? Please rephrase for clarity.





Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):

Comments for Author
Manuscript Review for Communications Medicine July 2025

Manuscript Title: Polygenic Risk-Informed White Matter Integrity Improves Deep Learning-Based Prediction of Youth Depression

General Feedback:
In this paper Min et al. address the issue of early detection of youth depression and present a model incorporating both genetic risk and neuroimaging to improve prediction of depression and suicidality in at-risk youths. Early detection of psychiatric disorders offers significant benefits, including improved treatment outcomes, reduced severity of symptoms, and prevention of secondary complications. This is particularly true for early-onset disorders, which tend to have more detrimental outcomes.

The over-all study design is good: the ABCD cohort is an excellent choice for this study; the results show good replication in an independent Korean cohort; and the 2-year follow-up prediction is good (better than other unimodal and machine learning models), though still below clinical AUROC threshold of 0.80. However, this manuscript is lacking crucial details for the design and implementation of the model, specifically for the PGS component of this study. Referring the reader to a second paper (Joo et al., BioRxiv, 2024) for all details of this central part of the project is insufficient (see detailed comment below). Moreover as the Results report that the model does not perform as well as the symptom-based model (retaining 80-90% predictive accuracy of the symptom-based model) it is unclear what clinical benefit this model provides in comparison to existing behavioural and symptomatic assessments. A better explanation of how an at-risk (pre-symptomatic) cohort would benefit from this approach (or be selected for MRI/genomic assessment) is required to support the benefit and usefulness of this approach in a clinical setting (“particularly when for-casting longer-term psychiatric outcomes”). That would counter the better performance of the symptom-based model. These points and the points outlined below need to be addressed before this manuscript is ready for publication.

Major:
1.    Results:
“Further details on PGS calculations are provided in the methods Genetic Data Preprocessing”. The section of the methods referred to in this quoted text recommends readers to refer to a separate paper by Joo et al. (BioRxiv, 2024) to get “a detailed description of the method”. However, the paper by Joo et al. uses a number of PGS scores (35 GWAS summary statistics for 29 traits, including two depression, one MDD and one cross-disorder GWAS) and it is not clear how these scores have been incorporated in the current study. For example, what depression PGS is used as the “DEP PGS” in this model? Joo et al. present multiple Depression GWAS summary statistics and it is not clear which one (or multiple?) was used by the authors. Similarly it is unclear what traits/PGS were included in the composite PGS. If a subset of the data from Joo et al. was used there are no details given of which PGS were included or an explanation for why that subset was selected.

The PGS used for both the Depression PRS and composite PRS need to be clarified and the selection criteria need to be justified.

2.    Genotyping and QC of the Korean youth cohort:
There is a section describing genetic variant pre-processing for the ABCD cohort but not for the Korean cohort (no details of the genotyping or QC of variants used to generate PGS). These data should be included so the reader can understand how the Korean PGS compares to the ABCD PGS and the cross-population applicability of the model.

3.    2y follow-up MDD/MDD + suicide predictions:
Does the ABCD cohort have symptom data for multiple time points? If so, what time-point was used for the symptom-based model (the symptoms from the initial screen or the follow-up screen)? I would imagine symptoms recorded at these two time-points would give different results, therefore this needs to be clarified.

4.    Use of MRI for screening:
The Discussion states that the proposed model could be used to identify at-risk children before symptom onset (sentence in last paragraph: “(identifying) at-risk youth before symptom on-set”.) I agree that the proposed model could be very useful in this context, but how to identify these “at-risk youth” to assess in the first place is not clear. Are they selected based on family history first or is this considered a screening program? How would using MRI in a screening program be feasible considering the cost of MRI? “for youth flagged by clinical or genomic indicators” is a vague statement, particularly when the clinical indicators are likely to include symptom/behavioural data, which has been shown to be a better predictor than this model.


Minor:
Results
Line 116: The N for the various datasets should include case and control numbers.
Line 316: provide not provides
Lines 324, 325, 329 and 331: consistency in capitalisation of “Cohen’s D”. Current text includes use of Cohen and cohen, D, d, and d.

Methods
Line 376: “inclusion/exclusion criteria are provided in Supp at Table S1” actually in Fig S1.
Line 425: “sampled from participants”. Delete “from”

General comment on Figures and Tables (main and supplementary):
•     highly pixelated and difficult to read. Labels are very small
•     Figures don’t print properly as they go beyond page boundaries.
•     SIA and SA are not defined anywhere in figures or text. Assume SA is suicide attempt and SIA is Suicide active ideation?
•     Figure 1: Composite PGS: give max PGS # included (e.g. PGS 1,2,3… 29).
•     Figure 2: Labels are very small and as image is pixelated they are not possible to read.
•     Tables 1-3 would benefit from inclusion of legends/descriptions.
