papers.title: Dear Editor-in-Chief,
papers.abstract:
Importance: Childhood overweight/obesity is a global health issue affecting risks for chronic diseases and mental health. While the brain’s role in obesity development is recognized, its predictive remains unclear.
Objective: To investigate whether brain structure, assessed by MRI, can predict future children overweight/obesity within 1 and 2 years using deep neural networks (DNNs).
Design, setting, and Participants: This study used brain structural MRI data from 11,316 children (ages 9-10 years) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large-scale longitudinal study conducted across 21 sites in the United States.
papers.content:
Editor-in-Chief
JAMA Pediatrics 

Dear Editor-in-Chief,

I am writing to submit our manuscript entitled "Brain-Based Predictive Modeling of Childhood Obesity Risk with Neuroimaging and Deep Neural Networks" for consideration for publication as an original article in JAMA Pediatrics. Our research combines advanced neuroimaging techniques and deep learning to address a pressing public health issue—predicting childhood obesity. This study is not only the first to leverage such a methodology for this purpose but also introduces significant advancements to the predictive analytics capabilities in pediatric health.

Childhood obesity is a critical predictor of long-term health outcomes, yet early identification remains challenging. Our study employs deep neural networks (DNNs) and transfer learning to analyze brain structural MRI data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. We have developed a model that not only accurately predicts current and future obesity status in children but also elucidates the neuroanatomical regions associated with these predictions. This approach significantly outperforms existing models, providing both higher accuracy and deeper insights into the underlying biological mechanisms.

Key Contributions of Our Research Include:

Advanced Deep Learning Integration for Pediatric Health: Our research enhances the application of deep neural networks in neuroimaging by integrating transfer learning to accurately predict childhood obesity and associated psychopathologies such as Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and anxiety disorders using structural MRI data. This methodology refines our understanding of the interplay between physiological and psychological health factors in pediatric populations.

Neuroanatomical Insights into Obesity and Psychopathology Risks: Using explainable AI techniques, we identified specific brain regions linked to obesity risk that also relate to increased susceptibility to MDD and anxiety disorders. This knowledge is essential for developing targeted interventions that can simultaneously address both physical and mental health challenges in children at risk.

Enhanced Predictive Models for Early Detection and Intervention: Our study advances previous models by significantly improving the early detection of obesity and its related mental health issues, facilitating timely and effective preventive measures.

Public Health Implications: The findings offer novel insights for early identification and integrated treatment strategies for children at risk of obesity and mental health disorders, supporting the creation of comprehensive public health interventions.

The findings from our study have the potential to inform prevention strategies that could be integrated into early pediatric care, ultimately aiming to curb the obesity epidemic from a young age. Given the focus of JAMA Pediatrics on impactful, open-access research, we believe that our manuscript will appeal to your readership, offering clinically relevant insights that are accessible to a broad academic and clinical audience.

Thank you for considering our manuscript for publication. We believe that the readers of JAMA Pediatrics will find our study both innovative and crucial for advancing pediatric healthcare. We look forward to the opportunity to contribute to your journal.

Sincerely,

Jiook Cha, PhD

Associate Professor of Psychology

Seoul National University

Brain-Based Predictive Modeling of Childhood Obesity Risk with Neuroimaging and Deep Neural Networks

Hee-Hwan Wang1,  Eun-Ji Lee2, Bo Gyeom Kim2, Gakyung Kim3, Yoonjung Yoonie Joo4,5, Jiook Cha1,2,3

Interdisciplinary Program in Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

Department of Psychology, Seoul, South Korea 

Department of Brain Cognitive and Science, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

Department of Digital Health, Samsung Advanced Institute for Health Sciences & Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, Seoul, South Korea

Samsung Genome Institute, Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

Keywords: Childhood Overweight/obesity, Deep Neural Network, Transfer Learning, Explainable AI, Depressive and Anxiety Disorders  

Key Points

Question: Can brain structure, as assessed by MRI, accurately predict future overweight/obesity status in children using deep neural networks?

Findings: In this study of 11,316 children aged 9-10 years, deep neural networks using structural MRI data accurately predicted current weight status and future overweight/obesity within 1 and 2 years. The models also identified brain regions associated with obesity risk and improved classification of prior obesity-related mental disorder diagnoses.

Meaning: Brain structure analysis using deep learning techniques shows promise for early identification of children at risk for overweight/obesity and related mental health issues, potentially informing targeted prevention strategies.

Abstract

Importance: Childhood overweight/obesity is a global health issue affecting risks for chronic diseases and mental health. While the brain’s role in obesity development is recognized, its predictive remains unclear.

Objective: To investigate whether brain structure, assessed by MRI, can predict future children overweight/obesity within 1 and 2 years using deep neural networks (DNNs). 

Design, setting, and Participants: This study used brain structural MRI data from 11,316 children (ages 9-10 years) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large-scale longitudinal study conducted across 21 sites in the United States. 

Exposures: Baseline year brain structural MRI data.

Main Outcomes and Measures: Prediction of current overweight/obesity status and future changes within 1 and 2 years, based on age- and sex-adjusted BMI z-scores. Explainable AI (XAI) algorithms were used to identify brain regions contributing to model predictions. Classification of prior diagnoses of obesity-related mental disorders (Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Social Anxiety Disorder), was performed by leveraging model pre-trained on the prediction of current weight status.

Results: DNNs accurately predicted current weight status (R2 = ; Mean Squared Error = ). Transfer learning, model pre-trained to predict current weight status were fine-tuned to predict future weight status, significantly improved prediction accuracy for both 1 year (ACC = ; AUROC = ; F1 = ) and 2 years (ACC = ; AUROC = ; F1 = ). XAI-driven neuroanatomical attribution scores identified key brain regions associated with obesity risk, including the brain stem, pituitary gland, and temporal lobe regions. These scores also revealed individual differences in the development of anxiety problems (Cohen’s d = 0.14, pBonferroni < 0.05). Furthermore, pre-trained model significantly improved classification of prior diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder (ACC = ; AUROC = ; F1 = ).

Conclusions and Relevance: This demonstrates the potential of DNNs and transfer learning for predicting future childhood overweight/obesity and related mental disorders from brain structures. These findings highlight a novel approach for early identification of at-risk individuals.

Keywords: childhood obesity, deep learning, neuroimaging, prediction, transfer learning

Introduction

	Childhood overweight/obesity, a strong predictor of lifelong obesity1, is a global health issue demanding urgent action due to its alarming increase over the past decade2. This condition not only increases the risk of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and liver cancer but also intertwines with the development of psychiatric disorders. Emerging research reveals a bidirectional relationship between childhood obesity and mental health problems, suggesting shared biological mechanisms including immuno-inflammation, increased oxidative stress, hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis disturbances, and neurotransmitter imbalances3–10. Despite known risks, early identification of children at high risk for obesity remains challenging, hindering timely intervention efforts.

	The brain plays a central role in regulating food intake, body weight, and energy homeostasis through intricate neural circuits11–15. Key neural circuits, including the orexinergic16–20, leptin-melanocortin11–14,21, and mesolimbic pathway11,14,22–26, regulate feeding behavior, sleep-wake cycles, energy metabolism, stress response, emotional process, and reward mechanism. Dysfunction within these critical components, often influenced by stress, can disrupt energy homeostasis and predispose individuals to obesity, sleep disorders, and various stress-related problematic behaviors11–15,22–25,27. Stress-induced alterations in these neural circuits affect the structure and function of various subcortical regions like the amygdala, ventral tegmental area, and nucleus accumbens, potentially leading to sleep disorders, emotional dysregulation, and obesity15,21,28–30.

	Genetic studies provide further evidence for physiological alterations within these brain regions, highlighting shared vulnerabilities across sleep disorders, stress- and emotion/mood-related problematic behaviors, and obesity. Genes associated with obesity, such as those encoding the leptin receptor31,32, POMC33, BDNF34,35 ,and MC4R36,37,contribute to sleep disturbances and anxiety-like behavior under chronic stress, often mediated through either the leptin-melanocortin pathway or the mesolimbic pathway. Epidemiological studies also support the close relationship between obesity, psychiatric disorders, and sleep disturbances38–41. 

	Neuroimaging studies have revealed significant structural and functional brain changes associated with childhood obesity, suggesting potential predictors of future weight gain. Obese children show alterations in prefrontal cortex thickness42–44, nucleus accumbens and amygdala volumes45,46, and functional responses to food stimuli47,48. In recent years, a large-scale longitudinal study on child development, the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, has provided further insights, showing associations between BMI and decelerated development in specific prefrontal regions, altered corpus callosum44, and predictive value of nucleus accumbens cell density for future waist circumference increases49. Conventional machine learning algorithms have shown moderate success (AUROC = ) in predicting rapid weight gain from brain morphology50. While promising, these findings necessitate further research to develop whole-brain structural predictive models for future overweight/obesity risk.

	Recent advances in deep neural networks (DNNs) and large-scale population studies pave a new way for human neuroimaging research51–53. DNNs trained on extensive neuroimaging datasets have shown remarkable accuracy in predicting biological sex, age, and body mass index (BMI) in adults using T1-weighted brain MRI images51–53. These studies also show that Explainable AI (XAI) algorithms provide valuable insights into the neuroanatomical features that these models leverage for individual predictions. Additionally, transfer learning, which leverages knowledge acquired by pre-trained DNNs54,55, has shown potential in analyzing smaller neuroimaging datasets for various brain diseases and psychiatric disorders56–58.

Despite these advancements, the potential of DNNs, transfer learning, and XAI for early detection of childhood overweight/obesity risk and exploration of associated neuroanatomical differences remains unexplored. This study aims to address this gap by investigating three main questions. First, we examine whether DNNs can accurately predict both current weight status and future risk of overweight/obesity in children using structural brain images. Second, we investigate if neuroanatomical features identified by DNNs as contributing to the prediction of individual risk for future overweight/obesity can differentiate individual differences in the progression of physical and mental health problems. Third, we investigate whether transfer learning can leverage pre-trained DNNs, originally trained to capture neuroanatomical features of current weight status, for the prediction of obesity-related psychiatric disorders in children. 

By addressing these questions, this study aims to advance our understanding of the neuroanatomical basis of childhood obesity risk and explore innovative approaches for early identification and intervention. This research has the potential to significantly impact public health strategies for obesity prevention and management in pediatric populations.

Methods

ABCD participants 

	We utilized data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a 10-year longitudinal study across 21 U.S. sites. Participants (N=11,316, ages 9-10 years at the baseline year) were selected from data releases 2.0 and 5.0, including those with complete baseline, first-year, and second-year follow-up data59. T1-weighted brain MRI images from baseline were used. The study was approved by the institutional review board, and informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Calculating Body Mass Index standard deviation score & defining future overweight/obesity 

BMI and Overweight/Obesity Classification Body Mass Index Standard Deviation Score (BMI-SDS) was calculated using the 2022 CDC Extended Growth Chart60,61. Children were categorized as "still normal" or "become overweight/obese" based on CDC age- and sex-specific cutoff points and changes in BMI-SDS between baseline and follow-up. Those maintaining normal weight (5th to 85th percentile) with BMI-SDS changes between -0.2 and 0.2 were classified as "still normal". Transitions to overweight (85th to 95th percentile) or obese (≥95th percentile) status, or BMI-SDS changes exceeding 0.2, were classified as "become overweight/obese". We excluded children above the 99.99th percentile for BMI. We established these criteria by referring to previous study1. 

Preprocessing T1-weighted Brain MRI Image

We applied established protocols to preprocess 3-dimensional brain structural MRI images provided by the ABCD study62. To improve geometric accuracy and reproducibility of image intensity, we applied gradient nonlinearity distortion correction63, intensity nonuniformity correction, and rigid alignment with a reference atlas to T1-weighted brain MRI images. For conventional machine learning experiments, we applied cortical surface reconstruction using Freesurfer (v6.0), obtaining 596 brain regions. For DNN experiments, images were skull-stripped64 and nonlinearly registered to the MNI152 atlas65 by using SyN algorithm66 provided by ANTs. Detailed preprocessing steps are provided in Supplementary Materials.

Polygenic Scores 

	We constructed polygenic scores for 13 complex traits related to overweight/obesity, sleep disorders, and anxiety/mood-related disorders. Genotyping was performed on baseline saliva samples using the Affymetrix NIDA Smokescreen array. After standard quality control, genotype data were imputed using the Michigan Imputation Server71 and 1000 Genomes reference panel (see Supplementary Materials). To address population stratification and familial relatedness, we estimated kinship coefficients and principal components, retaining 10,199 unrelated individuals (7,893 of European ancestry). Polygenic scores were calculated using European-only GWAS summary statistics and PRS-CSx72,73 (trait list in Supplementary Materials). For scores with corresponding ABCD phenotypes, optimal hyperparameters were manually validated; others used PRS-CS-auto74. Final scores were adjusted for population stratification.

Demographic and Behavioral Assessment Data 

	We used demographic data (age, sex, study site, ethnicity, parental education, marital status, and household income) from the ABCD study for DNN training and statistical analyses. Longitudinal changes in age, birth weight, parental education, and household income were included in statistical analyses. Sleep problems were assessed using the ABCD Parent Sleep Disturbances Scale for Children75,76. Behavioral and emotional problems were assessed with the parental-reported Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL)77. We calculated change scores to assess symptom severity variations over time (delta score). Detailed descriptions of subscales and delta score calculations are provided in Supplementary Materials.

DNN and Conventional Machine Learning Model Training

	Our DNN experiments, detailed in Supplementary Materials and Supplementary Tables 1~4, involved constructing two datasets for predicting overweight/obesity within 1 and 2 years. We implemented a 5-fold stratified dataset split using propensity scores based on demographic factors and baseline BMI-SDS, with each fold further divided into train (75%), validation (5%), and test (20%) sets. We evaluated three 3D-CNN architectures (ResNet3D78, DenseNet3D79, and EfficientNet3D80) using data augmentation, AdamW optimizer81, and early stopping. The selected DenseNet3D-121 underwent pre-training to predict baseline BMI-SDS, followed by fine-tuning for future overweight/obesity prediction tasks. For comparison, we trained conventional machine learning algorithms (Elastic Net, Linear SVM, Radial Basis Function SVM) on demographic and brain morphological features using 16-fold cross-validation. Training was conducted using NVIDIA RTX 3090 and RTX A5000 GPUs. Detailed hyperparameters and model performance are provided in Supplementary Tables 1~4. 

Identifying Brain Regions Contributing to Predictions Using Explainable AI 

We employed Integrated Gradients82 and SmoothGrad83 to generate voxel-wise attribution maps of brain regions contributing to predictions. XAI algorithms were modified to account for zero-valued background voxels in T1-weighted images by applying Gaussian noise (σ = 0.05) within brain regions, generating 50 noise-added images per participant. We implemented the XAI algorithm using the Captum library (version 0.6.0).

Using the same 5-fold stratified dataset split as in DNN training, we obtained individual attribution maps for each participant. We calculated attribution scores for specific regions of interest (ROIs) using three MNI-space atlases: Harvard-Oxford Cortical and Subcortical Structural Atlases84–87, CIT168 Reinforcement Learning Atlas88,89, and CIT168 Amygdala Atlas90. The Harvard-Oxford Atlases were thresholded at 0.25 maximum probability, and all atlases were aligned to a 1mm isotropic MNI152 template and resized to 128x128x128. Individual attribution scores were standardized, averaged across voxels within each ROI, and used to determine brain region importance in predicting baseline BMI-SDS and future overweight/obesity. Further details are provided in Supplementary Table 5~6 and Figures 1~3. 

Clustering and Statistical Analysis with XAI Attribution Scores

Clustering analyses were performed on children who became overweight/obese using brain ROI attribution scores. Optimal clustering parameters were determined using silhouette scores from K-means and hierarchical clustering (2-6 clusters, see Supplementary Table 7). Variations in attribution scores across clusters were investigated for 1-year and 2-year predictions (Supplementary Figure 4~5). After confirming no significant differences between weight status groups, we examined differences in polygenic scores, behavioral assessments, and their longitudinal changes (delta scores) among subgroup of children who became overweight/obese,. We used permutation t-tests (100,000 permutations) with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons within each brain atlas and category (e.g., genetic scores, sleep disorders, CBCL syndrome, DSM-5-oriented CBCL). Deus Ex Machina: Preparing the Age of AI

Abstract

The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) presents both unprecedented opportunities and significant challenges for society. This paper examines the potential dystopian consequences of rapid AI development, drawing parallels with historical technological impacts to underscore the urgency of addressing emerging risks. We human neurocognitive mechanisms, particularly the Free Energy Principle, to illustrate vulnerabilities in human-AI interactions that could exacerbate issues such as social inequality, the proliferation of fake news, and the erosion of democratic norms. Proposing an interdisciplinary approach, we advocate for policy reforms and research that prioritize human capital, social trust, and ethical AI development. By synthesizing insights from behavioral science, social science, and public policy, we outline a proactive strategy to harness AI's potential while safeguarding human values and societal stability. Our framework aims not merely to prevent AI from becoming a modern-day Big Brother but to transform it into a Deus Ex Machina—a powerful tool for enhancing human well-being and fostering democratic resilience.

Introduction

In March 2016, Sedol Lee, a renowned Korean Go champion, commented on his defeat by AlphaGo, stating, “I don’t think my defeat this time is a loss for humanity. It clearly shows my weaknesses, but not the weakness of all humanity” (Lee, 2016). Since then, artificial intelligence (AI) has continued to surpass human abilities in various domains, including complex games like Atari 2600 (Mnih et al., 2015), Starcraft (Vinyals et al., 2019), and Go (Silver et al., 2017). Advanced language models like ChatGPT have demonstrated capabilities  (OpenAI et al., 2023). 

Conversely, the human condition has faced significant adversities. The COVID-19 pandemic has persisted for three years, exacerbating global challenges. The escalating climate crisis has intensified natural disasters—floods, hurricanes, wildfires—resulting in substantial loss of life and economic damage. Concurrently, ongoing wars in Crimea, Palestine, Syria, and Myanmar continue to destabilize regions. Politically, the global landscape has witnessed a decline in democracy and a rise in authoritarianism, highlighted by the US Capitol attack on January 6, 2021, and the consolidation of authoritarian regimes in Russia and China (The Economist Intelligence Unit, 2024).

Amid these crises, the rapid advancement of AI might seem more a curse than a blessing. Beyond the fear of job displacement, AI poses broader threats. For example, the combination of generative AI with social media bots capable of producing and spreading disinformation en masse makes it difficult for individuals to discern truth from falsehood. This challenge facilitates the unchecked spread of fake news and hate speech, aggravating discrimination, social unrest, and authoritarianism (Acemoğlu, 2023).

Furthermore, the environmental impact of AI, such as the substantial energy consumption required to train models like GPT-3—equivalent to the daily energy use of a small town—raises significant concerns about sustainability (Patterson et al., 2021). With the ongoing AI arms race between major powers like the US and China, reminiscent of the nuclear arms race, the risks to humanity are escalating (Stokes et al., 2023). 

Given these concerns, the potential of AI to foster a dystopian future is evident. However, our objective should not be to allow AI to evolve into an authoritarian Big Brother. Instead, we should steer its development to become a Deus Ex Machina—a mechanical god-like entity capable of resolving humanity's multifaceted problems. Thus, the development of AI technologies should be intentionally directed to benefit human society and enhance the quality of life for all.

In 1947, Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno advocated for a critical understanding of science and technology. They emphasized the importance of harnessing these forces to benefit humanity as a whole, rather than allowing them to lead to domination or a new form of barbarism (Horkheimer & Adorno, 2002). Drawing from the horrors of the world wars and racial genocides, they promoted a meta-critical approach to science and technology, advocating for their utilization in ways that are conscious of potential harms and are aligned with the broader goals of human well-being and emancipation.

How can we ensure that AI is developed and used in ways that are mindful of potential harms and aligned with human well-being? Given that history seems to be repeating itself with grim realities similar to those of a century ago, there may be an underlying common cause: human neurocognitive decision-making mechanisms. In this paper, we first review the mechanisms of human neurocognitive decision-making and explore how these mechanisms are related to social phenomena. We then suggest policy implications and future research goals. We believe the discussions outlined in this paper are crucial for building an inclusive, positive future amidst the ever-developing landscape of AI.

Human’s Neurocognitive and Behavioral Mechanism: Free Energy Principle

This section delineates how human neurocognitive and behavioral mechanisms are governed by the Free Energy Principle, which suggests that the brain operates to minimize free energy. Rooted in physics and Bayesian statistics, this principle is applicable to all biological systems, ranging from single-cell organisms to complex social networks. It provides a unified framework for understanding how biological systems maintain order and resist entropy, integrating insights from evolutionary biology, systems theory, statistical physics, and machine learning (Friston, 2009).

According to this principle, the brain constructs an internal representation of the external environment—a world model—that facilitates prediction, sensory signal interpretation, and optimal action selection (Friston, 2010). These cognitive processes are organized hierarchically, with different levels of the brain processing information at increasing levels of abstraction and complexity (Adams et al., 2013; Clark, 2013; Iglesias et al., 2013). This hierarchical organization allows the brain to efficiently manage a vast array of cognitive processes, including homeostasis, memory, attention, and both perceptual and value-based decision-making (Barron et al., 2020; FitzGerald et al., 2015; Friston, 2010; Iglesias et al., 2013; Tenenbaum et al., 2011).

The Free Energy Principle posits that biological systems resist a natural tendency towards disorder by minimizing free energyThis principle extends beyond biological constraints to evolutionary and ecological contexts, refined through millennia of adaptation. It applies broadly across neurocognitive and behavioral activities, such as sensory processing (Iglesias et al., 2013), decision-making (perceptual or value-based) (FitzGerald et al., 2015; Lak et al., 2020; Lak et al., 2017), input information (sensory inputs or abstract knowledge) (Friston, 2010), or belief subjects (physical world or social judgments) (Veissière et al., 2020). Advances in statistical physics and machine learning reveal that biological systems adhere to these constraints through simple mechanisms, highlighting the principle's elegance and universality in explaining brain function and broader biological phenomena (Friston, 2009). Thus, the Free Energy Principle not only elucidates neurocognitive processes but also provides a robust theoretical framework for interpreting complex behaviors and system-level brain activities. 

Social Implications of Free Energy Principle in the Age of AI

Prejudice and Stereotyping

Reality presents complexities far beyond the capacity of any individual to fully perceive or comprehend. The intersectionality of identities, such as the experiences of a Black woman facing both racial and gender discrimination, illustrates the inadequacy of considering social categories in isolation (Crenshaw, 2013). Similarly, the diverse impacts of global events like the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate how varied the experiences of economic loss or health impacts can be across different individuals. This variability underscores the difficulty of accurate causal inference in social sciences, a problem exacerbated by the multidimensional nature of societal variables and the limitations of inductive reasoning. The example of Bertrand Russell's Chicken highlights a fundamental flaw in forming general rules from limited observations, emphasizing the unreliability of such rules in predicting atypical future events.

Our brains strive to maintain a coherent and stable world model, often simplifying complex information, which might lead to incorrect generalizations and spurious causal inferences. From an early age, humans are capable of forming causal maps from minimal data, a process prone to sampling bias, confounding, and overfitting (Gopnik et al., 2004; Tenenbaum et al., 2011). These simplified models are especially evident in our handling of social norms, where adherence to collective behaviors minimizes prediction errors and aligns individual actions with group expectations, thus reducing free energy (Veissière et al., 2020). Nonetheless, this often results in the dismissal of alternative perspectives as too risky, potentially cementing prejudices and stereotypes that are supported by dominant societal groups.

Neuroscientific research has identified that areas such as the striatum, orbitofrontal, and lateral prefrontal cortices, which are involved in processing concepts of prejudice and stereotyping, channel signals to the medial prefrontal cortex (Amodio, 2014), a region crucial in managing confirmation bias (Kappes et al., 2020). These areas overlap with those processing prediction errors of sensory stimuli (Iglesias et al., 2013; Kappes et al., 2020), illustrating how prejudices and stereotypes may be neurologically rooted in the underestimation of the high free energy of sensory inputs that challenge existing world models. 

In a world rich with diversity and intersectionality, attempting to fit complex social realities into overly simplified models leads to significant predictive inaccuracies. This issue becomes particularly pronounced during periods of high uncertainty—such as economic downturns, wars, pandemics, or rapid technological changes like the advent of AI— where the propensity to generalize from noisy environments increases, heightening the risk of overfitting to biased interpretations (Sun et al., 2023). Consequently, experiences and subsequent adjustments that could correct these biases often instead reinforce them, perpetuating a cycle of prejudiced perceptions and decisions.

This exploration not only provides insight into the cognitive underpinnings of societal issues but also underscores the importance of developing strategies to enhance the adaptability and accuracy of our cognitive frameworks in the face of complex social dynamics.

Ingroup Bias

Ingroup bias represents a pervasive cognitive inclination that amplifies preferential treatment towards members of one's own group over those from different groups. This bias manifests early in childhood; studies indicate that from as young as 5 to 6 months, infants show preferences for those who speak the same mother tongue (Kinzler Katherine et al., 2007; Kinzler et al., 2011) and empathize more with individuals of their own race (Avenanti et al., 2010; Azevedo et al., 2013). As individuals mature, they demonstrate heightened expectations of support (Chai et al., 2022; Jin & Baillargeon, 2017), an increased willingness to share resources (Dunham et al., 2011; Mulvey et al., 2016), and more forgiveness (Mulvey et al., 2022) towards ingroup members compared to outgroup members. Furthermore, individuals are more inclined to accept information that favors their ingroup, while discounting contradictory evidence (Dunham et al., 2011; Hastorf & Cantril, 1954). Such biases are supported by greater activity in brain regions linked to empathy and confirmation bias, such as the insula and medial prefrontal cortex, specifically in response to ingroup members (Amodio, 2014; Cikara & Fiske, 2011; Harris & Fiske, 2006).

The implications of ingroup bias extend to real-world discrimination and political consequences, influencing social interactions and contributing to conflicts beyond mere dislike or discrimination against specific racial, gender, national, or religious groups (Amodio, 2014; Han, 2018; Harris & Fiske, 2006). The tendency to distort information in favor of ingroup members (Dunham et al., 2011) and to show leniency towards ingroup errors (Koval et al., 2012; Mulvey et al., 2022) exemplifies a broader tendency towards confirmation bias, which discounts information conflicting with pre-existing beliefs. This bias is associated with activation in the medial prefrontal cortex, a region implicated in both ingroup bias and prejudicial judgments (Amodio, 2014; Harris & Fiske, 2006; Kappes et al., 2020). Thus, ingroup bias and confirmation bias appear to share a common neural mechanism, underscoring a neurocognitive basis for these social phenomena.

Furthermore, confirmation bias can escalate into extremism. When individuals repeatedly interact only with like-minded group members, they may reinforce incorrect beliefs and become entrenched in extreme ideologies. Recent studies have shown that individuals engaged in antisocial or extreme behaviors often exist within homogeneous social networks that continuously affirm their actions as morally justified, perpetuating a cycle of biased information processing and behavior (Atari et al., 2021; Mooijman et al., 2018).

Ingroup bias not only fosters group favoritism but also significantly diminishes empathy toward outgroup members, reducing the ability to understand their emotions or perspectives. This cognitive limitation can lead to severe moral disengagement when individuals, acting under the umbrella of group identity, commit heinous acts without substantial guilt. For instance, during the French Revolution, revolutionary forces, driven by a distorted sense of patriotism, perpetrated acts of violence against perceived societal outcasts, including widows and orphans, without remorse, even seeking rewards for such actions (LeBon, 2001). Similarly, Adolf Eichmann, during the Holocaust, orchestrated the deportation and systematic extermination of Jews across Europe with clinical detachment, a phenomenon Hannah Arendt described as the banality of evil. Arendt argued that this type of evil emerges when ordinary individuals, failing to empathize with the suffering of others, blindly adhere to authoritarian orders, contributing to the horrors of totalitarian regimes (Arendt, 1976, 2006).

The concept that ordinary people can commit atrocious acts under authority was empirically tested by Stanley Milgram (1974) and further explored in recent neuroscientific studies. For example, a study using electroencephalogram revealed reduced auditory N1 amplitude when participants inflicted pain under orders compared to actions taken at their own volition, suggesting diminished feelings of guilt under directed conditions (Caspar et al., 2016). This neurological response underscores the impact of social identity and ingroup bias in obeying commands, facilitating the occurrence of banality of evil, where unjust acts are performed under the guise of group directives.

Ingroup bias does not merely exacerbate social prejudices; it also fosters the formation of political groups prone to extreme and antisocial behaviors. Members deeply embedded within such groups are more likely to engage in grievous actions without substantial remorse, following ingroup directives. While ingroup bias is a necessary cognitive function for navigating social landscapes, unchecked, it can lead to dire political outcomes, especially in competitive contexts where resources are scarce (Deutsch, 2011; Fiske et al., 2002). The current global economic downturn and inflation are likely to exacerbate these negative phenomena, making it crucial to understand and mitigate the effects of ingroup bias to prevent further social and political degradation.

Scapegoat

As prejudice, stereotyping, and ingroup bias intensify, marginalized individuals increasingly experience despair and alienation, often due to economic crises and unemployment. These pressures can cause individuals to develop intense resentment toward outgroups. They may come to believe that their hardships are caused by specific groups, influenced by personal experiences or inflammatory propaganda. In an attempt to alleviate their suffering, they project their grievances onto these groups, engaging in scapegoating as a means to address their problems by suppressing and eliminating those they perceive as culprits (Girard, 1986). Importantly, the targeted group is not always a social minority; it can also include groups with vested interests, such as the royal family, clergy, and nobility during the French Revolution. Historical instances such as the Holocaust, the massacre of Korean residents in Japan after the 1923 Kanto earthquake (Ryang, 2007), and the rise of anti-Asian sentiment during the COVID-19 pandemic exemplify the scapegoating phenomena.

In the dynamics of scapegoating, the public may gravitate toward authoritative figures capable of swiftly stabilizing a polarized context, wielding significant authority, and enacting punitive measures against the vilified groups (Fromm, 1965). This tendency to seek out leaders who promise to reduce the high levels of free energy caused by societal uncertainty often leads to the endorsement of authoritarian, even fascist, leaders. This dynamic has historically underpinned support for figures such as Hitler and has contributed to the rise of authoritarian leadership in numerous countries (The Economist Intelligence Unit, 2020, 2024). Current global challenges, including the ongoing wars, economic crises, and climate change, exacerbate these conditions, further fueling the dynamics that lead to authoritarianism.

In conclusion, extreme disenfranchisement, aggressive propaganda, and societal agitation often precipitate the erosion of democratic values and the rise of fascism. This pattern highlights the critical need for vigilance and proactive measures to counteract these destructive forces in society.

Preparing for the Age of AI

So far, we have explored the complex interplay between human neurocognitive and behavioral systems and the escalation of adverse social phenomena such as increased hate speech, the erosion of democracy, and the rise of fascism. Additionally, we argue that the advancement of AI could potentially exacerbate these crises. As these issues intensify, they contribute to a vicious cycle of social problems, making their resolution increasingly challenging (Box 2). This dynamic suggests that even as AI technologies advance and potentially pose significant risks to humanity, effectively regulating these technologies to prevent harm and ensure their benefit to humanity becomes progressively more difficult.

Abstract 

Early life stress (ELS) may cause a long-term effect on the brain and cognition primarily during development. Despite the extensive research, however, there is a lack of research integratively revealing the impact of ELS on genetic factors, brain development, and cognitive capacity in humans. Here we hypothesize that ELS impedes the inherited genetic influence on the brain development of grey matter morphology and white matter connectivity, and that this impediment on the brain negatively affect cognitive function in children. We analyzed the multimodal data of DNA genotypes, brain imaging (structural and diffusion MRI), and neuropsychological assessment outcomes (NIH Toolbox) of 4,276 children (ages 9 to 10 years, European ancestry) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. The genetic influence on cognitive capacity was estimated using genome-wide polygenic score (GPS). Using brain morphometry and white matter tractography, we identified the brain correlates of the cognitive capacity GPSs. Regression and mediation analyses revealed the likely causal relationships for the gene-brain-cognition pathway. The brain structural variance significantly mediated the genetic influence (estimated with GPS for cognitive capacity) on cognitive intelligence (indirect effect = 0.016, PFWE < 0.001). Of note, this gene-brain relationship was impeded by abuse, leading to impoverished cognitive intelligence(Index of Moderated Mediation = -0.007; 95% CI= -0.012 ~ -0.002; PFWE < 0.05). Our results support a novel gene-brain-cognitive model likely accounting for the long-lasting negative impact of ELS on cognitive development in young children.  


Introduction

Early life stress (ELS), such as abuse, neglect, and household challenges, is a major risk factor for maladaptive cognition, behaviors, and psychiatric disorders1–4 with long-term sequelae5. ELS modulates the expression of the genes responsible for stress physiology, emotion regulation, cognitive control, and learning and memory6–10. Animal literature shows a causal effect of ELS on cognition and behaviors11–20 and the epi-/genetic mechanisms within the brain21–24. In humans, similar mechanisms may be involved in psychopathology25,26, stress physiology7, or emotion regulation27–29.  

Although extensive literature shows associations of ELS with poor cognitive outcomes and brain functional and structural representations1,3,8, exactly how ELS affects the brain development and cognitive function in children remains unclear. Addressing this will permit much-needed insight into who, when, and where to intervene regarding the negative neurocognitive outcomes of ELS. We hypothesize that ELS modulates the inherited genetic influences on brain and cognitive development3,5.

Cognitive development involves multiple dynamic processes regulated by the interplay of genetic and environmental factors30–32. Despite the significant impact, less is known about the biological mechanisms of how ELS interacts with genetic influences to impact cognitive development in children. The recent development of the genome-wide polygenic score approach (GPS) allows individual genetic loadings for cognitive capacity (e.g., accounting for up to 13% of the variance in cognitive outcomes in adults33) to be estimated quantitatively. Using this rigorous computational approach, we aimed to test whether ELS modulates the gene-brain-cognition development process. 

This study had two main questions. First, does a gene-brain-cognition pathway exist during development? If so, does ELS negatively affect the causal pathway? We investigated these questions using multimodal data, including genetics, brain imaging, psychological and cognitive assessment data in large samples of prepubertal children (ages 9 to 10 years) with a wide range of sociodemographic confounding. Methods

Study Participants

Participants were enrolled in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, an ongoing longitudinal multisite study of brain development and health of youth in the United States34. We used the de-identified neuroimaging, demographic, genetic, and behavioral data from the ABCD 2.0 Data Release, these data were collected across 21 sites from 2015 to 2018. The participants were 11,875 children from the U.S. who were aged 9-10 years. After removing participants who had at least one missing value from genetic, neuroimaging, and ELS data, 4,276 participants were included in our analyses.  

Genotype data for Genome-wide polygenic scores (GPS) 

Saliva samples were collected from study participants and were genotyped using the Affymetrix NIDA Smokescreen array (733,293 SNPs) at the Rutgers University Cell and DNA Repository. We removed any inferiorly genotyped SNPs with thresholds of (i) genotype call rate<95%, (ii) sample call rate<95%, and (iii) rare variants with minor allele frequency (MAF)<1%. We imputed the data using the Michigan Imputation Server35 based on the 1000 Genome phase 3 reference panel with Eagle ver2.4 phased output36. For the imputed 12,046,090 SNPs, we additionally removed data from any individuals with >5% missing genotypes; extreme heterozygosity (F coefficient > 3 standard deviation from the population mean); and SNPs with <0.4 imputation INFO score, >5% missingness rate, <1% MAF and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p<10-6). Genetic ancestry was determined with the fastSTRUCTURE algorithm37, available from ABCD release 3.0. Our analysis was restricted to individuals with European ancestry to control for population stratification. We estimated both kinship coefficients (K.C.s) and principal components (P.C.s) to control familial relatedness and ancestry admixture using PC-Air38 and PC-Relate39. We selected unrelated samples that were inferred to be more distant than 4th-degree relatives (K.C.>0.022) and removed any genetic outliers that fell significantly outside (>6 S.D. limits) the center in P.C. space.

To assess the subject-level genetic propensity for cognitive ability, we computed genome-wide polygenic scores (GPS) for cognitive performance and educational attainment using publicly available GWAS summary statistics based on the European population30. The scores were computed using PRSice2 software, version 340, with linkage-disequilibrium clumping threshold (R2) of 0.2 over 500kb sliding windows based on the 1000 Genome phase3 reference panel (GWAS p-value < 1). To control for population stratification, the scores were adjusted for the first ten principal components (P.C.s) of the genotype data (11,301,999 variants) of 8,523 unrelated European samples after Q.C. (Supplementary Figure 1). 

Brain Imaging-Anatomical Imaging 

T1-weighted (T1w) 3D structural MRI images were acquired in the ABCD study. We processed the images following established protocols34,41: The gradient nonlinearity distortion correction method was performed on structural MRI scans to improve geometric accuracy and image intensity reproducibility42. Based on tissue segmentation and sparse spatial smoothing, intensity nonuniformity was corrected. Then, the data were then resampled with 1 mm isotropic voxels into rigid alignment with an atlas-derived brain.  

Cortical surface reconstruction was applied using the following procedures: structural MRI scans were processed using FreeSurfer v6.0 (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu) for cortical surface reconstruction43, which includes skull-stripping44, white matter segmentation and initial mesh creation43, correction of topological defects, surface optimization45,46, and nonlinear registration to a spherical surface-based atlas47.

Brain Imaging-Diffusion Spectrum Imaging 

We used the diffusion spectrum images from the ABCD study that were preprocessed using the following protocol48 by the ABCD Data Analysis and Informatics Center (DAIC). Eddy current distortion correction was used with a nonlinear estimation using diffusion gradient orientations and amplitudes to predict the pattern of distortion49. Head motion was corrected by registering images synthesized from tensor fit50. Diffusion gradients were adjusted for head rotation50,51. To identify and replace dark slices due to abrupt head motion, we used robust diffusion tensor estimation52. B0 distortion was corrected with the reversing gradient method53. Gradient nonlinearity distortion correction was applied42. The data were resampled to a standard orientation with an isotropic resolution of 1.5 mm.  

To estimate accurate brain imaging phenotypes, we used individual connectome data. We applied MRtrix354 for whole-brain white matter tract estimation and individualized connectome generation. For connectivity metrics, we used streamline counts associated with fiber connection strength55,56 associated with fiber integrity. We decreased noise57, and performed bias correction with the Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs) pipeline’s N4 algorithm58. To obtain a connectivity index with a white matter pathway59, we performed probabilistic tractography by second-order integration over fiber orientation distributions60, with random seeding across the brain and target streamline counts of 20 million. These initial tractograms were filtered from preliminary tractograms using spherical-deconvolution informed filtering (2:1 ratio). With a final streamline count of 10 million, we generated an 84 x 84 whole-brain connectome matrix for each participant using the T1-based parcellation and segmentation in FreeSurfer. This pipeline ensured that individual participants' connectomes were restricted to their own neuroanatomy. We carried out the computation on the supercomputers at Argonne Leadership Computing Facility Theta and Texas Advanced Computing Center Stampede2.  

Dimensionality reduction of brain data 

To extract brain morphometric representations correlated with genetic influence on intelligence, we first performed generalized linear model analysis using cognitive capacity GPSs as independent variables and neuroimaging data as dependent variables adjusted for covariates (e.g., age, sex, maternal education, income, BMI, study site, and marital status). Among three different types of neuroimaging data (structural MRI, DTI-count, and DTI-FA), only brain morphometric features (i.e., structural MRI) showed significant associations with cognitive capacity GPSs (PFWE < 0.05; Figure 3, Supplementary Figure 2, Supplementary Table 1)(Python environment v3.7.7 using bioinfokit packages). We then performed principal component analysis to extract representations from brain morphological features associated with cognitive performance GPS or educational attainment GPS (R version 3.4.1). We used the first principal components as representations of the brain.  

NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery data 

NIH Toolbox Cognitive Function Tests61 were used to assess various levels of general cognitive ability of the participants. For each child, summary scores from the NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery were provided, including the crystallized intelligence composite score (mainly measuring prior learning and past experiences about language), the fluid intelligence composite score (mainly measuring abstract reasoning and learning ability in novel situations), and total intelligence composite score, which is the combination of both crystallized and fluid intelligence composite scores62. The crystallized intelligence composite score is a composite of the Picture Vocabulary Test and the Oral Reading Recognition Test outcomes, and the fluid intelligence composite score is a composite of the Dimensional Change Card Sort Test, the Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention Test, the Picture Sequence Memory Test, the List Sorting Working Memory Test, and the Pattern Comparison Processing Speed Test outcomes. Total intelligence composite score is a representation of general intelligence and is an aggregation of all the tests62.

Early life stress 

We derived ELS measures based on child exposure domains in the ABCD study63 (Supplementary Table 2). ELS measures were divided into three main categories: household challenges, neglect, and abuse. Subcategories of ELS data were as follows: parental separation or divorce, criminal household member, household substance abuse, mental illness in household, mother treated violently in household challenges, emotional neglect, physical neglect in neglect; and physical abuse and sexual abuse in abuse. We extracted the items of each subscale from the following various measurement tools (participant- or parent-reported): ABCD Family Environment Scale-Family Conflict Subscale Modified from PhenX, ABCD Diagnostic Interview for DSM-5 Traumatic Events, ABCD Family History Assessment, ABCD Parent Demographics Survey, ABCD Children’s Report of Parental Behavioral Inventory, and ABCD Parental Monitoring Survey. We averaged the measurements for each subcategory and transformed them into z scores. The higher the score, the more stressful experiences children had.

Statistical Analysis 

We performed a generalized linear model for three types of relationships — GPS-brain, GPS-intelligence composite scores, and brain-intelligence composite scores. We included the following covariates into those models: age, sex, maternal education, parental income, BMI, study site, and marital status. Family ID was not included because our analysis was performed in the dataset of unrelated individuals after excluding any relatives fourth-degree or closer during the genetic QC process. We used familywise error (i.e., Bonferroni correction) in each type of relationship for multiple comparison corrections.  

For path modeling, we first tested an initial mediation model to check whether the key relationship of the GPS-brain-cognition pathway was significant. Before examining the role of ELS in the GPS-brain-cognition pathway, we tested whether ELS directly affects cognition and whether ELS moderates the GPS-cognition pathway. After we determined the potential moderation effect of ELS on the GPS-brain-cognition pathway, we evaluated the first-stage moderated mediation models and the second-stage moderated mediation models, following the framework of moderated mediation analysis64–66. These models assessed how ELS and its interaction with genes or the brain, would affect the triangular pathway. We repeated the analyses with different subtypes of ELS and compared their effects. Lastly, we performed moderation analysis as an exploratory analysis to examine how the interactions between ELS and GPS affect behavioral problems with caregiver reported Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) from ABCD study63.

Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were performed in R environment v3.4.1 using the lavaan v0.6-7 package with 1000 bootstrapping samples. Mediation models included the same covariates used in the regression model. Parental separation or divorce had to be excluded in a moderated mediation model because of model convergence issues.

Results 

Participants 

After quality control, our study cohort comprised of 4,276 unrelated children of European ancestry with a mean age of 9-10 years from the ABCD study34. The demographic characteristics of the patients, stratified by records of ELS experience, are summarized in Table 1 (Supplementary Table 3) and Figure 1. Several covariates showed significant differences between the ELS and non-ELS groups (Supplementary Table 4). 

Correlation among GPS, Brain, and Intelligence 

Cognitive Capacity GPS-Brain 

Out of 992 brain morphometric features, 169 and 44 brain features correlated significantly with cognitive performance GPS (PFWE< 0.05) and educational attainment GPS, respectively (PFWE< 0.05), when adjusted for age, sex, maternal education, income, BMI, study site, and marital status (Figure 2). Of note, global brain features ─ including total gray matter volume, total cortex volume, subcortical gray matter volume, and total cerebral white matter volume ─ showed significant associations with both GPSs (Figure 2, Supplementary Table 1). White matter fiber counts and fractional anisotropy of the structural connectomes showed no significant correlations with either GPS (Supplementary Figure 2). To obtain cognitive capacity GPS-related brain representations, we reduced the dimensionality of brain morphometric features correlated with each GPS by performing principal component analysis. Accounting for the substantial variance of brain morphometric features (correlated with the GPS) (Braincognitive performance GPS: 44.5%; Braineducational attainment GPS: 54.9%) (Supplementary Figure 3, 4, 5), the first component significantly correlated with cognitive capacity GPS (Braincognitive performance GPS: β = 0.10, PFWE< 0.001; Braineducational attainment GPS: β = 0.15, PFWE< 0.001) (Supplementary Table 5). 

Brain-Intelligence Composite Score 

Both Braincognitive performance GPS and Braineducational attainment GPS significantly correlated with all three types of intelligence composite scores (PFWE< 0.001). Among the different types of intelligence composite scores, both brain representations showed the highest effect size on crystallized intelligence composite scores (Braincognitive performance GPS: β = 0.18; Braineducational attainment GPS: β = 0.18), with the lowest effect size on fluid intelligence composite scores (Braincognitive performance GPS: β = 0.05; Braineducational attainment GPS: β= 0.05). Total intelligence composite score was moderately correlated with brain representations (Braincognitive performance GPS: β = 0.12; Braineducational attainment GPS: β = 0.12) (Supplementary Table 6). 

GPS-Intelligence Composite Score 

Both cognitive performance and educational attainment GPS significantly correlated with the outcomes of all three of the different types of intelligence measures (PFWE< 0.05). Crystallized intelligence showed the strongest association with both GPSs (cognitive performance GPS: β= 0.17; educational attainment GPS: β = 0.15), followed by total intelligence composite scores (cognitive performance GPS: β = 0.14; educational attainment GPS: β = 0.10) and the fluid intelligence composite score (cognitive performance GPS: β = 0.09; educational attainment GPS: β = 0.05) (Supplementary Table 6).

Mediation analyses of the GPS-brain-cognition pathway (Figure 3-A) showed that the brain morphometry significantly mediated the causal effect of both GPSs on cognitive intelligence (PFWE< 0.001). Deep Learning Integration of Genetic Risk and White Matter Imaging for Youth Depression Prediction

Jung Youn Min1, Heehwan Wang2, Yoonjung Yoonie Joo3,4, Bo-Gyeom Kim5, Gakyung Kim1, Eunji Lee5,Jiook Cha1,2,5,6 †

Affiliations

Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Department of Digital Health, Samsung Advanced Institute for Health Sciences & Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, Seoul, South Korea

 Samsung Genome Institute, Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

Department of Psychology, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Institute of Psychological Science, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

Correspondence to: 

Jiook Cha, Ph.D. 

Gwanak-ro 1, Building #16, Suite M512 

Gwanak-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea 

connectome@snu.ac.kr 

Keywords : Child Depression, Polygenic Risk Score, White matter, Track-weighted imaging (TWI), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Multi cohort validation

Abstract 

Although genetic factors play a critical role in early-onset depression, their integration into neuroimaging-based analyses and understanding of neuropathophysiology remains limited, constraining efforts for early detection and intervention. We introduce a novel deep learning framework that pretrains diffusion MRI models using polygenic risk scores (PGS) as an outcome, enabling the discovery of latent associations between genetic risk and white matter microstructure. Using a large multi-ethnic cohort (N = 5,248) and an independent Korean validation sample (N = 108), our PGS-pretrained 3D-CNN significantly improves cross-sectional (AUC = 0.62, F1 = 0.64) and longitudinal (AUC = 0.61–0.66) depression prediction, including suicidal behaviors. To enhance interpretability, we employ Explainable AI (Integrated Gradients + SmoothGrad), revealing that key white matter tracts—superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum, corticospinal tract, and corpus callosum—strongly contribute to depression risk. Compared to traditional models, our approach boosts predictive accuracy across diverse populations, with cross-ethnic generalization (AUC = 0.67, F1 = 0.61 in Korean youth). Furthermore, we demonstrate that PGS-based pretraining outperforms standard deep learning and machine learning models, underscoring the importance of integrating genetic and neuroimaging data for psychiatric risk prediction. These findings establish PGS-informed diffusion MRI modeling as a scalable and interpretable tool for early detection of youth depression, paving the way for precision psychiatry applications in diverse clinical settings.

Introduction 

Youth depression is an increasing global public health concern, with prevalence rates rising worldwide  [1, 2]. Affecting approximately 2-7% of youth populations, depression often begins in childhood or adolescence [3].  Depression starting in this period poses significant long-term challenges, including higher chronicity, elevatedrecurrence rates, and reduced responsiveness to treatments such as antidepressants and psychotherapy compared to adult-onset cases [4-6]. Moreover, it has been linked to heightened risks of adult anxiety, impaired social functioning and suicidality [7, 8]. These findings underscore the urgent need for early identification and targeted strategies to predict and mitigate depression in at-risk youth [9]. 

The biological underpinnings of depression are complex, involving both genetic predisposition and neurobiological factors. Youth-onset depression exhibits stronger genetic associations, including higher polygenic risk scores (PGS) and twin concordance compared to adult-onset cases [10-12]. Twin studies have consistently demonstrated the high heritability of youth depression [13, 14] with genetic factors significantly impacting its persistence and stability [11, 15, 16]. These genetic vulnerabilities interact strongly with neurobiological substrates, particularly white matter, which provides the structural basis for long-range neural connectivity [17-19]. Fractional Anisotropy (FA), derived from diffusion MRI (dMRI), serves as a key marker of white matter integrity and demonstrates high heritability, with genetic factors explaining up to 88% of its phenotypic variance [17, 20, 21]. Specific tracts, such as the corpus callosum, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, are strongly influenced by genetic factors, supporting the notion that white matter differences are under strong genetic control [19, 21]. 

Converging evidence from human and animal studies implicates disruptions in specific white matter tracts in the pathophysiology of depression. Studies in humans with depression have reported reduced FA in tracts including the corpus callosum, cingulum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus [22-25], with some findings linked to genetic risk for the disorder [26-29]. Consistent with these findings, animal models of depression show reduced FA in the corpus callosum and related tracts [30, 31]. Developmental alterations in white matter, particularly in the corpus callosum, fimbria, external capsule, and internal capsule, have also been observed [32]. These findings collectively underscore the critical role of white matter impairments in the pathophysiology of depression.

The interplay between genetic predispositions and white matter integrity provides a critical framework for understanding the biological basis of depression. Genetic overlap between dMRI parameters and depression has been demonstrated, including negative correlations with FA in the corpus callosum and links to serotonin transporter gene DNA methylation [20, 33]. Additionally, forebrain white matter-related dMRI metrics have been associated with single nucleotide polymorphisms in genes encoding proteins involved in extracellular matrix and epidermal growth factor signaling, which are critical for myelin repair and synaptic plasticity and closely linked to major depressive disorder (MDD) [18]. These findings suggest shared genetic mechanisms influencing both white matter integrity and depression susceptibility. 

Despite these advancements, critical gaps remain in our understanding of childhood depression. Many studies rely on either genetic or neuroimaging data, overlooking the complex interactions between these modalities [28, 34-36]. Research in other psychiatric disordershas consistently shown that integrating genetic and neuroimaging data through multi-modal approaches significantly enhances predictive accuracy compared to single-modality models [37-39]. Deep learning methodologies offer a promising avenue for multi-modal integration [40],  but faces challenges, particularly in smaller datasets often used in developmental psychiatric research [41, 42]. Optimized strategies are therefore needed to apply deep learning effectively in such contexts. 

Additionally, most existing studies in both neuroimaging and genetics have been conducted on predominantly Caucasian populations, leaving other ethnic groups underrepresented [43, 44]. Addressing this disparity is critical to developing globally applicable predictive models for depression. 

Our study addresses these challenges by utilizing deep learning to integrate genetic and white matter data from a large cohort of American children. By combining gene-brain features using pretraining and a multi-modal joint fusion strategy, we overcome limitations associated with small sample sizes and uncover latent associations between structural disruptions in white matter and depression risk. Three key experiments were conducted: (1) cross-sectional classification to differentiate individuals with and without depression, (2) prediction of depressive symptoms two years later in held-out sets and (3) validation of our model’s generalizability using an independent Korean dataset of young adolescents. These findings provide new insights into the applicability of predictive models across diverse populations. 

Materials and methods

Participants

We used participants from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study [45] (N=11,868), and a Korean cohort (N=180) recruited through research collaboration with Seoul National University and Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology. Following rigorous quality control and exclusion criteria, the final analysis included 5,248 ABCD participants and 108 Korean participants. Full inclusion/exclusion criteria and preprocessing details are provided in Supplementary Materials.

Track-weighted FA (TW-FA) Imaging Processing 

Track-weighted FA (TW-FA) was used as the input in all experiments. dMRI provides measures of brain macrostructure (e.g. volume(mm3), length(mm), area(mm2)) and microstructure (e.g. white matter integrity), non-invasively [46]. The processing was conducted using software based on the MRtrix3 package [47] especially using the command tckmap after general MRI quality assessment. TW-FA maps were formed as described previous studies [48, 49], so we will describe them briefly here. In summary, reference map (here, FA maps) values were computed at each point along the streamline. For each voxel, a Gaussian-weighted mean of the reference map values was determined within the neighborhood along individual fiber streamlines (yielding the track-wise statistic). The voxel intensity for the TWI map was then calculated as the average of these track-wise values across all tracts passing through the voxel, resulting in the voxel-wise statistic. We utilized full-width-half-maximums (FHWM) of 15mm for gaussian neighborhood weightings, which is known to be more sensitive to focal abnormalities [50]. The TW-FA framework applies directional smoothing to tractograms by assigning each streamline a weight derived from the average FA value along its path, effectively creating a track-informed version of the FA map [50, 51]. Both cohorts followed the sample protocol to process TW-FA.

Demographic and Behavioral Variables 

Psychiatric Variables of ABCD Cohort

For assessing the children’s life-time MDD and depressive symptoms, our analysis employed Kiddie-Structured Assessment for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for DSM-5 (KSADS-5) and Child Behavioral Checklist (CBCL), child-reported and parent reported respectively and self-administered. Computerized KSADS have been well validated from previous study showing good to high reliability (AUC 0.89-1.0) comparing against clinician administered [52]. For current analyses, we generated composite variable for lifetime history of MDD meeting criteria in present, past or remitted MDD based on child or parent report. We excluded participants who were taking anti-depressant medication and who met lifetime psychotic or neurodevelopmental disorder (e.g. autism spectrum disorder) diagnosis [53, 54]. For the health control, we included participants who met none of the diagnosis criteria in child nor parent report past or current time point and met healthy control criteria of CBCL (<60) from the baseline to 2-year follow-up. We utilized lifetime indicators of suicidal behavior (including suicidal active ideation and suicide attempts) based on KSADS diagnoses, derived from child and parent reports. The criteria for health controls were consistent with those described earlier. 

We generated depressive symptoms score based on previous study [55] using summated score from module1 of the KSADS symptoms assessment score as depressive disorder. The score included both child and care-giver reports. This score incorporated reports from both children and caregivers and was subsequently used as the outcome variable for generating composite polygenic risk scores. Detailed methods for composite PGS calculations are described in the Methods section 2.4.

In conclusion, 4741 participants for pretraining set, 266 propensity score matched using age, sex, study site participants were used for MDD baseline prediction fine-tune set. To statistically evaluate the 2-year follow-up zero-shot prediction performance, we utilized 118 individuals with MDD symptoms at the 2-year follow-up and matched them with healthy controls randomly sampled from participants not included in either the pretrained or finetune sets. This matching process was repeated 10 times to ensure robustness through different samples, which leads to 10 datasets of 236 participants. For suicidal behavior we used same strategy, resulting in 10 datasets of 116 participants with MDD and Suicidal active ideation at the 2-year follow-up and 30 participants with MDD and Suicidal Attempt. However, we ensured that none of the participants overlapped with pretraining nor finetune sets.

Psychiatric Variables of Korean Cohort

	Validated Korean translations of depression measures were used to classify participants. Depression was assessed using the child-reported CES-D [56] and parent-reported CBCL [57]. Based on prior meta-analyses, a CES-D cut-off of ≥21, which accounts for gender and racial variations [58, 59], was chosen to align with ABCD study criteria. The depressed group included individuals with CES-D ≥21, while the healthy group had CES-D <16 and CBCL total problems T-scores <60. The final sample consisted of 108 participants (41 depressed, 67 healthy). For deep learning, data were split into 10-folds using iterative stratification by age, sex, and CES-D score, followed by propensity score matching for validation and test sets.

Genetic Data Preprocessing 

 In this study, we used polygenic risk scores (PGS), which were previously calculated and validated in [60], where a detailed description of the methodology is provided. Here, we briefly summarize the key aspects of the methodology. The PGS were calculated using PLINK version 1.9 and the parameters were optimized in PRS-CSx. According to previous study, multi-ethnic PGS showed improved accuracy in diseases risk prediction by combining transethnic information [61]. Since our study focused on childhood depression in the population of multi-ethnicity, we utilized PGS scores generated with multi-ethnic panel using publicly available Genome Wide Association Study statistics of multi-ethnicity population. PGS related to depression, BMI, post-traumatic stress disorder, Alcohol Dependency and Schizophrenia were included. 

	We included composite PGS in our analysis, guided by prior research. Previous studies have demonstrated the advantages of composite polygenic risk scores in enhancing risk stratification [62, 63]. Building on these findings, we adopted a composite PGS approach in our analysis. To address multicollinearity, we employed ElasticNet, a robust regularization technique. Composite scores were constructed from PRS derived using five multi-ethnicity panels, with a stepwise elimination process to optimize R² while minimizing the number of independent variables. This procedure was performed exclusively within the pretraining set, and model fitting was conducted across 5,000 resampled train-test splits to ensure robust and stable estimation. We ensured that none of the participants in pretraining sets overlapped with finetune or prediction sets.

 Model Optimization and Evaluation 

Deep Neural Network Training 

	We implemented a 3DCNN model with densenet3D121 as the backbone architecture across all our experiments. The model consists of an initial 3D convolutional module, four 3D dense-blocks, three 3D Transition layers and one fully connected classifier for each task. In the field of medical imaging, prior studies have demonstrated the superior performance of densenet3D121 model compared to traditional CNNs in tasks such as brain tumor classification [64], and Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis [65]. Also, we conducted experiments using a model where each participant's PGS score was directly incorporated. This was done by adding the PGS score before passing through the fully connected layer of the 3DCNN model, followed by processing through a multilayer perceptron layer (3DCNN+MLP). We optimized the model with Mean Squared Error loss for regression tasks and Cross Entropy for the classification tasks. Minimal augmentation was applied, including resizing images to 128x128x128, Random Rotation by 90 degrees (probability=0.5), Random Axis Flip (probability=0.5), and Random Affine Transform (probability=0.5). The deep neural networks were optimized using the AdamW optimizer with a cosine learning rate decay scheduler and a linear warm-up. Additionally, we implemented early stopping with a patience window of 30 epochs to prevent overfitting on the training data. 

We employed two types of comparison models to evaluate our approach. The first set of comparison models focused on modality: an MLP model using only PGS, a 3DCNN model using only TW-FA, and a from-scratch 3DCNN+MLP model trained directly on both PGS and TW-FA without any pretraining. The second set of comparison models included traditional machine learning models: support vector machine with a linear kernel (SVC_linear), support vector machine with an RBF kernel (SVC_rbf), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBOOST) using structural connectivity and PGS as their inputs. All experiments were conducted using 10-fold cross-validation, ensuring that the same training, validation, and test folds were used consistently across all experiments. Details on the training parameters for cross-sectional and 2-year follow-up MDD prediction, along with transfer learning, are available in the Supplementary Materials.

Explainable AI 

To identify brain regions contributing most to the model’s predictions, we employed explainable AI (XAI) techniques, specifically Integrated Gradients [66] combined with SmoothGrad [67]. Integrated Gradients generates saliency maps by integrating the gradients of the model's predictions with respect to the input features, providing a measure of each voxel’s contribution. SmoothGrad enhances this approach by adding Gaussian noise (σ = 0.05) to input images within brain regions, generating 50 noise-augmented images per participant and averaging their resulting saliency maps. This method was implemented using the Captum library (version 0.6.0).

To align our findings with prior research, we performed tract-level analyses and identified key tracts containing voxels that significantly contributed to depression classification and prediction. We analyzed only the voxels with statistically significant XAI attribute values between the control and depressed groups. We conducted voxel-wise t-tests with FDR multiple corrections and applied a cluster-based threshold to identify statistically significant regions. Then we calculated the proportion of significant voxels for each tract, by dividing the total number of significant voxels by the total voxels in the tract. This allowed us to determine the positive and negative associations of each tract in the depression classification task.

Results 

We analyzed data from 5,248 participants in the ABCD dataset, all meeting strict quality criteria for dMRI and genetic data availability. The dataset was divided into three groups: a Pretrain set (N=4,741), a Baseline Finetune set (N=266), and 2-Year Follow-up MDD Prediction sets (N=236), 2-Year Follow-up MDD & Suicidal Ideation Active sets (N=116) and 2-Year Follow-up MDD & Suicidal Attempt sets (N=30). To rigorously assess model performance, we generated 10 matched datasets for each 2-year outcome group, selecting diverse controls to evaluate statistical robustness. Demographics are detailed in Supplementary Materials (Table S1). To minimize selection bias, we used propensity score matching on age, biological sex, and ABCD site when creating finetune subsets. All the statistics of model comparisons are detailed in Supplementary Materials.
