Abstract 

Childhood brain development involves dynamic remodeling shaped by genetic influences contributing to long-term neurodevelopmental variation. Here we report integrative analyses of over 8,600 children, using 7 brain imaging-derived phenotype (IDP) modalities, polygenic scores (PGS) of 33 complex traits, and 266 cognitive and psychological phenotypes. Most brain IDPs show low-to-moderate SNP-based heritability, lower than typically observed in adults. Sparse generalized canonical correlation analysis reveals positive associations between cognitive-related PGS and structural MRI features (e.g., total grey matter and ventral diencephalon volumes) and N-back task-related activation, while PGS for ADHD, depression, and neuroticism showed negative associations. Cognitive PGS also correlates positively with diffusion MRI metrics (streamline counts, fractional anisotropy in subcortical-frontal tracts and inferior parietal–subcortical tracts), whereas health-risk PGS (e.g., BMI, ADHD) correlates negatively. This study delineates key gene–brain–behavior associations in preadolescence, providing a multivariate dissection of the polygenic architecture underlying neurodevelopment.

Introduction

Preadolescent childhood is a critical developmental period characterized by substantial neurobiological changes. During this period, white matter volume increases substantially, and grey matter undergoes region-specific growth, peaking in the frontal and parietal lobes1,2. This dynamic interplay between genetics and environment not only shapes the maturing brain but also shapes the course of cognitive abilities and mental wellness in later life. Studies show that genetic factors play a pivotal role in these developmental processes, with neural and genetic markers of psychiatric vulnerability potentially present at this early stage, prior to the onset of behavioral symptoms3-5.

Cognitive functions and psychiatric disorders share common genetic and neurological roots6. The heritability of cognitive and psychological traits generally increases with age. For instance, genetics accounts for less than 25% of the variability in cognition in infancy, but up to 70% in adolescence7. Similarly, the heritability of various psychopathologies, including externalizing behaviors, depression, and anxiety, also appears to rise with age8. This evolving genetic influence may be attributed to developmental changes in gene expression or neuroanatomical alterations that render the brain more susceptible or resistant to genetic and environmental inputs at different life stages9. Given these substantial genetic influences, elucidating the genetic basis of neural and cognitive development is imperative to advance our understanding of the neurobiological foundations of cognition and psychopathology.

The joint analysis of multimodal genetic and brain imaging data could offer valuable insights into the relationships between genetic variation and brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs), and their relationship to cognitive and behavioral processes. Advances in high-throughput data generation have made computational approaches linking genetics and neuroimaging central to biological systems research. Identifying brain structures or functions associated with polygenic signals may improve our understanding of their biological relevance to cognitive and psychological development. However, existing studies have often overlooked the developmental stage of preadolescence10. While prior works have demonstrated significant connections between the brain and genomic components11,12, no studies have yet examined the polygenic influences on specific brain IDPs and behavioral outcomes during preadolescence. 

We depart from traditional analyses to employ sparse generalized canonical correlation analysis (SGCCA)13,14, an advanced multivariate technique optimized for high-dimensional data characteristic of neuroimaging and genetic datasets. SGCCA achieves this by enforcing sparsity through penalization, effectively reducing the feature space by assigning zero weights to less relevant variables while retaining the most informative ones. This ensures that key genetic variants or brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) are prioritized, thereby enhancing interpretability. Moreover, SGCCA introduces regional specificity by focusing on distinct brain regions or networks of interest, addressing a critical limitation of earlier canonical correlation analysis methods, which often lacked the capacity to capture localized patterns in IDPs10-12,15.

In this work, we utilize a comprehensive suite of polygenic scores (PGS) across a diverse range of 33 behavioral, cognitive, and psychological traits to test the functional genetic associations with brain IDPs and behavioral phenotypes, which could provide interpretable and informative insights into trait variability. Also, this methodology contrasts with prior studies that relied on a narrow spectrum of PGS and could not capture the full genetic architecture influencing trait development11. With the novel application of this multivariate method to the genetic and brain imaging data, we aimed to reveal the interconnected variations of genetic signals, the brain, and cognitive and psychological outcomes in the preadolescent brain. Our estimates of genetic heritability for multimodal brain features set the stage for SGCCA, enabling us to explore the covariation between IDPs and polygenic scores across traits, potentially transforming our comprehension of the genetic orchestration of brain, cognitive, and behavioral development.

Results

Participants 

From the initial cohort of 11,875 participants in the ABCD study, 6,555 European-ancestry participants passed quality control (QC) for brain imaging and genetic data and were included in the analysis (8,620 multi-ancestry participants for exploratory analysis) (Table 1). We compared the estimated Ps between European-ancestry and non-European-ancestry individuals, and PGS showed no significant differences across ancestries except for the educational attainment (P = 0.006) and IQ PGS (P = 0.0018) (Supplementary Data 4). 

SNP-Based Heritability

We quantified the heritability of brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) and psychological measures using imputed autosomal SNPs. Out of 7,963 IDPs tested in 6,555 children of European ancestry, 1,237 showed significant heritability, ranging from 19% to 27% (Figure 1A, Table 2). The average heritability for brain IDPs (23%) was higher than for non-brain measures (19%) (Figure 1C). Structural MRI IDPs accounted for the largest proportion of heritable traits (63.2%), followed by diffusion MRI measures such as fractional anisotropy (33.9%), diffusion count (14.1%), and task-based fMRI measures (2.7%–4.1%). Resting-state fMRI (3.4%) and SST fMRI (0.8%) showed the lowest proportions of heritable IDPs.

Within structural MRI, cortical volume exhibited the highest heritability (27%), while curvature showed the lowest (22%). Structural MRI IDPs also displayed higher heritability than diffusion MRI IDPs (19%–22%), suggesting greater genetic influence on grey matter compared to white matter in this age group. This pattern contrasts with findings from adult datasets, such as the UK Biobank8, where white matter heritability typically exceeds that of grey matter. Task-based fMRI traits showed moderate heritability, with estimates of 25% for SST, 24% for N-back, and 22% for MID.

Neurocognition related phenotypes exhibited the highest heritability among psychological measures, averaging 29% (Figure 1B). Key traits with heritability exceeding 30% included the Flanker Inhibitory Control Test, Oral Reading Recognition, and Total Intelligence Composite Score. Behavioral measures, including externalizing problems and anxious or depressed behaviors, showed significant heritability, averaging 16%–18%. Specific traits such as Anxious/Depressed Syndrome Scale, rule-breaking behavior and externalizing problems exceeded 20%. Mental health conditions, including generalized anxiety disorder, eating disorders, and suicidal behaviors, also displayed significant heritability.

Bivariate Association of PGS with Cognitive, Behavioral, and Psychological Outcomes 

Bivariate correlation of PGS with Cognitive, Behavioral, and Psychological Outcomes were tested. Cognitive-related PGS (e.g., cognitive performance, IQ) showed strong effects, explaining up to 18% of variance in crystalized intelligence scores (β = 0.286, P<0.0001). BMI PGS accounted for 13% of BMI variance (β = 0.299, P<0.0001), while PGS for ADHD, depression, and PTSD explained up to 3% of their respective traits. Notably, PGS for brain volume exhibited weaker associations (e.g., Total Brain Volume PGS R² =2.8%). Detailed results, including findings for multi-ancestry samples, are available in Supplementary Data 5 and Supplementary Information.

Bivariate Correlation between PGS and Brain IDPs

Significant associations between 33 PGS and brain IDPs were mainly found in structural metrics, such as morphometric measures and dMRI (streamline count, FA) (P < 0.049; FDR correction) and N-back fMRI (P < 0.495; FDR correction) (Supplementary Data 6). Total brain volume PGS and cognitive-related PGS (e.g., cognitive performance, IQ) were linked to widespread brain regions. Except for N-back fMRI, functional metrics (e.g., resting-state fMRI) showed no significant associations, highlighting the stability of structural measures in detecting genetic influences. Advanced multivariate methods like CCA are recommended to capture complex genetic-brain relationships and provide deeper insights into cognition and behavior.

Multivariate associations among PGS, Phenotypes, and Brain IDPs 

Multivariate associations among PGS, brain IDPs, and behavioral phenotypes were analyzed using SGCCA. Significant covariation patterns were observed between PGS and brain phenotypes, particularly structural MRI (component (comp) 1, 2, 4 and 5), diffusion MRI (streamline count, comp 1, 2, 3 and 5; FA, comp 1), and N-back task-based fMRI (comp 1). Resting-state and other task-based fMRI modalities showed fewer significant components. Triadic relationships explored through 3-block SGCCA revealed consistent positive loadings for cognitive-related PGS (e.g., educational attainment, IQ) and negative loadings for PGS linked to behavioral and mental health risks (e.g., depression, ADHD). These findings highlight the genetic underpinnings linking cognitive and psychopathological traits with neural phenotypes. Full results are provided in Supplementary Data 10 and 11 and Supplementary Information.

Brain Morphometry (sMRI)  

We explored the covariation patterns between PGS, brain morphometric data (sMRI), and behavioral phenotypes using 2-block and 3-block CCA analyses. In the 2-block CCA, four significant components were identified, with Component 1 showing the strongest association between cognitive-related PGS (e.g., IQ, educational attainment) and increased brain volumes and surface areas. Other components highlighted tissue-specific genetic influences, including a white-grey matter dichotomy and distinct associations between risk-related PGS and brain shape metrics (e.g., curvature, thickness). In the 3-block CCA, cognitive-related PGS were linked to positive cognitive outcomes and brain morphometry, while risk-related PGS were negatively associated with behavioral and health variables. Full details, including component loadings and detailed metrics, are provided in Supplementary Data 12, Supplementary Data 13, and Supplementary Information.

Diffusion MRI (dMRI)

Streamline Count

We investigated the covariation patterns between PGS, streamline count, and behavioral phenotypes using 2-block and 30block CCA analyses. In the 2-block CCA, we identified four significant components. Component 1 linked cognitive-related PGS (e.g., IQ, educational attainment) to streamline counts in subcortical and frontal regions. Component 2 revealed opposing genetic influences, with white matter volume positively associated with motor-sensory connectivity, while mental health risk PGS were inversely associated with frontal-temporal connectivity. Components 3 and 5 highlighted associations with physical health and well-being, emphasizing distinct connectivity patterns in subcortical and temporal regions. The 3-block CCA analysis extended these findings, linking cognitive-related PGS to posterior cingulate cortex pathways and crystallized intelligence scores. Full results are provided in Supplementary Data 14, Supplementary Data 15, and Supplementary Information.

Fractional Anisotropy (FA)

In the 2-block PGS-dMRI fractional anisotropy (FA) CCA identified only one significant component of covariation. In particular, cognitive-related PGS (e.g., educational attainment, IQ) were positively associated with FA connectivity patterns involving the inferior parietal gyrus (IPG) and subcortical regions, while health-related PGS (e.g., BMI, ADHD) exhibited negative loadings. In the 3-block CCA, IPG-centered FA pathways were strongly linked to cognitive-related PGS and performance measures, such as crystallized intelligence, while health and behavioral traits showed inverse associations. Full results, including loadings and detailed connectivity patterns, are available in Supplementary Data 16, Supplementary Data 17, and Supplementary Information.

Resting-state fMRI 

Two significant components of covariation between PGS and rsfMRI data were identified in the 2-block CCA. Component 1 linked cognitive-related PGS (e.g., IQ, educational attainment) to connectivity patterns in retrosplenial-temporal, auditory, and cingulo-opercular networks, while mental health-related PGS (e.g., depression, neuroticism) showed negative associations. Component 2 revealed modest associations with eating disorder PGS and negative correlations with subjective wellbeing traits. The 3-block CCA extended these findings, linking cognitive-related PGS and rsfMRI connectivity to cognitive performance and favorable environmental factors, while mental health and behavioral risks negatively influenced these associations. Full results, including connectivity patterns, are provided in Supplementary Data 18, Supplementary Data 19, and Supplementary Information.

Task-based fMRI

In the 2-block CCA analysis, only N-back task-based fMRI yielded a significant component, while the 3-block CCA revealed significant associations across all task-based modalities (N-back, MID, SST). These significant associations linked cognitive-related PGS (e.g., IQ, cognitive performance) to activation patterns in key brain regions and behavioral phenotypes. N-back fMRI highlighted cognitive performance and emotional stability, while MID and SST tasks revealed associations with reward processing and inhibitory control, respectively. Behavioral challenges and adverse environmental factors were inversely linked to task-based activation patterns. Full results, including brain-behavior relationships, are detailed in Supplementary Data 20, Supplementary Data 21, Supplementary Data 22, and Supplementary Information.

Phenotypes

The 2-block CCA identified four significant components linking PGS to behavioral phenotypes. Component 1 associated cognitive-related PGS (e.g., IQ, cognitive performance) with neurocognitive strengths and socioeconomic advantages but inversely with behavioral challenges. Component 2 linked risk-related PGS to elevated behavioral symptoms, while Component 4 focused on physical traits (e.g., height) and emotional traits. Component 5 reflected cognitive and physical PGS alongside socioeconomic and behavioral risks. These results emphasize the intricate interplay between genetic predispositions, behavioral phenotypes, and environmental influences. Full results are provided in Supplementary Data 23 and Supplementary Information.

Predictive performance of the PGS-based models

We evaluated machine learning models incorporating genomic polygenic scores (PGS) to predict mental health outcomes. PGS-based models demonstrated statistically significant improvements in predictive performance for several outcomes when compared to covariate-only models (Figure 6 and Supplementary Information).

Discussion

In this study, we leveraged genetics, multimodal brain imaging, and detailed environmental and behavioral data from a large cohort of preadolescent children to investigate the multivariate relationships underlying neurodevelopment. Using genome-wide polygenic scores (PGS) and canonical correlation analyses (CCA), we identified three key findings. First, SNP-based heritability analyses revealed significant genetic contributions to both brain and behavioral phenotypes, with brain phenotypes exhibiting higher heritability than behavioral traits, underscoring the genetic basis of neurodevelopmental trajectories. Second, integrative analyses with SGCCA linked PGS for educational attainment and IQ to robust positive associations across multiple brain imaging modalities, including structural MRI (sMRI), diffusion MRI (dMRI), and task-based fMRI, while PGS for depression, neuroticism, and BMI showed consistent negative associations. These patterns highlight the interconnected genetic influences shaping cognitive abilities and mental health during development. Third, machine learning models trained on the 33 PGS demonstrated moderate to robust prediction of cognitive outcomes but showed lower performance for psychopathologies.

Our heritability analysis identified numerous brain IDPs in preadolescent children that exhibit significant genetic associations with different neuroimaging modalities. While these findings align with prior studies in adults that demonstrate substantial genetic contributions to cortical, subcortical regions, and functional connectivity16-18, they also revealed developmental distinctions. Specifically, the heritability of brain structure and function appeared lower in children compared to adults, suggesting that genetic influences on neurodevelopment are dynamic and evolve with age, potentially due to increasing gene-environment interactions during maturation19,20. Application of multimodal deep learning in identifying autism spectrum disorder in children with global developmental delay

Jubin Choi BSca; Miri Suh MDb; Danny Dongyeop Han BSca; Jundong Hwang MEngc; Jong-Hwan Lee PhDc; MinYoung Kim MD, PhDb*; Jiook Cha PhDd,e,f*

a Interdisciplinary Program of Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea

b Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, CHA Bundang Medical Center, CHA University School of Medicine, Seongnam, Korea

c Department of Brain and Cognitive Engineering, Korea University, Seoul, Korea

d Department of Psychology, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea

e Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea

f AI Institute, Seoul National University, Seoul, Korea

*Correspondence: Jiook Cha (connectome@snu.ac.kr), Gwanak-ro 1, Gwanak-gu, Seoul, 08826, South Korea

ABSTRACT

The early differentiation of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), a condition of impaired social communication and restrictive behaviors, from Global Developmental Delay (GDD), defined by significant delays across multiple developmental milestones, is essential for guiding effective interventions but is often difficult in young children. To address this clinical need, we aimed to develop and evaluate deep learning models using multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to objectively distinguish between these conditions. We retrospectively analyzed T1-weighted and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data from 357 children (79 ASD, 278 GDD). To ensure a robust and unbiased evaluation, we implemented a rigorous framework featuring a nested cross-validation design with propensity score matching to control for confounders like sex and age. Multimodal deep learning architectures were trained to classify diagnoses. The models achieved moderate performance, with a multi-channel model utilizing all DTI metrics demonstrating the strongest predictive power. This model yielded a mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) of 0.648 and an accuracy of 57.1% on balanced test sets. Importantly, statistically validated saliency maps revealed that classifications were driven by interpretable neurobiological differences. These were primarily found in the microstructure of white matter tracts crucial for motor, sensory, and interhemispheric functions, and notably, also by variations in the mean diffusivity of cortical gray matter. While performance requires refinement for clinical application, this study validates a methodologically rigorous approach and underscores the potential of interpretable deep learning to enhance early diagnosis, ultimately leading to more personalized interventions for children with complex developmental disorders.

Keywords: Autism Spectrum Disorder, Global Developmental Delay, Multimodal Deep Learning, Neuroimaging, T1 weighted image, Diffusion Tensor Imaging, Explainable Artificial Intelligence

Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by deficits in social communication skills and restrictive, repetitive behaviors [1]. The global prevalence of ASD, currently about 1%, continues to rise worldwide [2]. Early diagnosis of ASD is crucial for timely intervention and improved outcomes. However, distinguishing ASD from other developmental disorders, including global developmental delay (GDD), remains a significant challenge, particularly in young children. GDD is defined as a delay in reaching developmental milestones across motor, speech, language, cognition, social functioning, and activities of daily living in children under five [1]. The co-occurrence of ASD in children with GDD is notably high, with estimates suggesting a prevalence of over 50% [3-5]. This distinction is critical because early intervention for ASD during key developmental periods is associated with improved long-term outcomes [6].

Recent advances in neuroimaging have provided valuable insights into the structural and functional abnormalities associated with ASD. Studies using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have reported increased total cerebral white and gray matter volumes in young children with ASD [7-9]. Additionally, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies have identified microstructural differences in brain connectivity, which are critical in understanding ASD's neurobiological underpinnings [10-12]. 

However, research comparing neuroanatomical differences between children with ASD and those with developmental delays (DD) has yielded contradictory results. For instance, an early study found no significant differences in brain volumes between children with ASD and those with DD in the 2-7 year age range [13]. In contrast, a later study reported that children with ASD exhibited larger gray and white matter volumes, higher fractional anisotropy (FA), and lower mean diffusivity (MD) in certain brain regions compared to those with DD [14]. Given these contradictory findings, there is a clear gap in our understanding of the neurobiological distinctions between ASD and GDD in young children.

Moreover, a study focusing on toddlers at high familial risk for ASD has demonstrated that the ASD group exhibited higher growth rates of total brain volume, surface area, and cortical thickness compared to controls [9]. These findings suggest that neuroanatomical markers may vary significantly with age, highlighting the need for age-specific diagnostic criteria and the consideration of developmental trajectories in research.

To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel framework built on three key methodological advances. First, we employ multimodal deep learning to integrate structural (T1-weighted) and microstructural (DTI) data. This allows the model to learn from complementary information sources—anatomical shape and white matter connectivity—to capture a more holistic neurobiological signature than any single modality can provide. Second, to address the influence of confounders, we implement a rigorous sampling method using propensity score matching within a nested cross-validation design. This forces the model to identify true pathological differences rather than learning demographic biases related to age or developmental level. Finally, to ensure clinical relevance and transparency, we use Explainable AI (XAI) methods. By generating statistically significant MRI saliency maps, we can visualize which brain regions drive the model's predictions, moving beyond a "black box" to discover scientifically valid and interpretable biomarkers.

Therefore, this research aims to develop and rigorously validate a multimodal deep learning model for differentiating ASD and GDD. By leveraging this advanced analytical framework, we seek to identify reliable and interpretable neuroimaging biomarkers that could lead to more objective diagnostic tools and facilitate earlier, targeted interventions for these young patients.

METHODS

Participants

This study analyzed clinical registry data from 362 children at the CHA Bundang Medical Center, Seongnam, South Korea. The cohort included participants diagnosed with ASD or GDD who underwent brain MRI scans in the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine between August 2010 and October 2021. Clinicians with over five years of experience used the Childhood Autism Rating Scale or the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-IV and V for ASD diagnoses. GDD was identified by significant delays in two or more developmental domains including gross/fine motor, speech/language, cognition, social/personal behavior, and activities of daily living. We employed Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID)-II and BSID-III [15], Sequenced Language Scale for Infants, Preschool Receptive-Expressive Language Scale, Receptive and Expressive Vocabulary Test, Beery-Buktenica developmental test of visual-motor integration, Child Behavior Checklist, and Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory to detect those under two standard deviations in standardized measurements. Participants with poor-quality data were excluded from this study.

 Data acquisition and preprocessing

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

We utilized structural (T1-weighted) and diffusion (DTI) imaging to provide a comprehensive view of neuroanatomical and microstructural characteristics associated with pediatric ASD. T1-weighted MRI and DTI scans were acquired on a 3T GE Signa HDxt scanner. The enhanced fast gradient echo 3D sequence, the fast spoiled gradient echo brain volume sequence, and the T1-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequence in the axial plane were used for T1-weighted MRI. The single-spin echo planar imaging sequence was used to acquire DTI. Infant FreeSurfer [16] was used for T1w MRI preprocessing. MRtrix 3.0.4 [17] and FMRIB Software Library (FSL) [18] were used for DTI preprocessing. Four DTI metrics were used: FA, MD, radial diffusivity (RD), and axial diffusivity (AD). Further details regarding MRI acquisition, preprocessing, and quality control are provided in the Method S1.

Medical Records

Demographic (sex, age) and diagnostic variables, including functional measurement scores, were acquired for each participant. The Data Review Board of Bundang CHA Medical Center approved this process.

 Analytic plan

Cross-validation

To enhance the robustness and generalizability of our findings, we employed a nested cross-validation approach combined with propensity score matching (Figure 1A). To control for confounders between the ASD and GDD groups, propensity score matching was applied to the test set in outer cross-validation loops, isolating the effect of confounders (sex, age, and BSID developmental quotients) using PsmPy [19]. By doing so, we evaluated the model’s performance, ensuring it was unbiased for covariates, similar to confounder-isolated cross-validation [20]. Iterative stratification with multi-label metadata [21] was also used to ensure a balanced distribution of confounders across folds in training and validation sets. Missing data for BSID diagnoses were imputed using linear regression based on sex and age.

An additional experiment was conducted with a test set of 38 children including 7 with ASD and 15 with GDD who had pre-diagnostic MRI scans (>30 days before diagnosis).

Model architecture

A 3D DenseNet [22] architecture, a type of 3-dimensional deep neural network, served as the baseline model. We developed three model types: unimodal models using a single image modality (T1w, FA, MD, RD, or AD) and a single encoder, multi-channel models using all DTI metrics or a T1w image combined with DTI metrics (T1w+FA, T1w+MD, T1w+RD, T1w+AD, T1w+all DTI metrics) with a single encoder using multimodal data stacked in the channel dimension, and multi-fusion models using a T1w with DTI metrics and employing two encoders (one for each modality) excluding the last fully connected layer (Figure 1B). Features from each encoder were used for embedding alignment (L2 loss) and classification (cross-entropy loss). In total, 16 model types were investigated.

Training and evaluating model

Due to class imbalance, both the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and average precision (AP) were used as model selection metrics. Hyperparameters were searched using one outer cross-validation loop and then applied to each model type in the remaining outer loops. Test performance for each outer loop was averaged using the four models from the inner loops. Overall test performance was calculated as the average of all outer loops.

During hyperparameter tuning, we compared performances using the validation set in the inner loop. We performed a grid search that included three learning rates (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4) and three weight decays (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4) of an optimizer. We trained models for a maximum of 400 epochs with early stopping, a batch size of 16, AdamW optimizer, and a cosine annealing warm-up restarts learning rate scheduler. For the unimodal and multi-channel models, we employed weighted cross-entropy loss to amplify the loss from the minority class, which is ASD. 

To reduce computational overhead, we cropped and resized each image. First, we cropped the background of each image (originally 256x256x256, 1mm voxel size) using the brain as a boundary. Next, we zero-padded all images to match the maximum brain size of 206x206x206. Lastly, we resized the images to 138x138x138 so that the images would have an approximate voxel size of 1.5mm. We randomly augmented each image with rotations between 0 and 30 degrees and translations up to ten voxels along all axes with a 50% probability. We scaled all voxel values of each image to a range between 0 and 1 using min-max scaling.

Model interpretation with mean saliency maps

Saliency maps provide an interpretable visualization of model predictions, which is crucial for clinical and neurological translation, ensuring the models are not black boxes and can be used reliably in a clinical setting. To investigate which brain areas contributed most to the model’s prediction, we first generated five individual saliency maps for each input image from the best-performing models using Integrated Gradients [23] and averaged them using SmoothGrad [24] to reduce noise. 

A multi-step warping and transformation process was then implemented to analyze these maps in a common anatomical space (Figure 2). The initial saliency maps were generated at the resolution of the model's input (cropped, resized, and padded to a 1.5mm voxel size). Therefore, we applied a series of inverse transformations to these maps to ensure precise alignment with the original MRI orientation and resolution in native space.

Next, non-linear warping was used to transform each subject's native-space MRI and its corresponding saliency map into the MNI infant brain atlas space (for ages 33-44 months) [25]. To facilitate anatomical localization of our findings, the HCP 1065 Population-Averaged Tractography Atlas [26] was also warped from the standard MNI-152 adult space into the same infant MNI atlas space.

To create mean saliency maps, each map was separated into positive and negative values, scaled respectively (0 to 1, 0 to -1), and combined into one. After min-max scaling, we averaged the maps of correctly predicted subjects. To identify statistically significant voxels in the mean saliency map, we applied AFNI 3dttest++ to saliency maps for a 1-sample t-test [27, 28] and used only those voxels for further analysis.

Finally, we calculated two metrics to find important white matter tracts in the saliency maps. Peak Saliency Voxel Percentage is the proportion of the top 1,000 peak saliency voxels that fall within each tract. Tract Overlap Percentage is the proportion of the top 10,000 saliency voxels in the mean saliency map that overlap with each tract. These metrics were calculated separately for positive and negative saliency values to account for the directional contribution to the model’s prediction. 

Latent feature analysis

We estimated correlations between confounders (sex, age, BSID mental/motor developmental quotients) and output features extracted from the model using distance correlation [29]. Distance correlation is a metric for multivariate independence for random vectors of any arbitrary dimensions [30]. Additionally, we used Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) for dimension reduction and visualization of the output features [31]. 

RESULTS

Demographic characteristics of participants

Our final study cohort comprised 357 children (79 with ASD, 278 with GDD). The groups differed significantly in age at MRI scan and BSID-II Mental developmental quotients (Table S1 and Table S2). Most children underwent MRI on the day of their diagnosis; however, some had pre-diagnostic scans, allowing us to assess the model’s predictive ability using data obtained before formal diagnosis (Figure S1).

Prediction performance

Our multi-channel model incorporating all DTI metrics demonstrated the strongest predictive performance. When evaluated on the balanced test sets created via propensity score matching, this model achieved a mean accuracy of 57.1% (CI 95%: 54.2%-60.0%) and a mean AUROC of 0.648 (95% CI: 0.626-0.669) as shown in Figure 3.

In a separate analysis that classified prognostic ASD diagnoses from GDD using early MRI scans, the multi-channel model using all DTI metrics achieved the highest accuracy of 63.2% and AUROC of 0.615. This included the correct classification of 4 out of 7 children with ASD (ages 12-50 months) and 11 out of 15 with GDD (ages 7-104 months), demonstrating the model's ability to differentiate between ASD and GDD using pre-diagnostic DTI data (Table 1).

Table 1. Average test evaluation metrics of models. All models are evaluated on the balanced test set using propensity score matching and nested cross-validation. Bold text indicates the best model in all results and underlined text indicates the best model in each strategy. Abbreviations: AUROC - area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; AP - average precision; T1w - T1-weighted image; FA - fractional anisotropy; MD - mean diffusivity; RD - radial diffusivity; AD - axial diffusivity; DTI - diffusion tensor imaging.

Model interpretation

Saliency map analysis of the best-performing multi-channel model revealed that white matter tract integrity, especially FA was crucial in differentiating between ASD and GDD. High positive saliency values were observed in corticospinal, corticopontine, corticobulbar, and dentatorubrothalamic tracts, indicating higher voxel values increased the probability of predicting ASD (Figure 4, Figure S2). Conversely, low negative saliency values were observed in the anterior corpus callosum, anterior corticostriatal tract, anterior thalamic radiation, uncinate fasciculus, and right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. Additionally, microstructural differences in both white matter (e.g., middle cerebellar peduncle) and cortical gray matter (e.g., areas within the prefrontal cortex and temporal lobe) contributed to the model’s predictions.

UMAP visualizations of the latent features from the best two models suggest that the age of the subjects may not directly influence the classification criteria (Figure 5). Furthermore, Table 4 shows that distance correlation analysis indicated minimal correlation between the model’s predictions and potential confounders (0.033 for age, 0.079 for sex, and less than 0.001 for developmental quotients). These results indicate that our model effectively identified brain-based features distinguishing ASD from GDD independently of these factors.

Table 4. Distance correlation of confounders with latent features from the best two models. Abbreviations: DTI - Diffusion Tensor Imaging; T1w – T1-weighted image; FA - Fractional Anisotropy; ASD – autism spectrum disorder; GDD – global developmental delay; BSID - Bayley Scales of Infant Development.

Discussion

This study is the first to apply multimodal deep learning models to differentiate between ASD and GDD using T1-weighted MRI and DTI data. Analyzing data from 357 children, we found that models utilizing multiple DTI measures demonstrated the most effective diagnostic capabilities, yielding AUROC ranging from 0.61 to 0.68. Furthermore, in classifying prognostic ASD diagnoses from GDD using earlier MRI scans (taken when ASD subjects were 12 to 50 months old), our model showed a modest predictive accuracy of 63.2% and an AUROC of 0.615. These results highlight the potential of deep learning in aiding early diagnosis of ASD in children with GDD.

Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for children with developmental disorders, underscoring the need for developing diagnostic assistance tools to help physicians distinguish between ASD and GDD and enable more targeted treatments. Title: Polygenic Risk-Informed White Matter Imaging Improves Deep learning -Based Depression Prediction in Youth

Jung Youn Min1, Heehwan Wang2, Yoonjung Yoonie Joo3,4, Bo-Gyeom Kim5, Gakyung Kim1, Eunji Lee5,Jiook Cha1,2,5,6 †

Affiliations

Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Department of Digital Health, Samsung Advanced Institute for Health Sciences & Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, Seoul, South Korea

 Samsung Genome Institute, Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea

Department of Psychology, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea

Institute of Psychological Science, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

Correspondence to: 

Jiook Cha, Ph.D. 

Gwanak-ro 1, Building #16, Suite M512 

Gwanak-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea 

connectome@snu.ac.kr 

Keywords : Child Depression, Polygenic Risk Score, White matter, Track-weighted imaging (TWI), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Multi cohort validation

Abstract 

Although genetic factors play a critical role in early-onset depression, their integration into neuroimaging-based analyses and understanding of neuropathophysiology remains limited,  efforts for early detection and intervention. Using a large multi-ethnic cohort (N = 5,248) and an independent Korean validation sample (N = 108), our PGS-pretrained 3D-CNN significantly improves cross-sectional (AUC = 0.62, F1 = 0.64) and longitudinal (AUC = 0.61–0.66) depression prediction, including suicidal behaviors. To enhance interpretability, we employ Explainable AI (Integrated Gradients + SmoothGrad), revealing that key white matter tracts—superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum, corticospinal tract, and corpus callosum—strongly contribute to depression risk. Compared to traditional models, our approach  predictive accuracy across diverse populations, with cross-ethnic generalization (AUC = 0.67, F1 = 0.61 in Korean youth). Furthermore, we demonstrate that PGS-based pretraining outperforms standard deep learning and machine learning models, underscoring the importance of integrating genetic and neuroimaging data for psychiatric risk prediction. These findings establish PGS-informed diffusion MRI modeling as a scalable and interpretable for early detection of youth depression, paving the way for precision psychiatry applications in diverse clinical settings.

Introduction 

Youth depression is an increasing global public health concern, with prevalence rates rising worldwide [1, 2] . Affecting approximately 2-7% of youth populations, depression often begins in childhood or adolescence [3].  Depression starting in this period poses significant long-term challenges, including higher chronicity, elevatedrecurrence rates, and reduced responsiveness to treatments such as antidepressants and psychotherapy compared to adult-onset cases [4-6]. Moreover, it has been linked to heightened risks of adult anxiety, impaired social functioning and suicidality [1, 7]. These findings underscore the urgent need for early identification and targeted strategies to predict and mitigate depression in at-risk youth [8]. 

The biological underpinnings of depression are complex, involving both genetic predisposition and neurobiological factors. Youth-onset depression exhibits stronger genetic associations [9] , including higher polygenic risk scores (PGS) and genetic risk associated with other psychiatric disorders, compared to adult-onset cases [10-12]. Twin studies have consistently demonstrated the high heritability of youth depression [13, 14] with genetic factors significantly impacting its persistence and stability [9, 15, 16]. These genetic vulnerabilities interact strongly with neurobiological substrates, particularly white matter, which provides the structural basis for long-range neural connectivity [17-19]. Fractional Anisotropy (FA), derived from diffusion MRI (dMRI), serves as a key marker of white matter integrity and demonstrates high heritability, with genetic factors explaining up to 88% of its phenotypic variance [17, 20, 21]. Specific tracts, such as the corpus callosum, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, are strongly influenced by genetic factors, supporting the notion that white matter differences are under strong genetic control [19, 21]. 

Converging evidence from human and animal studies implicates disruptions in specific white matter tracts in the pathophysiology of depression. Studies in humans with depression have reported reduced FA in tracts including the corpus callosum, cingulum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus [22-25], with some findings linked to genetic risk for the disorder [26-29]. Consistent with these findings, animal models of depression show reduced FA in the corpus callosum and related tracts [30, 31]. Developmental alterations in white matter, particularly in the corpus callosum, fimbria, external capsule, and internal capsule, have also been observed [32]. These findings collectively underscore the critical role of white matter impairments in the pathophysiology of depression.

The interplay between genetic predispositions and white matter integrity provides a critical framework for understanding the biological basis of depression. Genetic overlap between dMRI parameters and depression has been demonstrated, including negative correlations with FA in the corpus callosum and links to serotonin transporter gene DNA methylation [20, 33]. Additionally, forebrain white matter-related dMRI metrics have been associated with single nucleotide polymorphisms in genes encoding proteins involved in extracellular matrix and epidermal growth factor signaling, which are critical for myelin repair and synaptic plasticity and closely linked to major depressive disorder (MDD) [18]. These findings suggest shared genetic mechanisms influencing both white matter integrity and depression susceptibility. 

Despite these advancements, critical gaps remain in our understanding of childhood depression. Many studies rely on either genetic or neuroimaging data, overlooking the complex interactions between these modalities [28, 34-36]. Research in other psychiatric disordershas consistently shown that integrating genetic and neuroimaging data through multi-modal approaches significantly enhances predictive accuracy compared to single-modality models [37-39]. Deep learning methodologies offer a promising avenue for multi-modal integration [40],  but faces challenges, particularly in smaller datasets often used in developmental psychiatric research [41, 42]. Optimized strategies are therefore needed to apply deep learning effectively in such contexts. 

Additionally, most existing studies in both neuroimaging and genetics have been conducted on predominantly Caucasian populations, leaving other ethnic groups underrepresented [43, 44]. Addressing this disparity is critical to developing globally applicable predictive models for depression. 

Our study addresses these challenges by utilizing deep learning to integrate genetic and white matter data from a large cohort of American children. By combining gene-brain features using pretraining and a multi-modal joint fusion strategy, we overcome limitations associated with small sample sizes and uncover latent associations between structural disruptions in white matter and depression risk. Three key experiments were conducted: (1) cross-sectional classification to differentiate individuals with and without depression, (2) prediction of depressive symptoms two years later in held-out sets and (3) validation of our model’s generalizability using an independent Korean dataset of young adolescents. These findings provide new insights into the applicability of predictive models across diverse populations. 

Materials and methods

Participants

We used participants from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study [45] (N=11,868), and a Korean cohort (N=180) recruited through research collaboration with Seoul National University and Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology. Following rigorous quality control and exclusion criteria, the final analysis included 5,248 ABCD participants and 108 Korean participants. Full inclusion/exclusion criteria and preprocessing details are provided in Supplementary Materials.

Track-weighted FA (TW-FA) Imaging Processing 

Track-weighted FA (TW-FA) was used as the input in all experiments. dMRI provides measures of brain macrostructure (e.g. volume(mm3), length(mm), area(mm2)) and microstructure (e.g. white matter integrity), non-invasively [46]. The processing was conducted using software based on the MRtrix3 package [47] especially using the command tckmap after general MRI quality assessment. TW-FA maps were formed as described previous studies [48, 49], so we will describe them briefly here. In summary, reference map (here, FA maps) values were computed at each point along the streamline. For each voxel, a Gaussian-weighted mean of the reference map values was determined within the neighborhood along individual fiber streamlines (yielding the track-wise statistic). The voxel intensity for the TWI map was then calculated as the average of these track-wise values across all tracts passing through the voxel, resulting in the voxel-wise statistic. We utilized full-width-half-maximums (FHWM) of 15mm for gaussian neighborhood weightings, which is known to be more sensitive to focal abnormalities [50]. The TW-FA framework applies directional smoothing to tractograms by assigning each streamline a weight derived from the average FA value along its path, effectively creating a track-informed version of the FA map [50, 51]. Both cohorts followed the sample protocol to process TW-FA.

Demographic and Behavioral Variables 

Psychiatric Variables of ABCD Cohort

For assessing the children’s life-time MDD and depressive symptoms, our analysis employed Kiddie-Structured Assessment for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for DSM-5 (KSADS-5) and Child Behavioral Checklist (CBCL), child-reported and parent reported respectively and self-administered. Computerized KSADS have been well validated from previous study showing good to high reliability (AUC 0.89-1.0) comparing against clinician administered [52]. For current analyses, we generated composite variable for lifetime history of MDD meeting criteria in present, past or remitted MDD based on child or parent report. We excluded participants who were taking anti-depressant medication and who met lifetime psychotic or neurodevelopmental disorder (e.g. autism spectrum disorder) diagnosis [53, 54]. For the health control, we included participants who met none of the diagnosis criteria in child nor parent report past or current time point and met healthy control criteria of CBCL (<60) from the baseline to 2-year follow-up. We utilized lifetime indicators of suicidal behavior (including suicidal active ideation and suicide attempts) based on KSADS diagnoses, derived from child and parent reports. The criteria for health controls were consistent with those described earlier. 

We generated depressive symptoms score based on previous study [55] using summated score from module1 of the KSADS symptoms assessment score as depressive disorder. The score included both child and care-giver reports. This score incorporated reports from both children and caregivers and was subsequently used as the outcome variable for generating composite polygenic risk scores. Detailed methods for composite PGS calculations are described in the Methods section 2.4.

In conclusion, 4741 participants for pretraining set, 266 propensity score matched using age, sex, study site participants were used for MDD baseline prediction fine-tune set. To statistically evaluate the 2-year follow-up zero-shot prediction performance, we utilized 118 individuals with MDD symptoms at the 2-year follow-up and matched them with healthy controls randomly sampled from participants not included in either the pretrained or finetune sets. This matching process was repeated 10 times to ensure robustness through different samples, which leads to 10 datasets of 236 participants. For suicidal behavior we used same strategy, resulting in 10 datasets of 116 participants with MDD and Suicidal active ideation at the 2-year follow-up and 30 participants with MDD and Suicidal Attempt. However, we ensured that none of the participants overlapped with pretraining nor finetune sets.

Psychiatric Variables of Korean Cohort

	Validated Korean translations of depression measures were used to classify participants. Depression was assessed using the child-reported CES-D [56] and parent-reported CBCL [57]. Based on prior meta-analyses, a CES-D cut-off of ≥21, which accounts for gender and racial variations [58, 59], was chosen to align with ABCD study criteria. The depressed group included individuals with CES-D ≥21, while the healthy group had CES-D <16 and CBCL total problems T-scores <60. The final sample consisted of 108 participants (41 depressed, 67 healthy). For deep learning, data were split into 10-folds using iterative stratification by age, sex, and CES-D score, followed by propensity score matching for validation and test sets.

Genetic Data Preprocessing 

 In this study, we used polygenic risk scores (PGS), which were previously calculated and validated in [60], where a detailed description of the methodology is provided. Here, we briefly summarize the key aspects of the methodology. The PGS were calculated using PLINK version 1.9 and the parameters were optimized in PRS-CSx. According to previous study, multi-ethnic PGS showed improved accuracy in diseases risk prediction by combining transethnic information [61]. Since our study focused on childhood depression in the population of multi-ethnicity, we utilized PGS scores generated with multi-ethnic panel using publicly available Genome Wide Association Study statistics of multi-ethnicity population. PGS related to depression, BMI, post-traumatic stress disorder, Alcohol Dependency and Schizophrenia were included. 

	We included composite PGS in our analysis, guided by prior research. Previous studies have demonstrated the advantages of composite polygenic risk scores in enhancing risk stratification [62, 63]. Building on these findings, we adopted a composite PGS approach in our analysis. To address multicollinearity, we employed ElasticNet, a robust regularization technique. Composite scores were constructed from PRS derived using five multi-ethnicity panels, with a stepwise elimination process to optimize R² while minimizing the number of independent variables. This procedure was performed exclusively within the pretraining set, and model fitting was conducted across 5,000 resampled train-test splits to ensure robust and stable estimation. We ensured that none of the participants in pretraining sets overlapped with finetune or prediction sets.

 Model Optimization and Evaluation 

Deep Neural Network Training 

	We implemented a 3DCNN model with densenet3D121 as the backbone architecture across all our experiments. The model consists of an initial 3D convolutional module, four 3D dense-blocks, three 3D Transition layers and one fully connected classifier for each task. In the field of medical imaging, prior studies have demonstrated the superior performance of densenet3D121 model compared to traditional CNNs in tasks such as brain tumor classification [64], and Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis [65]. Also, we conducted experiments using a model where each participant's PGS score was directly incorporated. This was done by adding the PGS score before passing through the fully connected layer of the 3DCNN model, followed by processing through a multilayer perceptron layer (3DCNN+MLP). We optimized the model with Mean Squared Error loss for regression tasks and Cross Entropy for the classification tasks. Minimal augmentation was applied, including resizing images to 128x128x128, Random Rotation by 90 degrees (probability=0.5), Random Axis Flip (probability=0.5), and Random Affine Transform (probability=0.5). The deep neural networks were optimized using the AdamW optimizer with a cosine learning rate decay scheduler and a linear warm-up. Additionally, we implemented early stopping with a patience window of 30 epochs to prevent overfitting on the training data. 

We employed two types of comparison models to evaluate our approach. The first set of comparison models focused on modality: an MLP model using only PGS, a 3DCNN model using only TW-FA, and a from-scratch 3DCNN+MLP model trained directly on both PGS and TW-FA without any pretraining. The second set of comparison models included traditional machine learning models: support vector machine with a linear kernel (SVC_linear), support vector machine with an RBF kernel (SVC_rbf), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBOOST) using structural connectivity and PGS as their inputs. All experiments were conducted using 10-fold cross-validation, ensuring that the same training, validation, and test folds were used consistently across all experiments. Details on the training parameters for cross-sectional and 2-year follow-up MDD prediction, along with transfer learning, are available in the Supplementary Materials.

Explainable AI 

To identify brain regions contributing most to the model’s predictions, we employed explainable AI (XAI) techniques, specifically Integrated Gradients [66] combined with SmoothGrad [67]. Integrated Gradients generates saliency maps by integrating the gradients of the model's predictions with respect to the input features, providing a measure of each voxel’s contribution. SmoothGrad enhances this approach by adding Gaussian noise (σ = 0.05) to input images within brain regions, generating 50 noise-augmented images per participant and averaging their resulting saliency maps. This method was implemented using the Captum library (version 0.6.0).

To align our findings with prior research, we performed tract-level analyses and identified key tracts containing voxels that significantly contributed to depression classification and prediction. We analyzed only the voxels with statistically significant XAI attribute values between the control and depressed groups. We conducted voxel-wise t-tests with FDR multiple corrections and applied a cluster-based threshold to identify statistically significant regions. Then we calculated the proportion of significant voxels for each tract, by dividing the total number of significant voxels by the total voxels in the tract. This allowed us to determine the positive and negative associations of each tract in the depression classification task.

Results 

We analyzed data from 5,248 participants in the ABCD dataset, all meeting strict quality criteria for dMRI and genetic data availability. The dataset was divided into three groups: a Pretrain set (N=4,741), a Baseline Finetune set (N=266), and 2-Year Follow-up MDD Prediction sets (N=236), 2-Year Follow-up MDD & Suicidal Ideation Active sets (N=116) and 2-Year Follow-up MDD & Suicidal Attempt sets (N=30). To rigorously assess model performance, we generated 10 matched datasets for each 2-year outcome group, selecting diverse controls to evaluate statistical robustness. Demographics are detailed in Supplementary Materials (Table S1). To minimize selection bias, we used propensity score matching on age, biological sex, and ABCD site when creating finetune subsets. All the statistics of model comparisons are detailed in Supplementary Materials. 

PGS-Pretrained 3DCNN outperforms Comparison Models in Cross-Sectional and 2-Year Follow-Up MDD Prediction

The PGS-pretrained 3D-CNN using TW-FA consistently outperformed uni-modal and other multi-modal baselines for cross-sectional MDD classif
